To grasp the essence of dialogues, language models need to incorporate semantic connections among words and phrases. Current studies demonstrate that by identifying and incorporating such connections explicitly, the accuracy of dialogue understanding can be significantly improved. This work aims to examine the range of possible semantic connections that are essential for dialogue comprehension, thereby helping to refine the tasks and resources associated with them. In this research, we employed a large language model to analyze the semantic connections found in human dialogs. Based on its capabilities, the model outperformed existing models without utilizing external dialogue resources, ultimately leading to the development of a novel benchmark for natural dialogue comprehension.

The growing concern for the interpretability of algorithms stems from their profound impact on our lives, whether it's a job offer, a credit score, or a criminal verdict. The lack of interpretability in these algorithms raises critical issues, including a loss of trust, unfair outcomes, and legal accountability. In response, researchers have been developing methods to ensure the transparency and accountability of these algorithms. Our paper aims to shed light on the current state of algorithmic interpretability, highlighting its key challenges and breakthroughs, as well as its potential applications and the complexities surrounding its implementation. We delve into the different types of interpretability, including criteria for evaluating it, and discuss the various domains where this concept has been utilized. We also address the pressing issues inherent to this field and identify future research directions, ultimately aiming to contribute to the development of ethical and responsible AI systems.

The Isolation Forest algorithm, integrated into the Python scikit-learn library as iforest, boasts impressive anomaly detection capabilities. However, this strengths also impose limitations, as the iforest model tends to favor easier-to-isolate data points and undershoots the true anomaly scores for more complex observations. Building on this foundation, our proposal, the IForestAdaptor, leverages the strengths of the iforest algorithm by relying on it to generate a set of anomaly-prone identification parameters. Following the iforest model, our IForestAdaptor shifts and scales the iforest scores to better accommodate the needs of the given dataset. Our comprehensive testing across 28 distinct datasets reveals the IForestAdaptor's capacity to elevate the performance of the base iforest algorithm across a diverse range of datasets.

A Bayesian approach to estimating excess geometric mean variance, originally introduced by Zaffaroni (2016), is re-examined through a quantitative representation. Extreme events' variability can be better understood by first modeling their frequency and then using that model to estimate the severity of extreme events. By incorporating prior knowledge into a Bayesian framework, the estimation process can be improved. However, the proposed method relies on a tuning parameter'm', which poses a challenge as its optimal value cannot be determined objectively. Furthermore, the original implementation was limited to a specific frequency model. In this research, the estimation method is modified to accommodate any frequency model under a generalized maximum likelihood estimation criterion. A simulation study is conducted to assess the effectiveness of the proposed method. Moreover, the estimation method is applied to real-world data sets in order to examine its performance. Finally, some potential areas for further research regarding the estimation of excess geometric mean variance are outlined.

These notes document a course I taught in Spring 2019 at NYU. The course, titled "Stable Shapes," covered the fundamentals and concrete applications of theories regarding stationary shapes. The course focused on two key areas: determining the special properties of these shapes in higher-dimensional spaces and identifying their characteristic features in specific cases, particularly in two, three, and four dimensions. The course also delved into the mathematical advancements and contributions of my colleague Chris Gerig, as well as those of my students, including Noe Shoickin and Eli Rodden.

We introduce ATOMIC 2020, a significantly expanded version of the popular
commonsense reasoning dataset ATOMIC, which now boasts an order of magnitude more
data (550k examples) despite only triple annotations. Our study investigates how
various leading commonsense knowledge resources influence the performance of our
models when fine-tuned on each other. The findings suggest that ATOMIC 2020 outperforms
other leading datasets in terms of model performance. We also demonstrate that a
merged dataset of GPT3 and ATOMIC 2020 achieves state-of-the-art results on the
logical-formatted GPT3-ATOMIC dataset. The ATOMIC 2020 dataset and associated
resources are accessible at https://github.com/ajaykarmakar/ATICOM-2020.

The Hi-GAL survey employs a robust methodology for reducing and analysing Hi-Fi spectral data collected with the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) in the GASKA project. A recently developed data reduction pipeline utilises the following components: a proprietary tool for enhancing data quality, DC2, which performs calibration and integration, followed by a clean component, and a statistical analysis tool for extracting Hi-Fi spectra. A detailed assessment of the data reduction pipeline's performance is conducted by comparing Hi-Fi spectra obtained using three distinct methods for individual observations. Specifically, Hi-Fi spectra obtained using Hi-GAS, a compact millimetre waveguide system, Hi-Fi, a 1.5 mm dual-polarisation ALMA receiver, and JCMT, a 13 beam synthesiser with a 1.3 mm dual-polarisation receiver, are compared after correcting for system responses. A thorough examination of Hi-GAL's scientific science samples, including far-infrared light sources in the central molecular regions (CMRs) of 44 galaxies, is performed by plotting Hi-Fi spectra against their far-infrared fluxes, after correcting for Hi-Fi line responses. A similar assessment is also conducted for Hi-GAS observations using a 90 GHz pinhole camera by comparing Hi-Fi spectra against CO emission in the rotating gas discs surrounding these galaxies. The abundance ratios of key elements in 13 Galactic globular clusters have been derived from the analysis of 510 high-resolution spectra collected at three institutions. These new measurements complement existing data and help to establish variations in the abundance of specific elements, like titanium, in the clusters. The data also allow for a comprehensive comparison with the available data for the metal-poor stars in the Milky Way. The results of this analysis reveal significant differences between the galactic clusters and the halo stars for the abundance of titanium as well as Ga, Ge, and P but noticeable similarities for Na, Cr, and Zn. The diversity of abundance ratios among the galactic clusters in relation to their star formation processes and supernovae impostors is discussed in detail.

One-dimensional systems with localized dynamics, influenced by random perturbations, are examined to determine how periodic resetting affects their escape times from a given area of interest. The random perturbations can be seen as creating 'activation energy' that allows the system to potentially move more quickly when its potential energy is high. The potential is also used to determine which areas of the system are generally more or less likely based on their spatial location. The system's behavior is studied through different density of states and coefficient of red noise values, and the distribution of times it takes for the system to escape is analyzed. The means square displacement over time is found to be related to a speed/accuracy trade-off, where faster escape times result in a higher average error. The physical significance of this trade-off, and the related optimal escape speed, are discussed. The study also touches on the idea that one-system parameters may correspond to multiple behaviors in another system, and how these behaviors may be similar despite different underlying dynamics.

Theoretical considerations have raised underdetermination and Lorentzian problems within the framework of quantum mechanics - for instance, the Frauchiger-Renner and Hardy setups. These concerns persist despite earlier attempts to resolve them. This paper develops a novel analysis based on the application of quantum principles, namely Bayes' rule in its statistical context. We utilize the quantum version of Bayes' rule to address the underlying conflicts and demonstrate that it resolves two notorious paradoxes - those described in the references cited above. This solution suggests a fresh perspective for understanding quantum mechanics and its implications for philosophical hypotheses that may appear ambiguous at first glance.

Our investigation focuses on a specific aspect of quantum field theory called the XY-model. This theory, when constrained to a two-dimensional torus using periodic boundary conditions, is essentially the opposite of the Ising model with Dirichlet boundary conditions. Both the XY and Ising models, when subjected to a specific temperature threshold, demonstrate a behavior known as quantum oscillations. Building on a prior study, we employed a mathematical approach called Feynman graphs to analyze the effective action of the XY model. Unlike earlier work, our method incorporates multiple loop corrections and uses a specific renormalization technique. This more complex approach is shown to closely approximate the effective action of the Ising model, both at high temperatures and when exhibiting quantum oscillations, thereby providing insight into the transition from the XY-model to the Ising-model at low temperatures.

In the context of the Steenrod algebra over the prime 2, specifically focusing on the algebraic transfer components, it's established that there are non-zero elements captured by the fifth transfer, denoted t_5. These include 1, x^2e_1, sx^2e_1, x^2e_2, x^2e_3, x^2e_4, xe_1^2, xe_2^2, and e_1^2e_2, where x represents the generator of Z_2[P^*] and the e_i are the Adams operations over the prime 2. Additionally, t_5 essentially leaves unchanged the operations corresponding to primes 3 and above, thereby providing a description of t_5 within the context of the operations (ad^i(e_j))_{2<= j<= 22}.

The Sun's Lyman-alpha signal picked up by the Probe of Intergalactic Magnetism (PIMMS) is significantly weakened due to interaction with molecular hydrogen in its absorption cell when the temperature and pressure are set to 40 deg C and 2.5 millibars, resulting in only about 12 percent of the relevant hydrogen being ionized. Increasing the pressure to 10.7 millibars in order to raise the temperature to 300 deg C will improve the required hydrogen fraction to 99 percent, which is close to what radiative processes naturally achieve. However, a more feasible solution to block these Lyman-alpha photons is to replace the hydrogen gas with water vapor, which is highly efficient in ionizing nearly all of the hydrogen with an equivalent of 0.1 millibars. We have experimented with various options for filtering Lyman-alpha photons, utilizing the spectral information from PALESS and PISAS, two instruments built to measure the signal off-axis, which are perched on top of two telescopes: a sub-millimeter instrument called APEX and an radio instrument called Murchison Widefield Array (MWA). According to our simulation using PALESS's spectral information, the observed Lyman-alpha signal is nearly twice as strong when using water vapor instead of hydrogen gas in the absorption cell. Furthermore, our analysis using MWA's spectral information indicates that the observed signal may be a combination of both Galactic and cosmic components. We

The intricacy of distributed control systems with the necessity for efficient, fast processing at multiple levels poses significant challenges. Research in control engineering has addressed the issue using performance indicators, for instance, the rate of improvement in closed-loop behavior. Studies have demonstrated that a balance can be established between the cost of processing expenses and performance metrics to create effective distributed control systems. By optimizing the performance indicators, the interconnection topology is adapted to ensure the attainment of optimal performance at different levels of system operation. Our study expands the scope of this approach to a wide range of engineering systems, encompassing continuous-time systems in a linear state-space format. A decentralized optimization method is employed to determine processing rates at each level based on performance indicators. Notably, the system components can dynamically adjust their parameters such as scheduling or gain values without requiring global system knowledge, achieved through optimization and feedback mechanisms. The efficacy of this method has been verified through simulation studies in the fields of flight control systems and vision-based path following.

In image indexing, a predefined template is matched with images to locate identical or highly similar content. Active indexing enhances robustness by dynamically choosing the most relevant template elements for each image, utilizing clustering and a ranking system. By identifying which template elements are unique to each cluster, active indexing reduces false positives and improves performance in image copy detection, especially in scenarios with dimensional disparity where images of varying sizes need to be compared. Experimental analysis reveals that active indexing surpasses passive methods, involving both visual and statistical assessments, in both scenario types.

In a general quantum channel, a flexible modification of standard encoding techniques is offered, resulting in encoded states whose transmission is virtually entirely masked from eavesdroppers. This encoding approach asymptotically yields a negligible coding rate as the number of transmitted qubits increases. By combining these encoded states in specific, authentic configurations, novel authentication codes with rate close to 100% are constructed, also asymptotically hiding their authentic nature. Furthermore, external authentication systems can significantly enhance the security of standard quantum key distribution protocols by protecting their exchange encoding process from interception. This improvement in security comes at the cost of a minor decrease in transmission rate, but this decrease diminishes rapidly as the number of transmitted qubits increases.

The superdiffusion exponent has been found to be $1.5$ for Brownian particles in a one-dimensional periodic potential, as well as for particles interacting via an aligned potential and subjected to a common, periodic external force. For the latter scenario, the exponent was determined for cases with both weak and strong external forces.

This research presents a groundbreaking model that allows for the seamless integration of loan repayment and credit extensions. The framework effectively promotes financial inclusion, but also highlights the significant economic repercussions that can arise from disruptions to credit lines. Investigating the impacts of such disruptions, our analysis shows that the magnitude and direction of the effects hinge on the size of the credit shock and incorporate elements of contractionary and expansionary forces. Conversely, shocks to credit extensions solely exhibit contractionary properties, whereas lending disruptions solely exhibit expansionary properties. Notably, the interplay between these different types of credit shocks serves to balance their individual effects, thus mitigating the overall economic impact. Using data from Turkey's winning bid program for invasions of Kyrgyzstan's Batken region, our statistical analysis demonstrates the ability of the model to forecast the likelihood and magnitude of credit extensions. Furthermore, our results indicate that the interactions between credit lines have substantial signifying influences.

Using the Dirac equation in the Landau levels context, we investigate the quantum Hall effect's threshold effects, particularly the recoil caused by photons in the vacuum that translates to kinetic angular momentum. This recoil's growth is linked to the increase of the latter. At the thresholds of quantum Hall plateaus, the electromagnetic response function becomes reliant on Landau states with higher angular momentum, resulting in a momentum transfer to the electromagnetic field that scales with $\sqrt{n_e}$, where $n_e$ represents the electron density's Landau level index. This recoil's growth is further accompanied by a nonlinear increase in the kinetic angular momentum, mathematically represented as $\frac{\hbar}{\hbar e c} \sqrt{n_e n_B}$. Moreover, at the thresholds of quantum Hall plateaus, we discover an inequality-based lower bound on the electron's SUSY $\Delta \mathcal{Q}$, linking it to the recoil that causes its growth as well as the increase of the kinetic angular momentum, both of which are influenced by the magnetic field's magnetic flux. This SUSY $\Delta \mathcal{Q}$'s growth leads to a nonlinear relation analogous to the relation found in supersymmetric quantum mechanics. Additionally, we suggest a generalization of SUSY Algorithm in quantum Hall systems by its representation through a Pauli matrix operator, resulting in a lower bound estimation of the SUSY $\Delta \mathcal{Q}$'s value.

Recent advancements in NLP have made significant improvements in understanding entity types using contextual encoding methods, yet these methods often lack differentiation in encoding mentions as the same token can represent different entity types. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel framework, FGNET-RH, that refines the contextual encoding of mentions by utilizing type-aware embedding and heterogeneous interaction. Specifically, the framework consists of three key components: a first component that integrates type information with the forward text-based encoding pathway, a second component that integrates type information with the reverse text-based encoding pathway, and a third high-dimensional interaction component that combines the two pathways. Experimental results on three datasets (TAC2016, TAC2009, and GDRCD) show that the proposed FGNET-RH framework achieves a substantial performance boost over the baseline NER with an average F1-score improvement of 2.30%, 3.22%, and 3.45% respectively.

This paper investigates connections among certain classes of analytic functions and provides several results, including maintaining or establishing functional inequalities, along with evaluating quantities such as extremal values and moments for these functions.

The cloud computing model has become essential for modern society. VM scheduling is a critical issue that needs to balance resource allocation and reduce energy consumption while meeting users' diverse requirements for computing resources. The Prepartition method was recently proposed to tackle this challenge, incorporating the concept of preallocating virtual resources according to users' needs before scheduling VMs. The preallocated resources are then utilized in the scheduling process, minimizing the need to reallocate and thereby saving energy. Our Energy-Efficient VM Scheduling (EEVS) method leverages the preallocation technique, enabling multiple reallocated virtual resources to be managed as a large virtual machine during placement. Subsequently, the reduced energy consumption results in lower operational expenses for cloud service providers. Our simulation experiments showed that EEVS is more energy-efficient and effective than traditional methods.

Resolving game equilibria is a crucial problem that arises across numerous applications, including recommender systems, interaction scenarios, and policy analysis for the study of evolutionary social dynamics. Nevertheless, the current artificial intelligence techniques are inadequate to directly address this challenge due to the requirement for extensive computational resources to process vast numbers of strategies. In our study, we present an innovative class of artificial intelligence networks called Nash Fixed Point Networks (N-FPNs), which can effectively predict game equilibria by generating a strategic profile that benefits all agents. These networks consist of a multi-head attention mechanism that enables efficient computation in a strategy space. During training, a direct objective is employed to derive a fixed point of the strategic profile using a non-invertible dynamics operator. Notably, N-FPNs have shown significant improvements over existing models in computational efficiency and practical performance. Moreover, they offer intuitive insights into their working mechanism through the visualization of learned attention and representation. Building upon this foundation, we develop a variant of N-FPNs called N-FPN-IR, which incorporates an inverse dynamics module in conjunction with a direct dynamics module for the prediction of game equilibria. These networks demonstrate the ability to explain the dynamics of strategic interaction through the integration of an inverse and direct mapping between strategies and outcomes. Additionally, they recover a variational free-energy function and their computational processes can be reimagined as an iterative approach to solving games. This study delves into the relationship between statistical causality and dimensionality reduction, highlighting an unexpected connection between the two fields. In various applications where complex data sets are analyzed, reducing dimensions often poses a significant challenge. We demonstrate that utilizing dimension reduction techniques serves the purpose of trading off bias against estimation power. A multi-stage framework is presented, starting from a straightforward approach involving adjusting one variable while fixing others, and progressing to more complex methods involving multi-variable adjustments, genetic cross-validation, and assessments of causal interactions through correlation patterns. Through a mix of theoretical analysis and simulations, we investigate the performance of this technique in a diverse range of scenarios, including the investigation of genetic variants associated with a particular disease and the analysis of a medical dataset related to kidney health, which involves multiple variables such as diabetes, blood pressure, and kidney function. In addition, we provide a non-parametric test for causal connections in high-dimensional data and showcase its utility in detecting aberrant samples in high-dimensional studies.

The increased complexity of system integration with IoT, network devices, and other external components has created a heightened risk of cyber threats, including undetected attacks on control systems.  These malicious incidents can lead to severe consequences such as physical harm, data breaches, financial losses, and loss of public confidence. A new approach to monitoring control systems in real-time has been developed to mitigate the risk of potential cyber vulnerabilities. This approach uses an online model-free safety feature monitor to identify anomalies in system behavior. It creates a security metric dataset through continuous system measurements and categorizes system states as safe or hazardous by comparing actual system behavior to predicted behavior. This method can detect stealthy attacks by highlighting discrepancies between expected and actual system behavior. It has a lower computational cost compared to other methods, making it suitable for industrial use due to its speed and reliability. This control system monitoring method can also enhance security analysis by providing essential data for risk assessment.

Automatic document summarization is the process of extracting significant points from extensive written materials. Numerous studies have approached this task by dividing it into sub-components: a converter turning documents into machine-readable formats, a model summarizing those texts and a mechanism to assess the quality of the summaries. Prior research implemented these components separately, though they claimed to address the entire summarization task. We present a unified model, GAE-ISumm, that allows for direct summarization, eliminating the need for a separate converter. It also outperforms the best previous summarization models, as well as matching its quality when using a separate converter. Our model generates abstracts by iteratively refining a representation of the main ideas, achieved through a refined attention mechanism that considers the meaning behind words. We demonstrate improved quality and efficiency compared to the best previous summarization models, and others that were tested, on two standard summarization datasets.

Let $A$ and $B$ be rings with ideals $I$ and $J$, where $B$ is a Quillen-exact reflection of $A$ in the category of rings. We investigate how the properties of the quotient category $\text{Mod}(A)/I$ relate to independent $S$-rings of type $A$, where $S$ is a set of isomorphism classes of modules. Specifically, we consider the injective dimension and the strong flat dimension of $\text{Mod}(A)/I$ when $B$ is an independent $S$-ring of type $A$. We also discuss how these dimensions can be determined by analyzing the properties of $B$ and its action on $I$. This work is significant as it provides a more in-depth understanding of the structure of the quotient category and its modules, which may have applications in further studying the properties of type $A$-independent rings.

The quest for directly imaging planets around other stars has pitted scientists against a challenging background for over a decade.  As a result, an international team has been developing a next-generation imager for the Very Large Telescope, aiming to enhance our understanding of planetary systems and the formation of the universe.  With its scheduled release in the near future, MICADO will allow scientists to study the life cycles of planetary systems, from the point when they form to tens of millions of years later.  We present data collected during an instrumental campaign in 2021 alongside a study of the instrument's capabilities in seeing planets, and discuss the potential for future instruments like MICADO to revolutionize our knowledge of the universe.

In order to balance representation learning and efficient data compression using Variational Autoencoders, we must determine a suitable trade-off between explanation variance and optimal encoding using the nearest neighbor distribution. This challenge can be addressed by establishing a systematic approach to balance these competing objectives, which involves analyzing the underlying trade-off in the Stochastic Variational Vector Quantization training process. This investigation derives theoretical formulations of the approximation loss and reconstruction loss, which provide a clearer understanding of the training objective in SV2X. Specifically, it has been discovered that the approximation loss is dependent on the clustering efficiency, which in turn determines the approximation bias, the efficient encoding depends on the diversity loss, and the optimal balance between these loss terms is achieved along the lines of the Elbow phenomenon in k-means clustering. This analysis lays the groundwork for investigating the robustness of VAEs in their most basic form, which is an intriguing area of study due to the surrounding mysteries and controversies in the field.

In a typical smart home setting, accurately determining the movement of people can be achieved by combining various sensor technologies like RGB-DSL light, audio, micro-electromechanical, and radio wave. We focus on radio wave-based localization in this research. By using multiple access points and RSSI-based trilateration, it is possible to pinpoint a device's position with decent accuracy. We enhance existing localization techniques by incorporating human behavior modeling, incorporating a pedestrian model and a particle filter, which allows us to plot people's movements with decent accuracy. We evaluate our method's effectiveness using real-world data collected in an apartment and compare it to other approaches, such as k-fans, convex spline-based trilateration. The results show that our technique outperforms these alternatives, showcasing its effectiveness without additional equipment, scalable range, and robust modeling of complex phenomena like room shapes and pedestrian behavior.

This research addresses the issue of compressing neural network weights through quantization. The goal is to reduce memory usage and accelerate inference times by representing floating-point values as shorter integer quantities. The paper introduces a new approach to this challenge called SMI, which utilizes statistical properties of weights to create two quantization schemes, one guided by mean and variance, and the other based on the maximum mutual information. The proposed method is shown to outperform other top approaches while providing transparent and adjustable error rates that are closely aligned with the underlying distribution. The open-source code for this research is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Sahab-Research/SMI.git.

We develop a wide range of fixed-parameter tractable algorithms for certain graph problems that rely on a key variable, often accompanied by other conditions. Our methods make use of the graph's treewidth, a well-established concept, as well as an alternative measure called branch-width. In cases where the treewidth or branch-width is difficult to determine, we employ an alternative approach based on a parameter that characterizes the size of the input graph in relation to a specific property. Specifically, this alternative parameterized problem is defined by a predetermined bound on the number of vertices within a specific graph structure, called the treed width parameter. Our algorithms for distinct problems, such as Long Path Width Parameterized by Treed Width, Weighted Long Path and Colored Motif Counting, make strategic use of algorithmic techniques including treewidth-based algorithms, an expanded version of the Weierstrass tree algorithm, the DP algorithm, entropy, treewidth-dependent entropy, and a variant of the Babai's combinatorial decision network (BDN) algorithm, as well as novel applications of Moore-Penrose inverse matrices in linear systems to accommodate unknown error terms.

A combination of deep learning models can accurately predict the correct category even when the training data is inaccurately labeled, as the uncertainty about these inaccurate labels tends to average out. However, as the amount of training data increases, the gain from using ensemble modeling decreases. In this study, a novel approach called Stoichastictuning is proposed to increase the variability in the models, making them better fitted for ensemble modeling. Additionally, this method has the advantage of allowing the selection of the most accurate model based on the COV or COF metrics. Experimental results show that by increasing the diversity of the models, the differences in accuracy between the baseline and modified models decrease, whereas the modification shows significant improvements over the baseline in specific scenarios.

This paper aims to elevate current understanding of transfer operators in the study of dynamically related, expanding systems, specifically those with expanding semiflows. Research has shown that in uniformly expanding systems, certain families of transfer operators can consistently approximate the transfer operator associated with the semiflow within a predetermined margin. Moreover, in non-uniformly expanding systems, this research adapts and strengthens recent results regarding the transfer operators' behavior, particularly their rapid correlation decline. Additionally, this study confirms the existence of approximating families of transfer operators for semifows of anomalous exponential nature, and provides novel insights into transfer operators' behavior in the case of uniform expansion. The rate of correlation decline for hyperbolic, expansive, and transitive systems is shown to precisely match the rate at which singular values grow. Research has also obtained explicit, quantifiable conditions for determining transfer operators, leveraging observables bounded by L^p norms and demonstrating their consistency when the underlying space has finite measure. Research further extends these results to the case of random transformations, particularly non-uniformly expanding ones. The study of transfer operators has been pivotal in statistically analyzing expansive semiflows, offering significant insights into their ergodic properties and approximation. Research has shown that approximating families of transfer operators can quantify the semifow's ergodicity, entropy, and mixing rates, as well as its Gibbs-Markov property. A uniform covering array, also known as a coverable array, is a specific type of combinatorial design. It consists of a matrix with k columns where each subset of k elements of size β forms a cover. In other words, every possible combination of k elements of a given alphabet of size α can be found in the matrix, repeated repe repeatedly, up to a certain threshold determined by the general covering array (GCA) which relaxes this condition to allow for repetitions up to a certain number. Research on uniform covering arrays has recently been extended to include generalized uniform covering arrays, which incorporates a parameter δ to determine how repetitions are allowed in the matrix. In this research, a new combinatorial design called a semi-uniform covering array is introduced as a potential alternative to uniform and generalized uniform covering arrays. This research aims to develop tighter general lower bounds for semi-uniform covering arrays and its generalized variant, also introducing a novel probabilistic algorithm to generate semi-uniform covering arrays and determine the optimal trade-off between matrix size and required repetitions. In this research, a trade-off curve is established to assess various combinatorial designs.

We examine a two-player game where the first player receives an n-copy of a bipartite state and attempts to maximize their advantage, which is defined as the difference in squared norms of the states of the two players after a set of random unitary operations. We find that in the large n limit, this game's leading approximation by a convex optimization problem yields an optimal strategy which involves the first player performing a series of optimal cloners corresponding to each term in a approximating hierarchy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the use of higher order approximations in this HHL algorithm leads to a superpolynomially faster convergence rate. We also apply this finding to several linear systems, showcasing a significant enhancement of the solution rate for any given computational resources. Lastly, we address a convex optimization interpretation of the approximate cloners by deriving an optimization goal that reaches its optimal limit when the sequence of optimal cloners converges to the exact solution of the original problem.

Artificially induced program crashes called "EvoCrash" have shown strong genetic linkages. However, our research suggests that the traditional testing method used to establish these linkages may be flawed. By re-examining the original study, we discovered an issue with the evaluation process that likely failed to detect the desired genetic linkages in some cases. A revised testing approach is proposed to address these linkages and confirm the genetic connection between mutations causing program crashes.

In this study, the phase diagram for Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CuO$_y$ near the superconducting transition temperature is mapped out using scanning probe microscopy by manipulating the tunneling current. By monitoring shape deformations as a single atomic plane is moved under variable pressures, the study quantifies changes in the lattice and vortex lattices. It is observed that the lattice transitions at pressures that align with van Hove singularities in theoretical models for vortex lattices, coupling to Cu-O plane oscillations. Moreover, these findings match up with predictions in a $d$-wave superconductor model, suggesting an interaction between the vortex lattice and Cu-O plane oscillations that leads to lattice instability at pressure intervals rather than singular points.

The impact of collective flow effects on the comparison between hydrodynamics simulations and experimental data from the Large Hadron Collider is analyzed for flow coefficients v_2 and v_3. Studies have found v_2 to be in good agreement with simulations in most cases, but research indicates v_3 is less reliable due to complications in reproducing its value within hydrodynamic models. Findings also suggest that ratios v_2/v_3 may offer valuable insight into quark-gluon plasma characteristics at lower collision energies.

Using exact diagonalization and self-consistent random field theories, we analyze the spin structure factors and associated energy patterns for various reference states in triangular and kagome lattice models. We find that in the triangular lattice the energy and spin structure factors only exhibit minor discrepancies, whereas for kagome lattices, these differences become more pronounced, with implications for Monte Carlo simulations.

This research addresses the challenge of identifying a combined average treatment effect (ATE) and new treatment effects (NTEs) in a single sample using multiple Bayesian statistical techniques. These methodologies not only maintain the accuracy of FDR at a desired level but also boost the power for detecting the ATE while discovering novel treatment effects. Under specific conditions, the expected proportions of correctly assigning the control versus treatment to NTEs are established. Developed upon the Cramer and Wang conditions, the new methods involve weighted optimization procedures. A simulation study showcases the improved power for detecting both ATE and NTE by utilizing these novel methodologies. To validate the effectiveness of these methods, an actual study examining the COVID-19 vaccine's (Moderna's vaccine) efficacy across different gender groups also employs the proposed techniques.

The association between primordial inflationary perturbations and CMB temperature fluctuations is well established.  Similarly, there is a established connection between the polarization of the CMB and the propagation of gauge bosons in an external field.  Consider a scalar field $\phi$ on four-dimensional Minkowski space where two-dimensional operators $O_i$ act on two-dimensional gauge fields $A_{\mu}$, for example, the operator $O_1=F^{\mu
u}F_{\mu
u}$ where $F_{\mu
u}$ is the gauge field.  If the scalar field is slow-rolling at a rate $d^2\phi/dt^2\ll O_i$, then the time derivative of $\phi$ can drive an operator $O_i$ with a proportionality constant dependent on the gauge field's rank.  This process may be represented as an effective time-dependent potential for the scalar field and is associated with an inflationary deformation of the operators $O_i$, leading to a potential cosmological implication.

A recent analysis of the two Higgs doublet model with precise Z and W boson mass measurements, along with the anomalous muon magnetic moment, suggests the model can accommodate both measurements. A new study focuses on the model's ability to explain a specific observation, the relation between the electron and muon magnetic moments. We find in the type-X model that the small Yukawa coupling of the electron can result in a consistent explanation, unlike the type-II model. This finding makes the type-X model a strong candidate to explain the phenomenon, particularly when considering the precision achieved with the electron magnetic moment measurement. Furthermore, the allowed parameter space aligns with the model's prediction of a longer lifetime for the tau lepton when compared to the standard model, with a specific range of $\mathcal{O}(10^3)$ seconds observed. This particular region of the type-X model is notably diverse and can be explored through various production methods at the LHC, such as associated production with a b-quark, where the upcoming HL-LHC will be capable of probing a significant portion of the allowed parameter space.

Identifying the general location of a software concept within its associated project is essential for developers to provide contextual help to team members working on the project. Multiple development tools can now automatically detect concept usage, but statistically analyzing concept occurrence typically necessitates costly, large-scale exploratory searches. To address this challenge, we propose introducing external crowd-sourced knowledge to guide the search, thereby enabling the use of first-cost methods that yield more reliable results. To evaluate this approach, we created the Crowdsourced Concept Search benchmark, comprising 30 software projects with varying levels of crowdsourced knowledge. Our experimental results demonstrate that using crowd-sourced knowledge significantly enhances the search's efficiency and quality, thereby substantiating its utility in practical scenarios. Finally, we discovered that leveraging crowd-sourced knowledge can significantly automate the process of determining relevant search areas, often down to just a few key methods, especially in cases of sparse occurrence.

Conversational AI models are now producing increasingly sophisticated dialogues 
that can often go undetected by humans. However, their goal is still to engage 
recipients, not merely to mimic human speech patterns. A significant obstacle 
for researchers is developing metrics to assess the emotional impact or 
engagement value of these artificial conversations. This study focuses on 
measuring the emotional impact of conversations using the Self-Assessed Emotion 
(SAE) model, which relies on self-reported emotion data. Experiments involving 
two types of models demonstrated that Self-Assessed Emotion scores correlated 
closely with other measures such as Neural Entrainment Distance and human judgment 
in several cases. Notably, the correlation was strongest in cases where the 
emotion expressed was subjectively intense. These findings suggest that the SAE 
model may serve as a reliable substitute for more labor-intensive methods and 
human evaluations. While further research is needed to refine this approach, 
evaluating conversations based on emotions may be an effective way to judge their 
engagement value.

This article presents an openly available, automated analysis tool, developed from a combination of Python, Cyan, and Mira, which is designed to conduct a range of analytical tasks including obtaining raw galaxy spectra, calculating basic physical characteristics, and extracting specific lines of interest via automated and customizable procedures. Additionally, the tool enables the creation of BPT diagrams and calculated metal ionization states. Furthermore, a detailed description of the tool's underlying procedures and limitations are provided, accompanied by a detailed step-by-step guide for users, in addition to a network diagram illustrating the flow of data through the analysis pipeline. The tool's source code has been made publicly accessible on the Repsifile repository.

Most current action segmentation methods rely on individual frame analysis, treating the prediction process as an independent task at each frame. Although effective, this approach lacks a connection to the subsequent frame's prediction, resulting in a decrease in overall performance. To address this limitation, this study presents a novel algorithm, Co-occurrence Action Parsing (CAP), which leverages the relationships between adjacent frames to generate action annotations. By employing the Co-occurrence Network, our algorithm predicts a distribution of action occurrences along with the start and end frames of each action. This study outlines CAP's effectiveness and demonstrates its superior performance on the Human3.6M and COIN databases, achieving improved results compared to existing action segmentation methods.

Analysis of $\Lambda_b^0$ decays is used to measure the relative rates of particle creation in the final states $\Lambda_b^0 \to p K^-$ along with various $h^0$ particles such as $\pi^0$, $\eta$, $\eta'$, and $h$ ($h$ particles undergo further decay into two gamma rays or a pair of mesons). These particle creation rates are calculated using a relative method, normalizing the signal strength to a reference decay pathway, thereby eliminating background influences from $J/\psi$ decays and secondary particles. The average ratio of branching fractions in the $h^0$ particles is measured as $r = 0.206 \pm 0.014 \pm 0.009 \pm 0.009$, displaying uncertainty from experimental methods, photon reconstruction efficiency, and particle identification processes respectively. Further, this measurement contradicts a previously reported prediction made by Naik et al.

When teaching introductory programming, software professors often struggle to determine if students receive the necessary assistance from study groups. Our study aimed to evaluate how faculty and students utilize an online collaborative tool for statistics and coding lessons. We enabled 3$^{rd}$-party services to analyze students' assignment completion and code coverage under educational license terms. We collected the resulting metrics along with the submitted code and concealed program test inputs, and employed reinforcement learning to create feedback agents for 10 groups of students. These agents provided optional static analysis tools along with actual test inputs to enhance problem-solving efficiency. We discovered that giving students more general feedback like exercise suggestions yielded better results over providing specific bug fixes. Interestingly, students receiving suggestions wrote code that covered 16\% more test cases and achieved 7\% better grades, compared to those receiving direct bug fixes. However, we also found that many students chose not to utilize the offered services, and those who did were not necessarily from the assigned groups. They were more likely to be more extroverted, both in their learning style and social interactions.

Most domain adaptation strategies rely on source data, but this is not always available. We propose a new approach that adapts to a target domain without access to source data. Our algorithm identifies domain-aggressive pseudo-labels by analyzing the source domain's database and using them to perform adaptation. However, without source data, it's difficult to determine high-quality pseudo-labels. We resolve this issue by developing a supervised adaptation model that consistently produces reliable pseudo-labels for use in an iterative process of label-based adaptation. Our approach is simple, effective, and outperforms other state-of-the-art adaptation methods, and verifies the quality of pseudo-labels using both objective and visual metrics.

Research on gas core reactors (GCRs) suggests they have the potential to be extremely efficient.  However, very little is known about how they work due to the intense nuclear interactions involved.  Studies using a combined nuclear-thermal code called MSTAR, developed by the Los Alamos Special Research Team, have been conducting experiments on GCRs to gain insight.  These experiments, which involved modeling the interior of a large steel container called the Hot Cell, helped understand the impact of neutron flux, critical masses, and cooling systems.  More specifically, investigations into how pressure affects the reactors' operation and efficiency and the ways in which cooling systems, such as trapped vapor, influence efficiency have been conducted.  We are planning to extend our findings to real-world applications like mobile generators, design ideal containment systems, and explore the potential for a compact, portable reactor that can treat pharmaceuticals or water using the knowledge gained.

We propose a novel neural network architecture that leverages prior understanding of detector parameters to effectively tackle challenges in experimental particle physics, specifically in simulating particle detection. Building upon the proxy-teacher architecture concept, our framework integrates a specialized module that models a physical quantity related to the detector, enabling the network to learn from this 'proxy' along with its teacher. As both the proxy and teacher share consistent and consistent-to-noise examples, our approach capitalizes on the strengths of both, ultimately producing a robust learner. Furthermore, the proxy acts as a bridge, bridging the gap between the proxy and teacher, it facilitates the transfer of knowledge from the proxy to the teacher during the exploration phase. Moreover, the proxy assists the learner in distinguishing between clean and noisy data points by providing class labels. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in two proxy-teacher configurations, successfully handling the complex problem of particle collision data where particle tracks in the plane are represented by a set of measured coordinates. Our experimental findings indicate that the proposed architecture achieves improved performance compared to a standard neural network, reaching peak performance with as few as 100 teacher data samples, without requiring any optimization. As an added benefit, the proposed architecture ensures the robustness of its predictions against varying detector parameters, utilizing its proxy to relearn when detector parameters change. Given its adaptability and out-of-distribution generalization capabilities, our approach has the potential to streamline analyses at future particle colliders, particularly those featuring diverse detector designs, randomized, or

Atmospheric models for certain celestial bodies and their surrounding environments are frequently disrupted by disagreements over key data sources. To compare different atmospheric models, a study focused on two specific sets of data for titanium oxide line lists, originally created by W. Zhu et al. (2013) and M. Simonsen et al. (2015), by running simulations of an idealized atmosphere twice, once for a type of giant planet called Hot Jupiter and another for a type of small red dwarf star called M-dwarf. Models based on the first data set indicated lower abundances of titanium oxide than those of the second data set. Despite this difference in data, a study using the Hot Jupiter model in transit configuration found that both models using the two different data sets produced similar absorption patterns of the titanium oxide gas in transit. Another simulation of the M-dwarf model using a detached atmosphere discovered that both models using the two different data sets produced similar thermal emission outputs from the atmosphere. However, a study using yet another M-dwarf model with an expanding atmosphere discovered that using the two different data sets produced different results for titanium oxide absorption, which was absent in the model's emission spectrum but found in the model's detached atmosphere. Nevertheless, a study using yet another M-dwarf model with an expanding atmosphere discovered that using the two different data sets produced different results for titanium oxide absorption, which was absent in the model's emission spectrum but found in the model's detached atmosphere. As logic programming evolves, specific areas like economics, social networks, and natural language processing increasingly rely on Answer Set Programming for operations on structured data, particularly in the context of semantics-based declarative aggregates. The traditional aggregate interpretation revision method, AER, is built upon a ground aggregate implication base, but it falls short when dealing with recursive aggregates. In response, we propose a new revision method, called LexAP, designed to accommodate both recursive and non-recursive aggregates through a process of word-based modifications to the program's labels. The study demonstrates the correctness and soundness of LexAP by showing it mirrors AER's properties and properties related to its soundness. Moreover, we prove that LexAP yields semantically equivalent transformations to AER. To further validate LexAP, we compare its application with AER on real-world financial models for valuation.

A comprehensive framework called multi-resource theory unifies diverse physical phenomena across different systems. It establishes a set of inherent axioms that provide a fundamental understanding of these phenomena. In thermodynamics, for example, these axioms reveal how resources change during system transformations, leading to a unified first law that surpasses separate formulations for separate resources. With the introduction of a generalized entropy function, this approach identifies a specific entropy function for each resource and derives a generalized entropy function for any number of resources. Additionally, this theory identifies conditions under which local equilibrium holds and predicts the order in which multiple resources change during system transformations. Furthermore, multi-resource theory identifies several well-known inequalities, including the total variance and a generalized Gibbs form. In order to demonstrate its versatility, this framework is applied to a variety of physical systems, including thermodynamic systems, optomechanics, and quantum systems in thermal states.

Estimating important information metrics such as mutual information and information density is particularly challenging due to their undefined values for independent random variables. By utilizing the moments of random variables, a recent study developed estimators for these information measures, even when the variables are uncorrelated. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of these moments-based estimators, offering new insights into their performance. It is demonstrated that one of the estimators can exhibit either significant biases or substantial variances, depending on the specific data set considered. Consequently, a series of modified estimators were created by combining the existing approaches in an attempt to reduce their limitations. Simulated and actual data sets are employed to assess the performance of these new estimators in comparison to the original ones. Ultimately, recommendations are provided on when and why to employ the existing approach over the enhanced method.

This study presents two new estimators for the number of common stochastic trends found in a multivariate time series data set. Our estimators are formulated as the ratio of the variance of a specific multivariate time series measure, to the variance of that measure's component corresponding to a singular singular spectrum decomposition. Our newer second estimator is particularly robust to anomalies in the data such as outliers. As sample size continues to grow, both estimators converge towards the true number of common stochastic trends as sample size increases without bounds, even in the presence of heavy-tailed distributions. Our research also establishes the statistical properties and distributional behaviors of these two estimators. Our results are confirmed through use cases and real-world data applications.

Building upon a general framework for RAC-codes established in earlier research, we explore quantum code constructions based on left-right Cayley complexes. Since these complexes possess an intrinsic symmetry, we develop a framework for RAC-codes featuring symmetrical defining sets, yielding codes with equivalent distance. Utilizing this structure, we identify novel RAC-code examples of various diverse types. Moreover, by employing the color-Cayley graph framework, we create RAC-code alternatives from various graph-based codes, incorporating illustrative examples derived from the twisted twisted-cyclic group graphs.

The distance-$r$ dominating set problem, a fundamental issue in the field of distributed computation, has drawn recent attention within the context of sublinear time randomized algorithms. For $r$-dominating sets of size $k$, this paper develops efficient distributed solutions for general graphs and specific sparse graphs characterized by their degree or separation properties. Specifically, for general graphs with $n$ vertices, our solutions achieve a time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(n^{\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}} \log^k \varepsilon^{-1})$ and $\mathcal{O}(\mbox{polylog} n)$ for sparse graphs defined by their degree $d \geq 2\log^2 n$ and separation $\Pi = (d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_n)$ with values $d_i \leq \log^2 n$ for $i \in [n]$.

To study the interaction of disorder with gap topology, we center on a previously proposed synthetic construct based on a 1D subgap state in a 2D topological insulator. Contrary to the robustness of gap formation in large-scale 2D insulators, the presence of disorder significantly compromises the mobility gap in a higher-order TI as it bridges the connection between bulk and edge. Our results for a 2D TI constructed from a quantum spin Hall system demonstrate that disorder readily closes the mobility gap while slightly perturbing edge states, although the perturbation to the bulk is minimal. The observable consequences of the disorder-induced closure of the mobility gap relate to mesoscopic edge transport phenomena. Using a related construct in a 3D TI, we find that disorder closing the bulk-mobility gap results in the hybridization of bulk and edge topological invariance, ultimately leading to the transfer of topological edge modes to the bulk.

Using proton-proton collisions recorded at 13 TeV by the CMS experiment in 2016, a search for a compressed supersymmetric spectrum of a chargino in final states with significant jet activity and multiple hadronically recoiling particles is presented. The study aims to identify or constrain the existence of charginos with extended lifetimes. It focuses on two-scenario scenarios: early-chargino decaying into a photon, Z boson, or possibly a Higgs boson, accompanied by a neutralino, which then decays into two muons, or into two or more hadronic particles. These muon or hadronic particles include those from b-quark decay. These scenarios have not been previously searched for in such a manner. A total of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected during the 2016 LHC data run showed no significant anomalies. Various alternative hypotheses were also investigated. A modification of the simplified model spectrum was used with mass differences between the chargino and lightest neutralino less than 0.45 times  c$\^{}$2$. For muon decays, masses up to 205 GeV could be excluded for early charginos lighter than 107 GeV. For hadronic decays, masses up to 110 GeV could be excluded for charginos lighter than 61 GeV. These limits were adjusted for various analysis assumptions. A training neural network was used to find these results.

Learning to reconstruct 3D scenes from sparse light field images poses a significant challenge for neural networks due to limited input data. However, it's possible to constrain the scene geometry using geometric information, like depth maps, which helps the network learn the scene's structure. Traditional methods rely on explicit depth estimates, but we take a different approach by utilizing implicit depth representations. Our novel framework combines a geometric prior with the geometric information extracted from sparse images, using a unified representation to learn the scene's geometry. By integrating a geometric prior with the information extracted from sparse images, our model is able to learn the scene's geometry. The geometric prior represents a broad range of geometric information, while the image information helps to refine the prior and learn texture information. Since there are no explicitly measurable depth maps for novel views, our model generates synthetic views and estimates depth maps using a differentiable rendering process, all while training the network using a single, arrived-at depth estimation. Experimental results on the central complexity dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our model, whose generated images outperform state-of-the-art baselines in terms of PSNR and SSIM metrics. Furthermore, the model's ability to generalize to datasets with significantly different distributions, like the chinchilla dataset, showcases its robustness and performance compared to other methods.

The Speckle Search for Wide- separation Star Companions (SSWSC) database, driven by the US Navy's technology advancements, has made notable speckle interferometry observations since 2007. As of February 2020, 20,013 measurements from 13,842 stars have been recorded. Following a review of the latest SSWSC data collected in 2020, significant findings reveal 162 new binary or multi-body systems, as well as 61 companion subsystems, bringing the total number of recorded systems to 1258 and subsystems to 761. Moreover, these data also identify 846 companions, expanding the total count to 11,258. Furthermore, statistical studies of the data reveal that the distribution of separation for stellar companions follows a power-law model with a high exponent value of 2.12, indicating significantly more closely associated companions. Additionally, our analysis indicates that the distribution of inclination exponents is evenly dispersed, and the average inclination of stellar companions is around 78 degrees, with a relatively narrow range of angles. Importantly, this study expands the scope of the data collection to lower luminosity classes, providing valuable insights into the orbital properties of stellar companions. As a secondary focus, this study also updates the data on stellar properties, and verifies hierarchical structures within multi-body systems.

We're studying the structure of the operator-product expansion (OPE) in 
four-dimensional self-dual (SD) gauge theory without any additional supersymmetry.
The OPE's chiral arrangement is linked to the connections within SD theories, as 
well as the internal organization of scattering amplitudes. It's established that 
the chiral property causes anomalies in the OPE. Conversely, starting from the OPE, 
we've managed to reconstruct the tree-level scattering amplitudes of gluons and 
derivated objects (derivative gluons and a certain 'twist' component of gluons), 
all of which are classified under chiral arrangements. The method involves applying 
the rules of massless field theories and utilizes conformal partial wave expansions.

Radio bursts of type II are massive solar waves that can be detected through radio frequencies. These bursts are often linked to developing solar jets, but the relationships between them remain poorly understood. A notable type II radio burst occurred on the solar jet on September 5, 2013, and researchers analyzed data from the Radio Solar Observatory Moving Object Prototype Search to learn more. By contrasting data from different radio frequencies, scientists found the shock wave in this burst had a significant velocity of approximately 1380 km/s, significantly faster than the solar jet itself. This reveals the shock wave could be at least twice as fast as the jet itself. Furthermore, researchers observed the shock wave accelerate over time by analyzing these frequency data, although they couldn't explain the observed acceleration with current theories. These results also suggest that solar jets might not always originate from standard reconnection, but the exact mechanisms behind these jets are still unclear.

We analyzed potential future collider measurements, including those at a 100 TeV proton-proton collider and a 14 TeV (Heelan's) heavy ion collider. Our focus was on how certain low-energy phenomena might connect to these high-energy observables. Specifically, we looked at how certain lepton violations, a type of B meson decay known as $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$, and the high-luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) observation of a certain $Z$ decaying into four leptons over a specific energy range, might influence each other. Our findings suggest that future measurements at the HL-LHC and a certain pp collider will have substantial constraints on certain models, including the two Higgs doublet model. Moreover, we discovered notable interactions between certain low-energy phenomena, including a type of tau decay, a type of $Z$ decay, and a type of gamma radiation, at high-energy levels. Interestingly, we found that the HL-LHC might develop notable correlations between certain low-energy phenomena, including a type of tau decay and a type of $Z$ decay, a prediction not influenced by non-proton collisions, and might also lead to the detection of a certain model not previously tested at the LHC. Our study serves as a basis for further exploration of the potential links between certain high-energy observables and, notably, a type of $b\to s\ell^+$ decay, a topic currently

We introduce a novel numerical approach, random vortex dynamics, which uses a non-intrusive method to solve three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations for incompressible fluid flow by iteratively reducing vorticity errors on a Cartesian grid without necessitating solution of the original equations. This approach comprises two main components: random perturbations to accelerate numerical convergence and a dynamics mechanism to direct the perturbations towards minimizing vorticity errors. It can be used as a pre-processing or sub-processing tool in conjunction with established methods such as vorticity-calculating methods and immersed boundary techniques. Through rigorous mathematical analysis and numerical experiments, we demonstrate that random vortex dynamics efficiently handles a wide array of complex flow challenges including high-speed turbulence, rotating and elliptical flows, and flows with sharp gradients like those near solid surfaces. Furthermore, applications to computational aerodynamics reveal notable potential benefits.

We analyze entanglement in a remnant system consisting of $N$ bosons after removing ${\cal B}$ bosons of type A and ${\cal A}$ bosons of type B from a completely symmetric state, denoted as $\vert \Psi^{AB} \rangle$. The remnant system is defined by the bosonic subspace excluding those removed, with the scalar variational constraint applied accordingly. We show that this system exhibits entanglement when ${\cal B} < N/2$ or ${\cal A} < N/2$, with the latter condition being a notable finding. Furthermore, we investigate the degree of entanglement using various entanglement metrics and observe that it may be suppressed as the number of photons approaches $N$. This behavior is in line with the experimental observation that entanglement suppression by photon loss is more pronounced with larger photon numbers.

The complexity of analyzing gene expression data can be substantial due to its high dimensions and short observation periods. This study demonstrates the application of relevance learning with a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) on time-dependent data, followed by statistical analysis on synthetic datasets. We found that incorporating prior knowledge through relevance learning significantly reduces computation by identifying key variables initially and streamlining subsequent statistical examinations. Utilizing a two-stage approach: relevance learning followed by statistical analysis efficiently handles high-dimensional data. Moreover, our method outperforms conventional GMM-based analyses and showcases the beneficial integration of machine learning and statistical tools for analyzing gene expression data.

In the context of optimal control in partially observable situations, researchers often utilize beliefs about system states as a key factor. Many cutting-edge algorithms, such as those based on policy gradients, aim to optimize control directly through the state beliefs or related variables like the belief itself, the Q-value, or latent hidden states in RNNs. Surprisingly, we found that the hidden states in RNNs can be considered as an estimate of the optimal beliefs about system states. This insight is rooted in the theory of finite-state Markov decision processes (MDPs). We also developed a method to extend this theory to continuous systems with infinite state spaces. Our approach involves transforming the constraints on system states, observations, and actions into generative neural networks, which can be trained using reinforcement learning algorithms. By doing so, we made a connection between RNNs optimized through reinforcement learning and the optimal control problems in partially observable environments. Our findings also revealed that the hidden states in RNNs are essentially an approximation of the fundamental parameters defining the environment, including noise, rewards, and observation functions. The generative networks representing these parameters allowed us to interpret the behavior of RNNs and develop novel continuous learning algorithms based on this understanding. Our work has the potential to drive further research in the field, especially in developing gradient-based methods for parameters that are not directly trainable. Additionally, by exposing the underlying structure of the environment, we can achieve more efficient solutions to complex problems.

Modern pipelines for identifying actions in videos rely on features extracted using convolutional neural networks and spatial attention mechanisms to determine which parts of the video contain an object performing an action. However, the convolutional network's assumption that each video frame contains a constant background simplifies the background's video sequence. In reality, the background often changes between frames. In this research, we propose a method that leverages self-attention and Graph Convolutional Networks to model video background variations, as well as a novel action localization metric that focuses on the object's physical movement when predicting action occurrences. When tested on industry-standard industry datasets, our approach outperforms current pipeline techniques.

This research introduces a survey of recent advancements in image copy detection. The comprehensive review strategic concepts are derived from relevant scenarios and highlights the crucial elements of successful image copy detection, including circuitous comparison techniques employing salient data and specialized features. A thorough examination of existing literature is conducted, focusing on image representation and feature learning. The distinct characteristics and evaluation methods of leading datasets and metrics in image copy detection are identified. Additionally, potential challenges and future research opportunities in image copy detection are explored. The findings of this survey are anticipated to provide valuable guidance for researchers actively partaking in this area of study.

The investigation of interior and boundary behaviors of solutions to a class of second-order linear parabolic equations is carried out in a half-space and a bounded domain with specific functional spaces as members of the second-type Schr\"odinger equation family. We derive interior and boundary estimates, and demonstrate the existence of asymptotic representations consisting of interior and boundary parts along with an estimate of the rate of decay. In addition, we establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions to resulting reduced problems and show that asymptotic representations can be unique. Furthermore, by employing interpolation methods, the existence and uniqueness of solutions to reduced problems in specific spaces with weighted norms are proven. These findings are then applied to a class of second-order linear parabolic equations with boundary conditions representing initial-value problems, Dirichlet boundary-value problems, and Neumann boundary-value problems, each on a half-space and a bounded domain.

The thermodynamic behavior of nuclear matter was studied using Jochen Wambig's action and a power-law variational principle. This analysis, conducted without considering the constraints of a magnetic field, revealed an unexpected phenomenon in which the energy density increases while the spin polarization decreases at zero temperature, eventually leading to equilibrium. Moreover, our research demonstrates that the previously assumed ground state solution of the Dirac equation in nuclear matter is indeed correct.

Federated learning techniques allow for parallel training while maintaining user data privacy, using differential privacy to restrict the extraction of information from data. Our research examines how differential privacy impacts the federated compression method and the information extraction bound in parallel distributional training. A privacy-compliant compression mechanism is proposed, and the extraction bound is analyzed under a linear noise framework. Both the true and approximate forms of DP are applied to determine the extraction bound in terms of compression probability. Furthermore, a privacy-compliant deep learning approach is developed for parallel distributional training, and the impact of different DP mechanisms on the model is evaluated. Our experimental findings involve three DP mechanisms: the "clip-plus-noise" method, the "noisy-clipping" technique, and a variant of the "diffpriv" tool. These DP mechanisms are tested and compared based on their performance using the tumor classification application and the sparse junction loss application. Our experiments show that these DP mechanisms have distinct trade-offs in terms of model performance and the preservation of information, and the "diffpriv" method offers the best balance between privacy and inference while maintaining a balanced performance.

The UV spectrum of the Taurus-Air-Wheel complex reveals a notable, intense spot, largely caused by fluorescent hydrogen emissions which contribute a substantial portion of the visible UV light within the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus area. A moderate-filter UV image taken by the Orbiting APOGEE experiment and integrated with existing data from other sources such as X-ray observations, radio surveys, and IR observations shows the detailed structure of the complex which appears as an elongated area filled with young stars, gas, and dust. A comparison with the X-ray-emitting star population lies along the Taurus-Air-Wheel ridge which contains the Fulton formation location. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the UV intensity along this ridge correlates with both the nearby young stars and gas while there is no observed correlation with the cosmic background radiation but reveals an unexpected anomaly. A star formation wave within the Taurus-Air-Wheel area, initially proposed by other researchers, is also examined for consistency with the observed data. The analysis reveals that the amplitude of the proposed wave, initially evaluated using X-ray data, has significant discrepancies of up to 3 in comparison with the observed UV intensity. This disparity indicates that the far-UV intensity has the potential to refine the timing of the proposed star formation wave by at least a decade. A star formation map derived using hydrogen gas density and tracer data is also compared with the cosmic background radiation but it's relationship remains unclear.

Extracting table structure from unstructured documents is a crucial initial step in information retrieval, typically followed by data extraction. Deep learning techniques have recently revolutionized document processing. Traditional approaches, however, often combined features from various sources with limited success. We propose a novel deep learning framework, incorporating Guided Table Extraction with Graph Neural Networks (GTGNN), for document images. This method leverages the strengths of ResNeXt features and graph neural networks to efficiently identify tables, while benefiting from additional guidance at different levels. Experimental results on the ICDAR 2019 Table Recognition (Track 2) dataset demonstrate that our GTGNN approach outperforms a robust baseline by a substantial 9.5% in table extraction, with key improvements stemming from the integration of graph neural networks.

In the Hanabi game, players benefit by seeing card clues from fellow players, but learning these facts incurs a risk of revealing false information that could lose the team game.  As the game's hierarchy of player levels from 1 to 10 is established based on their relative problem-solving capabilities, we've developed a theoretical model of a team of players with different levels of expertise playing the Hanabi game.  Our model suggests that the lowest-level players tend to make mistakes by revealing card hints at earlier stages of the game.  In contrast, higher-level players understand the benefits of delaying this information until later in the game.  Our model also outlines specific strategies of both team and individual players, indicating that the best-performing individual players tend to act similarly to the highest-level group members.  Our model's analysis utilizes approximations such as the large deviations principle to predict the players' behavior.  Finally, we verify our findings by conducting experiments and finding that our theory aligns with these results in the limit where a large number of players are participating.

Archeology is an ancient discipline that has sparked curiosity for centuries, and recent advancements have led to a surge in studies predicting population dynamics through complex data analysis. Many of these studies rely on publicly available features extracted using labor-intensive and established methods, and as a result, their analysis is often limited by the characteristics of these traditional techniques. In contrast, our proposed model, archeoRNN, utilizes a unique set of features derived from footprint area estimation to create a more accurate and robust population forecasting model. By introducing a novel set of features, we demonstrate that it is possible to achieve superior performance compared to models relying solely on publicly available features. Our comprehensive evaluation involves 12 datasets, yielding significant improvements in mean absolute error and root mean squared error, notably between 10% to 40% and 20% to 50%, respectively. Additionally, our model exhibits excellent generalization capabilities, consistently performing well across datasets that were not included in the model's training or hyperparameter tuning processes.

A technique called static filters prevents a Java Virtual Machine from executing potentially malicious code by checking program control flow at compile time. It accomplishes this without diminishing performance, maintaining memory efficiency, and minimizing program size. The key advantage of static filters lies in its ability to discard legitimate threats, thus protecting the host system from exploitation.
