During the control process, the feedback law is represented by a Convex Program, allowing the collection of online gradient information regarding the future state distribution prediction. Online gradient collection yields better results than the initial batch approach used in [1], resulting in fewer evaluation calls required to achieve the same performance. Moreover, enforcing a lower bound on the likelihood noise at the data generation stage grants the system dynamics model a level of robustness, even when the actual noise level is higher than that assumed during data collection. As a result, the learning control method developed here is capable of handling uncertain dynamics, robustly estimating models with noise levels greater than initially assumed, and yielding better performance compared to traditional learning control methods.

For any quiver $Q$, a family of linear maps defined on $Q$ enables the construction of a slice algebra by combining matrix or tensor algebras with a mapping algebra. This paper presents a method to calculate a higher syzygy of a module's structure in a slice algebra in a way that preserves module structure. Based on this approach, the text also offers a direct construction of homogenization for submodules within a quotient module, demonstrating that this process maintains exact relationships with the module's homogenization. Additionally, the text applies this operator to derive a matrix description of a toric algebra, further exploring its relationship with the algebra's Grobner basis when the underlying quiver is a path graph.

In their research, a group of analysts demonstrates the existence of reflected entanglement spectra within certain random tensor networks, which they go on to show can be precisely computed.  Unlike a traditional R'enyi spectrum, the reflected entanglement spectrum does not directly stem from a R'enyi quotient tensor but instead requires a specific "flipped" tensor.  Utilizing a specific example, the analysts reveal how the reflected entanglement spectrum can be utilized in the detection of area laws, and they further note its potential for applying a finite-time entanglement localization principle in fermionic systems.  The analysts also outline a method for free fermion spectra transformation and apply this method in exploring the entanglement spectrum of a specific edge excitation in a Majorana chain.  Lastly, a group of analysts proposes that the reflected entanglement spectrum can serve as an extended entropy of tensor network deformations and that the tensor network deformations corresponding to the reflected entanglement spectrum can serve as a dual to the tensor network deformations corresponding to the traditional R'enyi spectrum, with the tensor network deformations corresponding to the reflected entanglement spectrum can also serve as a dual to the tensor network deformations corresponding to the traditional R'enyi spectrum, which is a work that has not been done before this research.

We investigated probability events in two relatively straightforward dynamical systems 
characterized by a small number of degrees of freedom. Building on prior research at 
the Complex Systems Group of Moscow State University, we expanded the scope to 
evaluate numerous configurations of several systems, analyzing how different initial 
settings influence enduring patterns. Despite the simplicity of the dynamical systems 
and extensive data collection, accumulating evidence suggests that gathering a large 
set of independent realizations poses significant statistical challenges, potentially 
affecting our understanding of persistent events. This study's findings are rooted in the 
analysis of one-dimensional discrete-time iterated functions and vortex dynamics in 
the Boussinesq equation for approximate three-dimensional dynamics. While the latter 
is a area of research focusing on realistic fluid modeling, presenting a new approach to 
resolving three-dimensional chaotic dynamics through statistical comparison of 
configurations may be an inefficient method due to the considerable computational 
resources required.

We analyze the family of generalized H\'{e}non maps with one and two dimensions from a global perspective using bifurcation theory. The one-dimensional case serves as a reference point to understand the transition between scenarios where solutions converge versus those where they diverge. The incorporation of bifurcation sets enables us to visualize the dynamics in the larger parameter space, revealing that fixed points and periodic orbits play crucial roles in shaping the space's structure. The construction of bifurcation sets for the two-dimensional maps involves a novel approach, which is then used to examine the scenario where the maps serve as models for planet-orbit interactions. The results are also applicable to other parametric families of maps. Additionally, our method can be adapted to study other connected families of maps in various dimensions.

The Holonomy Transforms theory is developed as a non-Abelian extension of Gauge Theory's Holonomy, exhibiting both gauge invariant and covariant properties.  In contrast to Gravity's holonomy, which can be represented as a tensor product of subgroups, gravity's holonomy is defined by a subgroup's self-transformation.  The discussion includes $\mathcal{N}=1$ Seiberg-Witten Solutions for $SU(3)$ and $Sp(6)$ gauge theories, as well as an explanation of why gravity holonomy cannot be redefined as a gauge field.

We examine the asymptotic behavior of random variables of the form (1/Z)*f(T1/Tn) for the Lagrangian energies generated by systems of interacting particles on a 2D torus with fractional time T and momentum spaces, where the potential v(x) has several zeros and a smooth, convex shape. Given these conditions, we prove that the cumulative distribution functions of the variables converge as the number of particles n grows larger, ultimately tending towards an absolutely continuous limit equal to the integral of the given function f(x), with x ranging from 0 to infinity. Furthermore, we establish that the variables themselves converge in law, tending towards an absolutely continuous random variable defined by its cumulative distribution function f(x). This work builds upon previous research, specifically extending the findings of Teschl and Yngve.

The existing approaches to tunneling times are re-evaluated through a coherent quantum mechanical framework that incorporates the principles of Feynman's path integral formulation and the principles of quantum electrodynamics. It is demonstrated that previous tunneling time data collections, which have relied on transient electrostatic interactions, are inaccurate and misinterpret system evolution. A more accurate understanding of tunneling times is presented and it is shown that tunneling times are inherently tied to spin fluctuations in the tunneling system. According to this new understanding, tunneling times are measured by the average time it takes for a tunneling particle to transition between different eigenstates as influenced by spin fluctuations. A universal ATT formula is derived for the tunneling times of particles transitioning between two different eigenstates in the presence of electrostatic tunneling. It is shown that the ATT is directly proportional to $\hbar/(|E_{{\rm f}}-E_{{\rm i}}|)$ and that tunneling times can be tuned via external magnetic fields that influence spin fluctuations. A new ATT for the tunneling of electrons in quantum double well systems is presented and derived analytically, and it is shown that the ATT can be modified by introducing odd-numbered valence electrons into the tunneling system. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the average ATT can be modified by introducing even-numbered valence electrons into the tunneling system.

We've calculated relativistic corrections to the production amplitudes of P-wave charmonia mesons in $e+e-$ collisions. This study used a field-theoretic approach with a simplified linear sigma model, where charmonia mesons are described as quark-antiquark states. By applying a relativistic correction factor, specifically the 'quark rule', to each amplitude, we derived a general formula expressing relativistic corrections in terms of the specific angles between polarization vectors and fragmentation functions. We then applied this formula to calculate relativistic corrections for $\rho^0$, $\ kappa^+$ and $K_{1A}$ production amplitudes. Results showed significant relativistic corrections for polarization-dependent amplitudes but minimal effects for polarization-independent amplitudes. This study provides a theoretical basis that can be used for extracting polarization and anisotropy parameters from polarization distribution in future experiments.

To increase the precision of Ramsey interferometry involving multiple-path ways using trapped ions or cold atoms, we utilize a general efficient method to design and optimize higher-order, entangling gates. These gates, which entangle $m$ out of $n$ paths, increase the interferometric sensitivity compared to lower-order gates. Following the optimal protocol, we apply our method to design higher-order, entangling gates for systems with three-path ways and compare their efficiency to existing techniques. Furthermore, we explore a special case of systems with symmetric paths to develop an efficient approach for constructing higher-order, entangling gates specifically for these systems.

Building on the findings of a previous study (1905.12545), we further examine the impact of time-reversal and conformal transformations on the boundaries of our universe, specifically its extremal and non-extremal boundaries. These charges, known as eBMS charges, are inspired by a theoretical model called the extremal black hole-oscillator system. By proving that the ground states of this system, which are characterized by specific frequencies and degeneracies, are preserved under certain boundary transformations, we gain insights into the behavior of black holes. Importantly, our research confirms the "soft news" property and identifies the contributing factors to these charges. Furthermore, we demonstrate a connection between some of these charges and the principles of modular invariance and Schwarzian symmetry. The findings of our study provide a theoretical basis for further exploration of the relationship between thermodynamics and the BMS-type charges of black holes.

Ensemble method involvement within Neural Network training is a well-established technique that enhances generalization performances by reducing overfitting. Nonetheless, the current practices are largely dependent on heuristics rather than theoretical guidance. In this study, a theoretical framework inspired by a Gaussian process analysis is proposed, which suggests a variance-based ensemble approach. By selectively training neurons in an incremental manner, the proposed method aims to minimize the variance of the objective function, thereby facilitating convergence. Experimental results demonstrate that the variance-based ensemble technique achieves superior classification accuracy compared to standard ensemble methods, while also offering theoretical insights to guide the optimization of variance reduction and several other common objectives. Moreover, the proposed technique can be efficiently applied to tackle optimization problems in both functional and neural network contexts.

We explain generalized connections as a way to derive Ricci flat metrics from a given metric. Next, we discuss the realization of generalized connections through Atiyah sequences and show how this connection is related to $C^{\infty}$-bundles. Additionally, we derive generalized connections from twisted generalized calabi-yau structures and demonstrate that a specific type of generalized calabi-yau structure can lead to a metric having non-zero holomorphic curvature. We establish the relationship between generalized calabi-yau structures and hypercomplex structures derived from Atiyah sequences. Further, we discuss the Darmon-Conditch-Morris generalized calabi-yau structure and its association with $G_2$-manifolds.

Let's consider a d-dimensional cube built within the boundaries of the finite field $\mathcal{F}_q$ with $q$ elements, where each component $x_i$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}_q$. We define a complete mapping from this cube if there is an $q^d$-element set $\mathcal{S}$ such that for every function $f$ of $x_1, \dots, x_d$, and every $s \in \mathcal{S}$, there exists a point $x = (x_1, \dots, x_d)$ with the property that for every $y \in \mathcal{S}$, the condition $f((x_1, \dots, x_d)) + s = f((x_1, \dots, x_d)) + y$ holds. We will demonstrate that such a mapping exists within the family of polynomial functions over $\mathcal{F}_q$. Additionally, this finding leads to a generalization of the Lefshetz principle for complex manifolds to the scenario where we have a finite field $\mathcal{F}_q$.

Even with human visual inspection, diagnosing intestinal parasites can be challenging due to the laborious process and relatively high error rate. To improve the accuracy of such diagnoses, a computer-assisted system called ParaVision has been developed for supporting intestinal parasite diagnosis from microscope images. By integrating multiple advanced deep learning techniques, ParaVision's ability to detect and segment samples was refined, along with a classification system for identifying the present parasite types. A recent enhancement to ParaVision involves the inclusion of a stylization system that allows doctors to see the doctor's vision in the same image using a chosen style, thereby preserving the valuable expert knowledge embedded in it. By applying this concept to the field of intestinal parasite diagnosis, ParaVision can now display the doctor's insight about a sample's image by transforming the processed doctor image into an artist-style image that represents their vision. For the integration of this concept into ParaVision, a new neural network called Nascent has been designed. Based on normalizing flows, Nascent is capable of transforming a processed doctor image into a stylized art image while learning the underlying structure of the doctor's vision. Experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of ParaVision and Nascent, showing that they outperform existing models in task-specific linear evaluations. Furthermore, the stylized images generated by Nascent convey the doctor's insight into the processed image, thereby highlighting the added value of the incorporated expertise.

This study employs the direct approach from MacLean and Wiegand via the Hausdorff metric to find 
approximately consistent solutions of nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations, which consist of high-order integro-differential terms. This approach is specifically applied to a problem of flight trajectory optimization in the presence of uncertainties, which can be represented by the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation with an exterior convex solution. A verification algorithm is used alongside the Hausdorff metric method to generate approximations of solutions, which also allows for an analysis of error rates. This approach is demonstrated with two-dimensional flight trajectory optimization examples, which reveal the importance of incorporating flight path constraints.

Recent advancements in estimation algorithms have improved the accuracy of estimated states in quadcopters, yet the estimated states often diverge from the true states due to disturbances in real-world applications. To address this challenge, this research paper presents a novel control strategy called the Genetic Filter (GF), which uses the principles of Genetic Algorithm to enhance estimated state algorithms. The GF generates multiple state estimates through various initial conditions and evaluates their accuracy, selecting the most suitable one. By integrating the GF with a quadcopter control system, the quadcopter's stability was tested in both simulated and real-world environments. Results indicate that the integration of the GF significantly improved the quadcopter's flight stability, particularly in the presence of disturbances. Furthermore, the stability of the quadcopter's motion was achieved, as demonstrated by the minimal rise times and steady-state errors of the quadcopter's rotation and position.

We have performed a precise calculation of the pion-nucleon sigma term using lattice QCD, and our findings are consistent with recent findings from a different calculation method. Our results and their relationship to an on-going nuclear physics investigation are presented in this paper.

The CMS detector's silicon pixel detector has undergone upgrades since 2013,
which saw the implementation of an insertion based read-out system during
2016 and the integration of an on-processor trigger system in 2017. This
detector upgrade boosted the read-out speed and reduced dead-time, thus
enhancing the CMS's track finding capabilities. To handle the increased data rate
generated by enhanced jet transversity analysis resolutions following the 2018
upgrades, the CMS adopted an on-processor trigger system. This study evaluates the
efficiency of jets in the central barrel region following 2016-2018 data
collection, which includes 35.9 inverse femtobarns of luminosity recorded during the
LHC's Run II.

Using the multi-color image dataset from the COSMOS field, we have created a collection of deep-coadded images covering approximately 500 square degrees. These images incorporate more than 60,000 galaxy clusters spanning the redshift range from 0 to approximately 5. Utilizing a comprehensive set of 15 distinct filters, we employed two distinct methods for identifying galaxies hosting active galactic nuclei (AGN): an unsupervised approach that relies on a trained neural network and a second method incorporating neural networks and machine learning algorithms for determining galaxy classifications. In this study, we examined the properties of galaxies hosting active galactic nuclei across various intervals of redshift and found that neural networks are highly effective in identifying AGN hosts, especially at higher redshifts where broad-line AGN are prevalent. Additionally, we investigated the influence of neural networks on determining the types of active galactic nuclei within the COSMOS field.

A comprehensive approach is introduced to analyze the neutron skin thickness in terms of certain correlation functions. The impact of the short-range nuclear dynamics on the asymmetry of the radial nucleon density is systematically investigated using the Fourier transformation. Numerical results for selected isotopic chains are presented, revealing that the neutron skin thickness is significantly influenced by short-range correlations. Additionally, an empirical equation is proposed that seeks to minimize the contribution of the asymmetry density radius, yielding estimates of the neutron skin thickness that are consistent with data from neutron scattering experiments and other independent methods.

This research aims to improve the representation of images through complex-valued pyramidal scaling, incorporating the inherent link between color channels. Unlike traditional vector-based image representations, this approach utilizes complex numbers with separate real and imaginary components to capture inter-channel relationships. However, existing complex representations are limited by their inability to efficiently encode multi-channel images. We present a novel method that maps RGB images to complex forms while preserving key properties: across different scales, subtle color changes are minimized, and local pixel relationships remain consistent. This new representation is mathematically formulated as a constrained optimization problem and solved using an efficient algorithm. We demonstrate that our approach effectively captures inter-scale and inter-channel dependencies, as evident from its robust performance in tasks like image deraining, color naming, and single-image depth estimation. Experimental results and qualitative analysis confirm that our technique achieves superior outcomes and enhances interpretability.

The geometrical scaling phenomenon in hadron production has been observed across various reactions, including e+e- annihilation, deep-inelastic scattering, and heavy ion collisions. To better understand the geometrical scaling concept, a comparison is made between two processes: gluon emission from a charged quark and from a color-neutral gluon. By analyzing the latter process, a new formula is developed for gluon distribution, which accurately describes saturation and its connection to diffusion. This model expresses gluon distribution as a power law near the saturation point, closely related to that of a diffusion equation. At lower gluon densities, a new parameter is introduced, ensuring consistency with established QCD results. This model, which considers only the dominant Fock components, successfully describes gluon production across all stages, including the dilute and saturated phases. Specifically, it correctly predicts transverse momentum spectra in ultraperipheral collisions and describes saturation in semi-central collisions. Furthermore, it predicts novel phenomena associated with diffusion, including gluon production at zero momentum and its non-Gaussian distribution, both observable in future experiments. Ultimately, this model offers a unified description of geometrical scaling across all collision systems.

Enrichment of stars in the early universe with heavy elements came from explosive supernovae. By utilizing a simplified model, we analyzed the process of core-collapse supernovae (CCSN) and their impact on the formation of the early galaxy. The duration of a supernova event is significantly less than the time it takes for a star-forming region to solidify, an outcome of the rapid formation of dust due to CCSN. Therefore, subsequent star formation in the surrounding area can utilize newly synthesized elemental categories before they undergo changes through chemical interactions, an effect known as "elemental categorization". Using data from the GALACTICRUSHER simulation, we studied how chemical interactions influenced the formation of dust in the early galaxy. The simulation modeled core-collapse supernovae through stochastic sampling, reflecting the uncertainty of mass distribution at the time of a supernova explosion. The enrichment of elements from a single core-collapse supernova is enough to drastically alter the composition of surrounding gas, an effect observed in present-day star-forming regions of the galaxy. According to our model, CCSN and their supernovae explosions significantly accelerated the enrichment of elements in the early galaxy primarily because of their mass and the speed at which they form dust, far exceeding the effect of other supernovae types. The chemical interactions played a minor role in the early galaxy due to the rapid formation of dust from CCSN. The speed at which dust forms and the mass of a supernova are critical factors in the chemical

The concept of model stability in a statistical prediction model's framework, known as the BLR framework, is originally defined to assess the impact of newly added features on existing models. Models that prove stable under this definition remain highly predictive, even when new features are inserted. Originally, this concept was limiting because it solely focused on predictive accuracy. We have developed a more comprehensive definition, called the stochastic stability, incorporating a variety of performance metrics, such as predictive accuracy, robustness, and reliability. This revised definition is known as the S-stability. To facilitate the analysis of stochastic stability, the BLR framework is extended to encompass a broader range of models, known as the BLR+ framework. We employ the ELNNE model within the BLR+ framework to demonstrate the utility of S-stability for assessing the robustness of predictive models.

Variational quantum models, which utilize an ansatz with adjustable parameters to replicate quantum states, are being rapidly developed. It is essential to determine which output gates effectively approximate quantum circuit depth. Our research involves evaluating output gates based on three criteria: their ability to approximate quantum circuit depth, their scalability for gradient-based optimization, and the accuracy of Taylor expansions. We evaluated several output gates, including Pauli-Y, SU2, SU4, and SUN, through an approximation of quantum circuit depth and scaling tests. Furthermore, we used state-of-the-art quantum algorithms to train these gates for variational quantum algorithms. Our findings indicate that SU2 and SU4 gates can effectively replicate quantum circuit depth, while output gates with higher fidelity do not necessarily lead to deeper circuit approximations. Moreover, SU2 produces less variance in energy estimates compared to SU4. Interestingly, SUN failed to display the expected benefits of deeper circuits. Ultimately, SU2 emerges as a well-rounded output gate capable of achieving precise results, outperforming other output gates in scalability, despite having the simplest structure.

Researchers investigate pointwise semi-slant submanifolds of a particular type in Sasakian manifolds. Specifically, they identify new examples of warped product semi-slant submanifolds and, more remarkably, find the first-ever instance of a pointwise semi-slant submanifold of a Sigman manifold, which is a particular type of complex Sasakian manifold.

The Large Underground Xenon (LUX-ZEPLIN) experiment, a direct dark matter detection laboratory located at the SNOLAB laboratory in Canada, is studying a 10 kilogram liquid xenon detector to search for various types of particle interactions. A specific experiment, already underway, is analyzing coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CEvNS) interactions using a range of neutrinos sent through the xenon target. This work details a new analysis of the 2021 LUX-ZEPLIN dataset consisting of 2598 kg*years of exposure. Additionally, it includes considerations of the neutrino source, energy reconstruction, analysis selection, and background analysis in the context of standard and novel analyses within the double electron ionization (EE) region of the xenon nucleus. Specifically, it represents the first single-site CEvNS analysis based on the NOvA neutrino-nucleus response and includes a refined neutrino-nucleus response in the xenon context derived from quantum-echo-mixed-multiplicity-moment (QM$^3$M) calculations. As such, it has reached a CEvNS interaction rate limit of $0.0573 \pm 0.0198$ (statistical) $^{+0.1213}_{-0.0553}$ (systematic) events/(100 kilogram-year/(year)), with a 95% confidence interval excluding known neutrino-nucleus interactions from accelerator experiments using the Bayesian

To explore the active movement of molecules, we develop a basic theoretical framework and create a simplified model representing two-dimensional molecular structures with a balance system, able to generate circular motions from linear ones. We then use this concept to observe the rotation of molecular dimers across different temperature ranges and analyze the impact of external forces on their activity. Furthermore, by utilizing high-speed imaging techniques, we document the circular trajectories of actively moving dimers and quantify their rotation speeds, finding good agreement between these experimental results and our theoretical predictions.

Weyl particles, or chiralisites, of varying sizes are investigated in a
quantum system combining a one-dimensional wire of spinless fermions and a
magnetic field. The system's energy spectrum, which exhibits both polynomial
and exponential dependencies on the magnetic field, is illustrated by the
author's numerical solutions. The author also analyzes various low-lying states,
identifying two distinct 'chiral modes' and demonstrating that at a particular
ratio of magnetic field to particle density, one of these modes undergoes a
smooth transition while the other becomes singular. The phenomenon is tied to a
critical point in a related quantum parameter known as $
u=2/7$ and examined in detail. The author further develops a simplified
model, which in conjunction with numerical solutions not only confirms the
existence of two distinct 'chiral modes' but also indicates that at another value
of $
u=2/9$, the modes exhibit symmetry with respect to time reversal. The results
are further contextualised within the context of the field.

Our research investigates the dynamics of the $S$-permutation model on any type of network, essentially any set of connected points with associated risks. This work serves as a thorough examination of the stochastic process described by equitable relaxation on general networks and their corresponding equitable partitions. By relaxing the requirements for equitable partitions, we gain a deeper understanding of the variability of the model, enabling the computation of mean and variance for key indicators such as the size of the susceptible population and the time until the first individual contracts the disease. These findings are applicable to networks that are not necessarily regular and can be used in the study of epidemics on arbitrary contact networks by modeling the disease's spread through a Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered framework. Our work begins with a specific scenario where the disease's transmission probability is relatively low, and we use this base case to examine more critical situations.

There are numerous cosmic microwave background (CMB) estimators that aren't unbiased, meaning their performance can vary depending on the data's characteristics. Point sources can significantly impact these estimators by introducing systematic errors in CMB maps. In particular, estimators that are biased, such as those based on simple mean or median averages, produce skewed error distributions when dealing with strong point sources. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced when dealing with strong point sources, causing the standard deviation of the error distribution to be significantly higher than what's statistically expected. Despite this, the error distribution remains roughly Gaussian. By developing and analyzing the error budgets of the COBE- FIRAS and Planck missions, we explore the implications of these estimators and the impact of strong point sources on CMB estimators across various observational scenarios, including both ground-based and space-based missions.

This study explores the idea that by incorporating pedagogy and pragmatism into task instructions, researchers can create virtual interactions that not only provide practical information but also foster practical skills and practical wisdom. Drawing on theories from education and philosophy, we propose a framework for crafting task-based instructions rooted in these concepts. We demonstrate this approach by rewriting the instructions for the existing MTURK task and examine its implications for computational models of common sense reasoning.

A crucial yet underappreciated element in every optical experiment is shadowing. We are now able to quantify this phenomenon through a generalized tomographic protocol that determines shadow-induced distortion factors in any experimental setup. This protocol, known as shadow tomography, enables measurement of a state's shadowing matrix, thereby allowing for the identification of several key features. Firstly, we establish that shadow tomography is an intrinsic characterization method, free from dependent measurements. Furthermore, we reveal that shadow tomography is a special instance of quantum state tomography where the uncertainty relations of an ancillary qubit are utilized. This leads to the conclusion that the number of required measurements in shadow tomography must not exceed $4n$, with potential improvement possible in specific cases through clever experimental design. Lastly, we propose a novel approach using deep learning to accomplish shadow tomography, utilizing significantly fewer measurements than traditional methods.

In this study, we demonstrate that for any convex polygon with n sides, its inradius and circumradius satisfy the relationship $r\leq\frac{2}{3n}K_a$, where the area of the polygon is given by $K_a$. This inequality can be generalized to convex shapes in n-dimensional space as $r\leq\frac{2}{n(n-1)}K_n$, where the volume of the shape is denoted as $K_n$.

This paper investigates a novel challenge in creating a single UAV with multiple antennas that can move through the sky to facilitate the transfer of files to a group of users as quickly as possible. The file transfer times are determined by the UAV's distance to each user and can vary significantly. To tackle this issue, we reformulate the problem as a variation of the orienteering problem, a well-known problem in graph theory, and explore its complexities. Based on this insight, we develop a tabu search algorithm that uses a range of parameters, including route length, to improve upload speeds. The algorithm we created starts with a random route before applying diversification and intensification strategies to optimize loads and upload times at each stop. The algorithm we created was tested and found to be quite effective in simulating rapid file transfer.

Research on the quantum Hall effect in 2D materials has historically focused on the Dirac cone model. Recent studies of monolayer and bilayer graphene have revealed unique physical properties stemming from symmetry and interlayer coupling. In this work, we utilize tight-binding simulations of bilayer graphene to examine the quantum Hall phases and their underlying physics. By varying the coupling strength between layers, we find that the symmetry of lattice rotation changes from C_6 in the isotropic state to C_2 in the nematic state, while the energy dispersion shows breaking of C_3 momenta but intact C_1 symmetry, leading to a gapped Hamiltonian and suppressed Landau levels. As the gapping mechanism's primary driver is not the Coulomb interaction, we find that the integer quantum Hall phases remain unchanged. However, the energy cost for creating vortices in each layer, which is determined by the anisotropy of the interlayer coupling, varies significantly between the two phases, leading to distinct decay rates and drift velocities of quantized Hall states.

Recent studies have explored the placement of multiple endofullerenes on a substrate in research, specifically focusing on the arrangement of two endofullerenes in initial investigations. As these molecules interact with the substrate, they undergo a transformation, changing from a flat to a dome-like shape. Through calculations, researchers have discovered that both magnetic and electric properties are affected by the shape of the endofullerenes. Furthermore, the study indicates that, when close to each other, the endofullerenes' shapes can influence each other, leading to the possibility of modulating their properties simultaneously. These findings suggest that, by adjusting the substrate's interaction, the shape of the endofullerenes can be adjusted, leading to the potential to alter the endofullerenes' magnetic and electric properties.

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) brings numerous benefits but also raises critical issues of data security and privacy. To address these concerns, researchers have been seeking innovative, quantum-enabled solutions leveraging properties of quantum mechanics such as uncertainty, randomness, and non-locality. This research paper provides an in-depth analysis of the current advancements in quantum-enabled networks and technologies relevant to IoT security, before presenting potential roadmaps for integrating these technologies into IoT frameworks.

To efficiently optimize the experimental process, we use a Bayesian approach that identifies the optimal sequence of measurements to execute prior to a high-fidelity analysis, based on previous data collected. The designs of two protocols, one utilising an adaptive heuristic method and the other incorporating random variations, are compared to the Bayesian approach and high-fidelity protocols in a demonstration involving Ramsey measurements. The experimental process is modelled using a system where the evolution of a quantum system is studied by applying a series of -pulses to it, with the state being measured after each pulse. The experimental process is driven by a goal to optimise the accuracy of the fit to the data collection schedule, with the outcome being compared to the target spectrum. The designs were tested in a simulation involving low-fidelity measurements, with the results showing the Bayesian approach outperforms the other protocols. The simulation results also highlight the significance of the uncertainty in the system model, the limited number of measurements, and the non-linear influence of the system parameters on the spectrum for optimal experimental process planning. The study also develops a simulation interface for Bayesian experimental design, incorporating the necessary probability functions for realistic simulations of various experimental setups, including a programme for simulating magnetic resonance and developing a Gaussian distribution.

The Gromov centrality is a versatile metric that evaluates a node's importance relative to its immediate neighbors, offering distinct performances on various network types with different statistical properties. While a range of centralities are capable of differentiating among dominant and isolated nodes, the Gromov centrity effectively distinguishes nodes in networks characterized by a mix of these types. This node classification corresponds to key network functions, highlighting the Gromov centrality's utility in evaluating and distinguishing various types of nodes across different network configurations.

Our universe's mean spatial density must be thought of as a relatively high level, approximately 4.55 x 10^18 particles per cubic meter, based on observations of the increase in the Earth-Sun distance over time as recorded by astronomers. This density is a fundamental constant that reflects the mean density of the universe. It also serves as a reference point for determining the gravitational behavior of other celestial objects, such as the increase in the Earth-Sun distance over time. This prediction is a simple outcome of the gravitational behavior of one particle. Furthermore, we found that the inevitability of mass extinction occurs approximately every 50 million years, as well as the inevitable development of cancer in any human or animal over approximately 5 years, as described by our theory.

Within the field of multivariate polynomial matrix theory, several open sets are identified when matrices are complex, offering spectral insights. Building on this foundation, we define open sets related to bundles of matrix polynomials. By leveraging these sets, we derive a matrix factorization approach, explored in the context of quantum mechanics where it can contribute to understanding spectral problems. Two research directions are set aside for future investigation.

We investigate the connection between continuous-trace algebras and the classical version of T-duality in a string theory framework with non-geometric characteristics. Our analysis begins with a quantum model for T-duals that incorporate K-matrices, leading to a realization that continuous-trace algebras form a crucial component in the quantum transformation process. Consequently, our results imply that classical T-duality depends on the details of the underlying algebra representation. Building upon this insight, we develop explicit contextuality examples and establish a connection between state updates and geometric and non-geometric brane configurations.

We develop a concise and efficient embedding of metrics into simple graphs, specifically minor-free graphs, which takes O(n log n) time. This substantially reduces the processing time for the embedded metric, making it suitable for practical applications. In contrast, previous methods resulted in an exponential increase in computing the embedded metric once obtained. Building upon our technique, we swiftly adapt it to find metrics embedded into specific SPANDErs, which are graphs consisting of a single cycle and K edge divisions. These SPANDErs form a crucial element in algorithms addressing key problems, such as the Baker's problems, in restricted graph types. Our algorithm incorporates this new method, resulting in a significant running time improvement of a factor specifically proportional to the number of edge divisions in the SPANDEr, leading to near-linear algorithm applications for specific graph types. Moreover, we illustrate the new method's value by leveraging it in subset and extreme problems of metric embedding, thereby reducing the computational complexity by half in comparison to previous algorithms. Finally, we extend this concept to 2-point metric embedding, leading to faster algorithms with an improved factor of specifically proportional to the number of edge divisions in the SPANDEr, or in general, the number of divisions in the graph, resulting in near-linear algorithm applications for specific graph types.

In this study, we explore the prevalence of initial conditions that lead to a specific type of convergence toward periodic solutions in time-periodic parabolic equations. Specifically, under certain hypotheses, we demonstrate that a prevalent subset of the space of initial conditions leads to a forward semigroup that reaches a periodic steady state as time approaches infinity. Additionally, our research applies this principle to a model describing the dynamics of a population with periodic-oscillating movements and varying prey turnover rates.

An improved quantum algorithm, known as QEB-ADAPT-VQE, has been developed for generating optimal ansatzes in a quantum simulation of electronic structure. This method addresses the challenge of currying favor towards certain ansatz structures by utilizing a generalized ansatz platform that combines different tensor networks, specifically fermionic and matrix product states. Compared to its fermionic and qubit counterparts, the protocol shows accelerated convergence, increased efficiency, and faster computational speed. This advancement enables the performance of high-accuracy quantum chemistry calculations on more impaired quantum processors. The effectiveness of this method is successfully demonstrated through simulations of increasingly complex molecules.

A new method, the Deep Generative Decoder, aimed at uncovering a common underlying space for a set of data, has been developed. Initially designed for unsupervised representations, our studies found that the DGD can also produce representations that distinguish between different classes when given labeled data. This observation led us to propose a supervised version of the DGD, which consistently outperformed other representation learning techniques in our experiments based on different datasets, resulting in more precise recognition of classes in the representation space.

The cosmos' current state of tension regarding the Hubble constant can potentially be resolved by introducing a stiff component with negative pressure.  Following the parameters suggested by Baudry et al in arXiv:2103.04645, we examined a cosmological model consisting of a stiff component with a pressure coefficient of -1.5, coupled with a stiff component with an energy density parameter, omega_cs.  The Hubble tension is resolved at omega_cs = 0.64 with 68% confidence.  Furthermore, a cosmological model consisting of a stiff component and phantom dark energy, able to vary in pressure, is capable of solving both the Hubble and cosmic clock tensions at a confidence level of 90%.  In particular, this model suggests a pressure parameter, omega_dp, of approximately 0.43 with 90% confidence.

Our investigation into the activity of comet C/2015 ER61 involves analyzing spectral emissions from water and volatile organic molecules. We notice that CS, H2CO, HNC, and CH3OH originate from the gas phase, whereas HCN shows both gas and solid origins, with its release rate decreasing as the distance from the nucleus decreases. CS and H2CO exhibit typical jet behavior, whereas HNC and CH3OH display more dispersed emission patterns, possibly resulting from their formation mechanisms. We aim to compare the release patterns of CS, H2CO, HNC, CH3OH, and HCN, and investigate their origins by analyzing their spatial distribution, radial emission, and correlation with water. Furthermore, we discuss our findings in relation to the activity decay of the comet.

For our speech synthesis challenge submission, we developed an unsupervised TTS system that leverages a massive amount of public domain data. For synthesis, our system relies on a single-pass, unsupervised speech modification approach with minimal optimization. Despite this, our approach achieved a relatively close naturalness score to that of our supervised system, which was extensively trained on a large labeled dataset. Furthermore, our unsupervised system's intelligibility rating surpassed that of a comparable supervised system that employed a similar speech modification technique but with a focus on articulatory reconstruction. The impressive performance of our unsupervised system can be largely attributed to the efficacy of our speech model design and the use of a prolonged, dormant stage in the speech generation process, which significantly enhanced its ability to accurately pronounce out-of-vocabulary words without the need for a pronunciation dictionary.

We thoroughly investigate the property of entropy in Tsallis HDE model by utilizing a holographic energy density formula. Several parameters such as coupling parameter, entropy radius and its fluctuations are examined and analyzed. Findings indicate that interaction between matter and HDE does not alter the constant parameter of the Tsallis HDE, but it does affect the coupling parameter in a manner dependent on said constant. Additionally, the study explores the behavior of fluctuations in HDE entropy and entropy degrees of freedom within the framework of the coarse-graining hypothesis, yielding results that validate the applicability of the Tsallis HDE model across the universe, from the early universe to its present state.

Preprocessing is a widely used method to optimize computational efficiency for machine learning models, specifically for data reduction in supervision. A persistent problem is how to effectively assess various preprocessing techniques to identify the most suitable ones. In the context of clustering, we've developed the Investment Ratio (IR) to gauge the quality of solutions obtained from different methods by measuring the return on the time and effort invested in processing the data. A comparative study of the time complexity of different techniques is conducted, along with empirical evaluations of how the IR is influenced by specific data characteristics and parameters. Additionally, we've applied IR to multiple real-world datasets to determine its representativeness in practical scenarios. Based on this analysis, we recommend using IR as a unified assessment metric to evaluate the performance of different preprocessing techniques.

In the framework of synthetic differential geometry, we introduce the notions of source path and source simply connected groupoid, leading to the construction of étale local groups. Upon adding a differential structure, these groupoids can be transformed into 2-dimensional Lie groupoids. By treating the target map of the source path groupoid with Grothendieck topology, we establish a connection to Martin-Löef's work on relative prime numbers. Moreover, we demonstrate that any source simply connected groupoid with finite source path lengths can be discretely embedded within a simply connected groupoid of dimension equal to the maximum discrete width of its source paths.

Blockchain-based archiving systems are inherently secure, but their reach is limited due to the large amounts of data they can store, to the order of Exa-Bytes. Dynaswap, a solution protecting users' data and flow by integrating Multi-Cloud Storage, PKI, and Smart Contracts, was developed to address these limitations. This paper evaluates the performance of Dynaswap by focusing on its data transmission speed, the new concept of 'data wallet' storage, its virtual machine processing speed, and the level of security achieved with its integrated components. Furthermore, Dynaswap is compared to other solutions in terms of its blockchain-based archiving system's integrity, which it has proven, demonstrating its capability of handling complex data flows with several Virtual Machines.

Recent advancements in Self-Supervised pre-training have led to improved performance in Natural Language Inference from few-shot tasks. However, expressing personal opinions in reviews often relies on context that is not directly related to the product itself. As a result, general-purpose pre-training may fail to capture sentiment based on product features. To address this, our proposed method involves a Supervised Contrastive pre-training approach that aims to dissect high-level abstract concepts from low-level product details. This allows the model to focus on opinion-giving aspects, even if they are not semantically crucial. By doing so, our approach enhances the model's capacity to capture sentiment orientation in product reviews. To further refine performance, we have also devised a novel self-supervised few-shot NLI task. This task leverages a large dataset of product reviews paired with fake opinions to enhance the model's robustness to noisy sentiment influences. When tested with this dataset, our proposed method demonstrated significant improvements across all aspects, while outperforming baseline models, including BERT and RoBERTa, by a substantial margin.

Listeriosis is a severe foodborne illness caused by the germs in the GI tract, primarily affecting individuals whose immune system isn't working properly or has imbalances. Since the 1990s, the use of medications known to reduce stomach acidity, like antacids and PPIs, have become very popular to treat conditions like ulcers. Before the widespread use of acid-reducing meds, listeriosis tended to occur earlier, but their intake is linked to a later onset of the disease. A new research aims to understand the connection between reduced stomach acidity and increased risk of listeriosis. By building a mathematical model that looks at the numbers of pathogenic bacteria, immune cells, and gastric acid production, the researchers studied how these factors interact. The model, based on white blood cells' ability to fight infections, reveals that listeriosis tends to occur at a later time when gastric acid levels are lower, supporting the findings from clinical observations. Furthermore, the researchers discovered that reducing stomach acidity doesn't always mean a stronger immune response, but rather that listeriosis occurs after the initial battle between the immune system and bacteria, allowing the bacteria to multiply and reach toxic levels before the immune system can fight back.

We address the issue of secretive multiuser communication using reconfigurable, intelligent surfaces that are affected by hardware impairments. By formulating a nonconvex problem, we develop a two-stage solution to this challenge. First, we transform the initial problem into an alternative form through a unitary transformation. Next, leveraging this transformation, we apply an inexact algorithm incorporating successive interference cancellation to find a reliable solution. Numerical results demonstrate the substantial impact that surface reconfiguration has on improving secrecy performance under hardware impairments. Moreover, it's shown that an increase in the number of reconfigurable surfaces enhances overall secrecy performance.

Recent studies on hindsight summarization have revealed its potential to forecast outcomes more accurately than initial predictions made in real-time. Furthermore, hindsight summarization might serve as an optimal learning strategy for various domains, including those not necessarily subject to delays between input and outcome measurement. In this research, we bridge the gap between continuous and discrete time frameworks using a Hamiltonian formalism and an Lagrangian method to devise an algorithm. The algorithm combines hindsight summarization with stochastic optimization, taking into consideration the process by which memories are formed and lost over time. It is successfully applied to two distinct scenarios: a simple physical system with continuous variables and a challenging natural language task under time constraints. The results show that our method achieves significant improvements in predictive accuracy and speed relative to prior approaches. Additionally, the theoretical underpinnings of our method allow for its direct extension to other backward inference techniques, including backward generative modeling and the reverse engineering of complex systems.

A study a thousand times larger in volume than our solar system was carried out to gather data on the distributions of solar energetic particles, similar to those detected at 1 AU. By employing a novel parameterization that separates the energy requirements to escape solar gravitation from other particle distributions, it was found that the energy demands at close proximities to the sun are significantly lower than those observed at 1 AU. This close proximity range also demonstrated a more stable distribution stability compared to 1 AU, while also showing a systematic variation over time. These findings are compared against theoretical models that predict energy resources, such as those driven by coronal mass ejections, and against statistical models that forecast energy demands based on given path lengths. It is proposed that the energy resource parameterization can be used more widely to compare and contrast different solar energetic particle events and their statistical behavior.
We establish that a locally trivial G-C*-algebra has a free action on a M\"obius transformation group with a finite series, which generates the group via its elements.

In our investigation, we focus on fundamental inequalities involving large cardinals, rewritten in a logarithmic form, and analyze their consistency by utilizing $P$-points. A $P$-point is an ultrafilter on a set $X$, which gives a unique consistency result when it's stated that for every family of subsets of $X$, the intersection of the family is nonempty if and only if the intersection of the positive sets is nonempty. We show that this type of filter is consistent but cannot be constructed within the standard model of ZFC. Our analysis also reveals that the consistency results for these inequalities are distinct and independent of one another. Furthermore, we prove that the existence of a $P$-point is consistent, and its occurrence can be treated as an intermediate outcome between the scenarios where $\lambda^{\lambda_{1}}=2^{\lambda_{1}}$ and $\lambda^{\lambda_{1}}<2^{\lambda_{1}}$ are true. Lastly, we discuss the fundamental question of whether the occurrence of $P$-points can be anticipated by ZFC.

Our research involves studying a hypothetical system where the tunneling effect is taken into account in a two coupled optical cavity system that also interacts with an excited photon. By applying the $q$-deformation of the Poincar\'e group, we develop a wave function for the system, and then use the $q$-deformed Wigner functions to calculate the optical protonization ($O_p$) and polarization ($O_\gamma$) of the probe field. The studies show that $O_p$ and $O_\gamma$ have two distinct peaks. Furthermore, we find that by adjusting the tunneling strength and optomechanical coupling, the position of these peaks can be shifted in the spectral distribution. Additionally, the localization of $O_p$ can be enhanced or diminished by adjusting these parameters, and both peaks can be reversed by modifying the optomechanical coupling and tunneling strength. Conversely, the localization of the polarization can be enhanced or diminished solely by adjusting the tunneling strength.

We have developed a unified framework for describing scissors modes in atomic nuclei. By combining analytical and numerical methods, we have derived a general wave function for the lowest scissors mode in rare-earth nuclei, revealing a clear separation between positive and negative R-states. Our investigation also shows that R-negative states exhibit significantly stronger electromagnetic transition properties than R-positive ones. Utilizing the constructed wave functions, we have employed the collective model to describe photodoubleon experiments in even-even and odd-even isotopes within the $^{108-124}$C system. Our predictions display good agreement with empirical data. Moreover, our study covers a broad range of transitions involving the scissor mode and many-player collective excitations. We have further examined the impact of fragmentation in nuclear transitions caused by competing peaks other than the main scissor mode. By comparing our results to measurements of the differential radiated power $d^2P/d\mathrm{dE}/c$ in future experiments, we aim to achieve a more comprehensive and accurate understanding of these collective excitations.

This research explores the performance of neural networks in solving a specific type of hyperbolic differential equation with the ability to handle large fluctuations in data across various fields including astronomy, astrophysics, and meteorology. We test the resolution capabilities of central difference numerical schemes and neural network methods on a model equation known to generate intricate solution behaviors such as contact discontinuities and shock waves. We evaluate their performance by analyzing the characteristics of the resulting numerical solutions including contact thickness, error measurements, and the production of shock waves. The study reveals that despite expected similarities, there are notable differences in how these two methods perform. We find that in the absence of noise, the central difference method accurately captures shock waves, whereas the neural network method tends to smooth out shock waves. However, this smoothing effect is diminished when noise is present, and the neural network method consistently shows a stronger ability to resolve contact discontinuities compared to the central difference method. We also find that an increase in the size of the time step in the central difference method and the training data volume in the neural network perturbs the contact thickness in both methods. Despite this, the neural network method maintains a level of resolution capabilities far beyond that of classical numerical schemes and well beyond the limits that would ensure the preservation of shock waves.

The Longshore 3 ($\ell$3) experiment plans to deploy a state-of-the-art, high-intensity laser facility located at Brookhaven National Laboratory, aiming to conduct cutting-edge research on gluon behavior at rarely measured early stages of proton development. To significantly expand its research potential, we are developing two substantial upgrades for the $\ell$3 experiment. Firstly, we are introducing a highly sensitive, multi-layer ionization detector system for thorough event characterization, including enhanced spatial and temporal resolution, and precise timing capabilities. This advanced detector is expected to greatly improve the experiment's efficiency across its entire range. Secondly, we are introducing a cutting-edge, radiofrequency-based leak current monitor for precise and real-time gas flow control, and pressure safety checks, ensuring the smooth operation of the experiment. To ensure the smooth integration of these new components, we are conducting thorough comprehensive upgrades of the experiment's control systems, including the development of customized software. To achieve this, we are leveraging a cutting-edge, containerized infrastructure, which provides robust, long-term stability and flexibility in experiment operation.

We suggest using a time-varying QCD $\Lambda$-system for observing the timelike Unruh effect and rapidly accelerating particles. The novel, time-dependent relation between the CMW gauge and the spatial A gluon field may enable direct detection of the timelike Unruh effect with low acceleration and temperatures. Furthermore, we took into account the influence of a timelike Unruh mode's large negative energy density in a vacuum and produced a unified description of the timelike Unruh effect across all its aspects.

This study presents a technique to generate semi-markup events for non-English texts without any prior annotation, a necessity due to the scarcity of labeled data in languages other than English. Unlike English, for which Event Extraction is established, other languages face significant data limitations. They also often have different termings and grammatical structures, making things worse. We address these challenges with a innovative approach that semi-marks up texts into base events and related entities. This method leverages unlabelled texts, helping to overcome data limitations. Additionally, we establish criteria to assess event validation quality and show that our technique produces better results with validated events, surpassing even heavy manual supervision. Finally, we apply this technique in two real-world scenarios: zero-shot Event Extraction and cross-lingual Event Extraction, achieving top-notch performance. Crucially, most other methods rely on labelled data, but our technique achieves such impressive performance without any, including in English, under a zero-shot setting that mimics a typical production environment.

In a positive characteristic field, we establish a formalism for analyzing polynomial expressions involving Chern forms, ensuring their positivity. Our results, specifically for degrees 2 and 3, align with Griffiths' original conjecture regarding positive characteristic forms. These findings have real-world applications, enabling the computation of Chern forms from a projective variety's Riemann-Roch theorem. Furthermore, we leverage this tool to investigate Griffiths' conjecture, building upon a theoretical foundation established by Petrov, with significant implications for varieties in a particular Hilbert scheme.

Using the La Cornetta team's multi-band X-ray monitoring of NVe07b, a 14.1-s orbit high-mass X-ray binary system, we studied the evolution of fractional rms variability with energy. Our 7-year follow-up observations with the Arcus monitor revealed significant changes in soft and hard band light curves around 2013 and 2016, related to different states of the system. Our analysis suggests that the hard state enjoys more independence between energy bands due to reduced post-ejectile cloud coherence. Notably, in the 2016 soft state, heavy ejectile clouds cause interference between soft and hard band measurements, resulting in a lower hard band fractional rms compared to the hard state. Our findings also indicate that heavy ejectile clouds have a mitigating effect on measured hard band fractional rms, leading to underestimation of the hard band fractional rms if post-ejectile clouds are not considered. Our study sheds new light on variability properties of high-mass X-ray binary systems during their bright states.

A nonabelian version of the Weinberg-Quiros boundary condition is explored, leading to the formation of a nonabelian "aether" term at boundary vertices. This term influences radiation and induces a temperature-dependent Casimir energy and boundary Casimir pressure. Furthermore, the boundary condition gives rise to nonabelian and abelian gauge field configurations with non-zero boundary curvature. These insights are gaining significance in the context of early universe research, particularly when examining symmetry-breaking phenomena prior to cosmic inflation.

Our proposed model uses neural networks to analyze sentence structure and meaning simultaneously, and when trained on English data, it replicates patterns seen in other languages when analyzing those languages. This joint model uses a shared semantic space to capture concepts common to multiple languages, and we find that the shared space is similar across languages for concepts that have equivalent meanings. Furthermore, the model's ability to recognize semantic relationships between words is consistent across languages, and we highlight this by identifying analogous semantic pairs that are distinct from translation pairs. Additionally, the model's analysis of analogies such as "the_X of the_y is a/z_" reveals that the inferred representations form natural groups, and these groups correspond to parts of speech.

Radioactively driven astrophysical transients include events such as Fast Rising Evolutionary Transients along with Nova-like Phenomena generated by Binary Compact Object Mergers. Currently, researchers are only able to observe the brightest approximately 10,000 events of this type in the nearby universe with current technology. Employing the top-tier multi-color imaging system of the VLT Survey Telescope and the most comprehensive photometric database ever compiled across the entire visible spectrum, the study significantly expands its ability to detect these events by capturing a much broader range than previously possible. With its improved detection capabilities, the study identifies over 200 new sources for the first time and nearly doubles the previously known total count of approximately 100 such events. Analyzing the new data set reveals that these events exhibit luminosity levels anywhere from a few tens of solar luminosities up to $10^{10}$ solar luminosities, and last for time periods ranging from days to over a year in duration. Their speeds relative to nearby star fields vary greatly, and their infrared radiation capability appears to be significantly more extensive than previously thought with rates reaching up to 20 times more INOVAs generated by binary compact object mergers, and fast-evolving luminous agglomerations 9 times higher. Furthermore, the study discovers relationships between these transients and supernovae 1998bw-like events, and finds evidence of a pattern similar to what is seen with gamma ray bursts and their corresponding after effects in the distribution of their

This study examines the spatial distribution of dark and bright tidal features within the outer regions of 97 early-type galaxies, using a comprehensive dataset of 63 galaxies undergoing galactic mergers and 34 non-interacting galaxies. These tidal features are derived from DESPHOT deprojected images and the Gaia photometric data. The analysis focuses on tidal features with a brightness that is 4 magnitudes lower than the galaxy's halo to balance light and gravity. It shows that a consistent pattern exists across all galaxies, with tidal features consistently positioned at a specific radius. However, this pattern breaks down in galaxies with tidal features located internally, being offset both towards the galaxy's center and away from it. The research also finds that tidal features in more massive galaxies cover a higher percentage of the galaxy's surface. Furthermore, galaxies with tidal features have a significantly higher overall brightness and a more extended halo compared to non-interacting galaxies. Importantly, galaxies with tidal features held 3 times stronger gravity than those without, and those with tidal features have their stars moving at lower velocities. The research demonstrates that tidal features influence galaxies' movement, and the galaxies with tidal features tend to experience more friction than those without, resulting in the loss of their kinetic energy. The findings imply that tidal features play a crucial role in the development of galaxies' outer regions.

The Radiation Problem will be avoided in a developing star through an auto-regulating process that slows to a stop its conventional material contraction.  An alternative, more straightforward approach to tackling the Radiation Problem is offered by the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation.  This theory proposes a gravitational system unaffected by radiation pressure that accommodates the formation of massive stars.  To achieve this, it employs a unique gravitational component with an irregular motion that can cancel out a developing star's contraction when sufficient energy is available.  As a result, the feasible mass range for the stars is expanded to include those up to 100 solar masses, based on an estimate of the energy required for star formation and an analysis of the rate of energy release.  Furthermore, the theory offers an explanation for dark matter as a collection of these star systems, which can exist in a stable equilibrium state.

The investigation of simultaneous multi-color observations for fast radio bursts is crucial in understanding the precise nature of their emission processes, which current observations cannot constrain effectively due to the lack of sufficient data. Our research involved carrying out extensive, simultaneous multi-color observations for an FRB with a repeating pattern, yielding a significant dataset of >110 repeats, 35 observations, and a total of >380 f-modes. These observations covered a broad spectral and temporal ranges, with the assistance of an automated system identifying individual f-modes in vast amounts of data. As a result, we obtained a substantial advancement in our understanding of FRB 20210907A, including its spectral and temporal behavior. Our research provided over 110 repeat observations, facilitating the analysis of up to 32 simultaneous observations, spanning various frequencies and durations. With the aid of a highly accurate and automated detection algorithm for f-modes, we generated constraints on the emission properties, such as the light travel time for repeated bursts and the spatial coherence of its emission. Moreover, we developed new methods to analyze multi-color data, including a Bayesian model for concordance among different frequency spectra, used the polarization properties to identify the emission location, and analyzed the spatial distribution of repeating FRBs. The constraints on the emission models were also obtained by analyzing the data from multiple frequencies. The findings from our research still left several aspects of FRB 20210907A uncertain, such as its distance, location of its emission, and the exact nature of

Due to the numerous optical components found in high-level laser systems, it's challenging to achieve precise accuracy in modeling these systems using traditional methods. In this study, the reliance of higher-order photons in CPA and NLO-based laser systems makes it particularly hard to achieve accurate modeling using lower-order approximations. As a result, we utilize a frequency-resolved nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation to model the interaction of second-harmonic generation in a nonlinear crystal, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the process and its accurate simulation with a Fourier-Chebyshev method.

VisualMagick is a context-aware image-capting model based on the MAGIC framework. It combines an encoder-decoder architecture, including an Cross Attention mechanism, with a memory bank component storing image features and corresponding word features. At each step, the MAGIC model selects relevant image features and integrates them into its internal memory, updating its representation and producing a word output. This process is repeated until a stop criterion is reached, resulting in a full sentence generation. Since the MAGIC model can access the entire image during the generation process, it also uses a teacher forcing module to ensure that the generated text remains coherent by choosing relevant words in relation to the image and the context. Additionally, the model incorporates a convergence module for early termination of the generation process and convergence to a fixed sentence length.

We introduce Delegated RingCT, a novel protocol that efficiently combines the Delegated Proof of Stake consensus mechanism with Ring Signature technology to facilitate confidential transactions in a decentralized setting. Delegated RingCT adopts a multi-round signature approach, significantly improving the speed and scalability of transactions. The innovative use of round signatures and public key delegating results in enhanced privacy, compute efficiency, and reduced transaction fees. Furthermore, Delegated RingCT ensures the validity of its transactions through a Delegated Proof of Stake consensus mechanism, while its ring signature component provides theoretical resistance to various attacks. Nevertheless, we also identify a novel attack that compromises the confidentiality of transactions under certain conditions. Subsequently, we present two possible solutions to counter this vulnerability. The first solution involves discontinuing the use of confidential transactions, and the second proposes an innovative attack detection method that utilizes control points to block suspected transactions. To validate the effectiveness of Delegated RingCT, we conducted a performance comparison with different RingCT variations, revealing its superior efficiency. We also demonstrated the feasibility of integrating Delegated RingCT with the Pontic cryptocurrency, which employs a Delegated Proof of Stake consensus mechanism.

Closed orbit oscillation data collected at the LHC during 2017 reveals a precision measurable phenomenon where a perpendicular radial beam position discrepancy, approximately 0.4 microns, develops between opposing beams over a period of a few days, accompanied by an observable effect on luminosity and other measurable symptoms. Notably, this phenomenon not only affects proton beams but seems to spare electron beams, suggesting a need to reassess a previously proposed explanation that linked this anomaly to beam cooling techniques. Investigations involving LHC operators and based on over 100,000 individual beam measurements suggest other possible sources, such as electromagnetic forces, to be responsible for this occurrence known as "soliton-like" discrepancy.

To adapt various materials' plasticity behavior, which change over time and rely on past events, researchers have developed complex phenomenological models. These models, which describe complex relationships with many variables, are often difficult to use because they require a lot of data and cannot be used by traditional methods that learn from data. Because these models so far only work for a single material, researchers have had to retrain the model, which becomes very slow and inefficient as the model gets more complex, when they want to analyze a new material. Researchers have now used a new approach, called meta-learning, to create a more efficient way that doesn't need as many data points. They developed a type of model, called a neural network, that can learn about the various materials' properties by seeing a few examples from each one. This allows them to create a general model for a new material just by showing it a few examples, which takes much less time and is more efficient. This new approach also helps to reduce the size of the model, making it easier to use.

The application of \v{C}erenkov detection in experimental searches for rare hadron decays has proven recently to be an emerging trend with notable consequences. Notably, experiments have utilized this method in searching for decays of heavy mesons, which if identified, could provide valuable insights to reconstruct the excitation spectrum of quark-antiquark pairs. This paper presents a theoretical evaluation of the effects of two rare processes: the electroweak interaction of a bottomonium meson and the radiative transition of a double charmonium state. Our analysis exploits the $B\to{}X_{{\rm{B}}}{\rm{\bar}}{}{\rm{H}}$ reaction using the relativistic quark model and considers two types of $B$-meson decays. The first involves the ${{\rm B}}\to{}{{\rm J}/\psi{}{\rm{\pi}}^0{}_{\rm{l}}}$
decay, which if combined with a recent experiment reporting a ${{\rm J}/\psi{}{\rm{\pi}}^0{}_{\rm{l}}}$ mass peak at 4.26 GeV, suggests that the $\varepsilon(10753)$ may fit within the conventional bottomonium spectrum as the $2S$ state. The second considered $B$-meson decay is $B\to{}X_{{\rm{B}}}{\rm{}{\rm

A new approach to training neural networks that use quantized weights has been developed, different from the existing techniques that either don't account for quantization during the training process or rely on incremental adjustments after training. The new technique, called AskewSGD, treats quantization constraints as an optimization problem and has been successfully tested with a variety of optimizers. The results show that AskewSGD can achieve comparable or even better results than the standard approach, accompanied by significant reductions in memory usage and energy consumption. The effectiveness of AskewSGD was demonstrated across a range of deep learning tasks and hardware platforms, with the open-source code made available for public use.

The development of soft robots using continuous materials like rubber and fiber has gained attention due to their innate ability to absorb external shocks and adapt to their surroundings. To further the understanding and improvement of these robots through learning from biology, this research focuses on designing and testing continuum robots with appendages similar to those found in invertebrate and vertebrate animals. A robotic system featuring two flexible arms attached to a semi-spherical head with moving segments is developed to mimic the general structure of an invertebrate's head with appendages. To achieve precise control and movement, this research employs a robust approach combining motion planning algorithms for navigating around obstacles and implementing a dynamic model specific to these robots. Additionally, this research adapts a control approach originally designed for fully flexible robots to its new dynamic model. To test the robotic system's performance, this research sets up scenarios that mimic real-world conditions such as complex path following in tight spaces and obstacle avoidance at various speeds. To ensure safety, this research also simulated human-robot collisions and demonstrated the increased robustness of the proposed control approach. A more complex application of this robotic system is explored by developing an innovative food-gathering algorithm inspired by invertebrate's method of grabbing objects by bending their bodies to successfully collect artifacts placed on elevated surfaces, within reach of the robot's anatomy.

The Jacobi group combines with the Siegel-Jacobi upper half-plane to create a unique left-invariant metric, related to a specific Kähler metric. We compare this unique metric with its lower-bound limit, revealing a perfect match.
