a singular scalar plays a pivotal role in both the formation of dark matter and its interaction with heavy neutrinos. 
Although the dark matter particle is typically introduced as a $T$-odd scalar, its $T$-even counterpart is critical in facilitating its interaction 
with right-handed neutrinos, which is essential for its function as a dark matter candidate. 
This $T$-odd scalar's properties are often fixed by considering the relic density, but its $T$-odd counterpart's properties inevitably affect its relic density 
and thus impact its functionality as a dark matter candidate. 
This $T$-odd scalar's properties can be crucial in describing the formation of dark matter through $T$-odd scalar exchange and also influence its interaction with heavy neutrinos. 
These $T$-odd scalars can modify or complement the interaction between dark matter and heavy neutrinos, which is typically considered minimal. 
Although a $T$-odd scalar that facilitates the interaction between dark matter and heavy neutrinos may increase the momentum available to these particles from dark matter, 
a $T$-odd scalar in the scalar sector can also generate this momentum. 
These models, which feature a non-minimal extension of the Standard Model (SMS) in the scalar sector, are evaluated in terms of the thermal production of dark matter 
in two distinct scenarios: a model with a single

Using advanced learning techniques to develop optimal control strategies can be
very time-consuming due to the need for extensive data collection and computing resources. This research focuses on shortening the data collection time by utilizing simulation. A neural network is used to represent the dynamics of the system and initial parameters are established through experience. Then, a large-scale reinforcement learning algorithm is employed to refine the parameters using real-time data collection. A robust control algorithm is also introduced to tackle data imperfections. This method significantly reduces the data collection time by utilizing pre-simulated data and tackling data issues offline. Several case studies were conducted to test the approach's effectiveness, utilizing a multi-rotor system for validation. Experimental results show that the approach can learn optimal control strategies quickly, especially in scenarios with limited real-time data availability.

A careful examination of free four-dimensional higher-spin (HS) theories under an SU(4)_R symmetry has led to the identification of spin-three Ward identities that encapsulate HS symmetry. This identification has also revealed an underlying SU(4)_R invariant structure within HS kinematics. As HS theories in question are thought to encompass Toda conformal field theories (CFTs), the derived spin-three Ward identities have been used to expand existing HS Ward identities while including the generators of the underlying SU(4) flavor symmetry. A key discovery was that, for a general rank of the HS algebra, local (HS) local (SU(4) flavor) bilinears cannot be represented by the free HS action. However, this incompatibility was found to arise solely from the HS nature of the system and is not a characteristic of HS models derived from HS-Vasiliev theory applications to Toda CFTs. Furthermore, the derived spin-three Ward identities have been used to expand a previous key finding of Mincher and Pufu that demonstrates an (HS) local (SU(4) flavor) 4-tensor can be consistently consistently coupled to an HS field without resorting to non-local solutions. This study has significant implications for HS models derived from HS-Vasiliev theory applications to Toda CFTs and may also provide insight into the yet-to-be-resolved problem of mass depletions in Toda CFTs.

Recent years have seen the emergence of various Group Variable-BliSteer GANs (GBGANs) for efficient training of high-quality images. A novel architecture was introduced in the BGGAN-B1 model by extending the B1 architecture of the official Style-Based Diffusion Model (SBDM) and adding a relation network to the encoder, which improves the latent space. This improved latent space (LS) has better information transfer and enhanced interdependence. To capitalize on this, our work utilizes a relation network integrated with the SBDM's encoder to produce a refined latent space (RLS). This integrated relation network utilizes the multiple intermediate features from the SBDM's normalizing flow transformations to build a comprehensive image understanding. A latent space refinement mechanism is developed to further fine-tune the RLS. Two groups of learned latent codes are employed to build a comparative latent space (CLS) for the SBDM, thereby enhancing the diversity of the latent space. This integration led to the creation of the learned latent code diffusion model for the SBDM, which produces higher quality and has better training stability compared to the BGGAN-B1. Extensive experiments were conducted to verify the superiority of our model over BGGAN-B1.

A revised twin-field quantum key distribution approach leverages reference frames rather than fixed reference frames to establish a global phase reference, enabling all parties involved to, in effect, share a "watch that syncs with the correct time". Using the global phase reference, global unitary transformations can be applied to implement eavesdropping-detecting filters without needing individual devices. Our study shows that by equipping each link in the distribution chain with just three components - a global phase reference, a mirror, and a beam splitter - these links can, in fact, block all known forms of unauthorised access. Additionally, we demonstrate how the global phase reference can also serve as a form of "broadcast clock' that facilitates the distribution of quantum-based time signalling protocols.

This paper generalizes the research of Sun and Wu to partially complete p-Bergman and p-Fock spaces, with specific cases including the spaces of Schubert spaces and spaces of homogeneous polynomials of degree p. It introduces classes of Toeplitz operators that act on these spaces and shows their connection to classes of symbols. Furthermore, it develops a symbol calculus for these operators, with applications in recovering symbols from their inverses, as well as a multipliers theorem.

Recently, pseudo labeling techniques have contributed significantly to the advancement of object detection. This method, in particular, can be an affordable option for clients using Microsoft Detekt to run object detection algorithms without requiring extensive training data. Our research introduces a novel pseudo labeling method called Top Down Pseudo Labeling (TDPL) to enhance object detection performance. The proposed TDPL framework focuses on two essential aspects: accurately predicting bounding box annotations and refining top-down classification and localization abilities simultaneously. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of TDPL, leading to improved performance on COCO object categories. By applying TDPL, detectors achieved higher accuracy, with some improvements ranging from 2 to 5% after multiple iterations. This method can be applied universally to various object detectors.

Our research focuses on OIII emission observed towards G-type stars, identifying a relationship with their far-UV continuum but also an unexpected self-absorption effect for both neutral and ionized gas in the immediate surroundings. These findings are based on an analysis of IUE data for 30 nearby stars within 50-100 pc of Earth. The OIII emission and continuum are generated by chromospheric plasma, while gas within a few thousand km of the stars absorbs certain wavelengths. The apparent increase in OIII emission with increasing continuum intensity can be explained by the demonstrated self-absorption effect, which aligns with theoretical models of stellar atmospheres. The implied gas-to-dust ratio is consistent with expectations, but our results for the OIII absorption edge suggest that gas extends to higher velocities than currently estimated and that the neutral wind of the stars may also carry some ions. The model of the extended stellar atmosphere, developed using macroscopic models, is found to handle various observed features, including the OIII emission and the far-UV absorption, but a detailed comparison with the complex observations of the hot coronal regions and their shear motions remains a subject for future research.

Transformers have thus far been largely restricted to use within sequence-based models. This limitation arises from the slow absolute complexity of Transformer operations, which is dictated by the length of the sequence ($O(L)$). This paper demonstrates that by incorporating a new type of global attention known as Bounded Attention, alongside a compact formulation of the Transformer, complex two-dimensional scenes can be effectively processed using a model that incorporates a single layer based on the BERT architecture. In contrast to conventional models, our approach incorporates a single processing element that is scalable with input size ($O(\sqrt{L})$) and a fixed overhead independent of input size and image resolution. When compared to cutting-edge computer vision architectures, our approach achieves comparable performance within a fraction of the computational footprint, as exemplified by state-of-the-art performance on the ImageNet dataset within ImageNet Link, as well as comparable performance within a fraction of the computational footprint and a fixed overhead with networks like ViLT and BigTransfer-1001. We have made the source code and pre-trained models for our approach publicly available at the GitHub link.

The Bayesian Network model is a widely used tool for enhancing mortality forecasting. The model's key advantage is its ability to identify patterns in mortality trends across different regions by retaining the underlying risk factor structure. The traditional Bayesian Network framework assumes static relationships between risk factors and mortality rates, limiting its ability to capture complex trends. To improve mortality forecasting, we develop a new Bayesian Network framework that incorporates time-varying factor loadings. The update acceleration technique and the shrinkage priors for random effects are combined with a diagonal Gaussian covariance matrix, yielding an efficient algorithm. The proposed method demonstrates improved ability to capture underlying patterns in mortality data, and performance tests on simulated and historical data reveals better fit, more accurate one-step and multi-step forecasts, and tighter prediction intervals. The method is successfully applied to US men and women, as well as Spanish males, yielding highly accurate results and supportive model diagnostics.

The newly emerged field of neural architecture search (NAS) has yielded
impressive results similar to deep reinforcement learning but poses a
considerable challenge for efficient and scalable language-based structure
prediction, largely because current NAS models are non-parametric and lack
language understanding. We propose an NAS model that utilizes the CoCoLoT
framework, incorporating the CoCoLoT transformer with a parameter-
sharing mechanism. We further develop two strategies, one adapting the
GPT2 trick and the other incorporating a generator, to constrain our model
and facilitate efficient NAS. We evaluated our model against RoBERTa and
ELECTRA models on the CIFAR10 dataset and the NAS-Bench-301 benchmark,
achieving an average 0.32 and 0.18 higher accuracy, respectively, with our
model also demonstrating significantly fewer parameters and training epochs.
We have publicly released our code at the link below.

Time-series analysis is a critical component of several AI-driven monitoring solutions, as well as the foundation upon which most deep learning models for time-series forecasting are built. Despite being essential, a prominent and unified entry point for building such models is missing. The open-source package "theft' - a Python library for extracting relevant time-series features, aims to fill this gap by providing a comprehensive framework for the time-series community. This package offers a wide range of algorithms adaptable to various time-series data types. It ensures seamless integration with widely-used time-series data structures like Datadog's Mottron and Lightrun's LightDB, as well as popular deep learning frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow. By offering a vast library of popular time-series feature extraction techniques, 'theft' helps users tackle common time-series analysis challenges, eliminates the need for manual feature engineering, and simplifies the transition to deep learning-based time-series modeling.

We demonstrate that in a complete CAT(0) space, if the fundamental group has a bijective isometry, then the property of geodesic completeness is equivalent to the finiteness property of the translation length spectrum.

A crucial element in machine translation, translation quality assessment, involves evaluating the performance of both MT systems and human reviewers. To gauge the performance of MT systems, an automated metric is employed. However, the evaluation of human reviewers necessitates a more intricate approach. A comprehensive evaluation framework has been developed to assess reviewer performance, considering factors like reliability, reliability of standards, and correlation with an MT evaluation metric. Additionally, a subset of the framework focused on reliability has been employed in an MT post-editing task. Nevertheless, the entire evaluation framework has been utilized in studies involving automatic MT evaluation. In this study, we aim to examine the outcomes of using the evaluation framework in an MT post-editing setting, and we are presenting the results of an online experiment designed specifically for that purpose.

The connection between the system's eigenchannels and the wave patterns within, as described by the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, is well established but the original work lies in establishing a relationship between the eigenchannels and the intensity patterns, as well as their corresponding propagation channels, all of which are derived from solving the equation. This relationship enables us to construct these eigenchannels and intensity patterns in the paraxial limit using a modified Levinson diagram, a technique that normally handles linear systems. We apply this linearization by transforming the nonlinear equation into a linear one that incorporates a memory effect, and then use a frequency-domain approach to obtain a transfer function that describes the system's response. Using this transfer function, we can determine the eigenvalues, eigenchannels, and intensity patterns, and our findings are confirmed through numerical simulations of a nonlinear waveguide with a GaAs material. It is worth noting that these findings extend to solitons as they can be obtained from the eigenchannels in a non-localised regime.

Deep neural network architectures have recently demonstrated impressive performance on complex visual tasks, yet they are often hindered by limitations in computational resources at inference time due to their large size and computational requirements. The ability to efficiently deploy such models on resource-constrained devices is essential, particularly in applications requiring real-time processing. The question remains whether current pruning techniques effectively reduce model dimensions and computational costs. This study investigates the effect of iterative magnitude pruning on a variety of benchmark datasets, and finds that it consistently yields a significant reduction in model size and inference time without a corresponding improvement in performance. The results suggest that prior studies may have overstated the effectiveness of pruning in enhancing model performance. Building upon this finding, we propose a novel approach to dynamic neural network inference, and demonstrate its potential benefits by comparing it to existing state-of-the-art compression methods.

The growing concern for the environmental impact of modern technology has led to the proposal of an innovative energy source - data center drifting. The core idea is to utilize idle data centers that aren't in use due to a lack of power demand, and couple them with ships that travel the world traversing various sea routes. The data centers would be powered by the ship navigating through these routes and cycling back into the data network to facilitate computational tasks such as scientific calculations and data analysis. Notably, a ship traveling the North Pole could generate enough energy to run a data center producing 10^13 FLOPS and supporting 10,000 tasks per second with a task latency of 100 microseconds or less. Comparing this to the computational power of supercomputers and servers shows the potential of data center drifting. The process is also compared to data center free-rider, a method where a ship doesn't need to purchase fuel once it reaches a certain speed, and the energy saved can be used to power a data center. The difference in energy efficiency between the two methods, with data center drifting yielding 3-6 times more efficiency, is discussed along with the potential applications for scientific research and data analysis. The various routes that a ship can travel, such as the North Pole, around Africa, and around South America, are examined to demonstrate the versatility of data center drifting. The method is also compared to other methods such as data center sailing and cryptocurrency sailing. The potential challenges for implementing data center drifting

The presence of elastic and lattice distortion disturbance has significant effects on valley Hall transport. A valley Hall device functioning based on a valley selective barrier, in close proximity to a nonuniformly deformed area, effectively transforms an in-plane electric field into a Hall electric field component. This phenomenon is explained as a result of a valley Hall current being redirected by a barrier and further realigned by a Berry phase associated with curvature in momentum space. Constructing a valley Hall device incorporating a quantum point contact and a modulation doped layer, and positioning it near a distortion pattern, in fact extracts an in-plane electric field component, quantifies as $\sim0.6$ nV/μm. Additionally, valley Hall conductivity exhibits a non-linear response to in-plane electric fields with a proportionality constant of $\sim 3.5 \cdot 10^{-3}$ V/μm. This valley Hall conductivity measurement offers a new criterion for evaluating strain effects and triggers new research opportunities for controlling current flow and electric field directions at the nanometer scale.

Recent studies on domain adaptation have employed graph-based approaches to create domain-independent proximity graphs. These graphs, defined by pairwise domain-specific distances, facilitate domain-adaptive models. However, previously proposed methods relied heavily on time-consuming iterations to converge, leading to inconsistent performance. To address this issue, we propose the Model Soup scheme, allowing for a single, effective calculation. Model Soup consists of a database of pre-trained models for each source domain, each initialized with distinct starting points. During training, the models in the database are temporarily refined, incorporating domain-specific knowledge. The learned representation can then be used for a common task, and the process can be repeated to improve performance. When applied to adaptive clustering, the Model Soup scheme offers a novel, time-efficient method for producing consistent proximity graphs. The model itself is obtained by training a neural network to minimize the distance between model representations within the database, while maintaining performance on a general task. Experiments show that Model Soup outperforms previous methods, providing consistent generalization performance across diverse datasets. Moreover, Model Soup's performance improves significantly with an increased number of model iterations, thanks to its capacity to reduce variance and capture domain-specific knowledge. The code for Model Soup will be publicly available.

In recent years, various techniques have been employed to analyze and visualize massive spherical data sets generated by cutting-edge instruments.  Despite our understanding of Gaussian distributions being more comprehensive than those related to spherical data, techniques such as t-SNE still rely on Gaussian models for embedding. Our innovation involves modifying the underlying distribution model in t-SNE specifically for spherical data. This involves using a Zipf's supercontinuous superposition of point processes to model local data density instead of a Gaussian distribution, which results in better preservation of the dataset's spherical structure and more accurately capturing relationships among nearest neighbors. This concept is realized in sSNE, a spherical adaptation of t-SNE. Our results illustrate that sSNE effectively highlights the dataset's inherent spherical structure, particularly within spherical molecular datasets, and that its visualizations are both aesthetically pleasing and more accurate in capturing statistical properties of the data. Furthermore, the principle of using non-Gaussian distributions for embedding has been applied to visualizing two dimensions of MRI scans of the human brain from the NeuronJ 3D viewer with promising results.

The total polaron Z factor, calculated using a full series of diagrams, is compared to the one-particle-hole approximation, showing significant disagreement at high interaction strengths ($u>0.2$), which increases with the interaction strength. When considering only semi-simple types of diagrams in the full series, the discrepancy with the one-particle-hole result is reduced but the two still show distinct differences at high interaction strengths ($u>0.6$). There is an effective approximation method, which adds the double polaron contribution to the one-particle-hole approximation in a way that reduces the discrepancy with the full series results at high interaction strengths ($u>0.7$).

The Fermi-Hubbard model, a complex quantum system of interacting fermions on a lattice, poses a significant challenge for numerical simulations. However, researchers have developed a new approach using digital-analog quantum computing that can now efficiently simulate this model. The quantum Monte Carlo algorithm employs a digital-analog quantum computer to sample from a deterministically prepared quantum state, allowing for the calculation of physical properties based on the state's overlap with the Hamiltonian. The research presents the first implementation of the digital-analog quantum Monte Carlo algorithm, applying it to a 28-qubit IBM quantum processor to calculate the expectation value of the Hamiltonian for a 4-site Hubbard model with varying parameters. The study also discusses the potential for using this algorithm in analog quantum computers once true quantum supremacy is achieved.

A specific type of polynomial, known as a matching polynomial, expresses the count of a specific type of subgraph called a 1-factor in a given graph G, that is, the count of all its complete subgraphs of size |V(G)/2| for even-sized graphs. When it comes to graphs with an odd number of vertices, a different variant of the matching polynomial, called the odd matching polynomial, takes its place. In this study, we investigate the determination of graphs whose matching and odd matching polynomials are complete graphs and bipartite graphs.

Cohomology classes associated with mapping class groups can be linked to stable form representations that satisfy a positive Kirby-Carriek condition. We reveal that some of these classes have a connection to the actions of mapping class groups on Bauer's space of ordered ideal boundary geometric surfaces, particularly its subgroups. By establishing a relation with cusp shapes, we provide a reinterpretation of a projective generator in the 3-dimensional projective space of topological polyhedra. Our work also yields cohomology classes associated with the orbifold projective space resulting from gluing copies of one-sided surfaces along their boundaries. We further propose that a projective version of a certain mod 5 cohomology class associated with cusp shapes has its origin in the cusp shapes of hyperbolic 3-manifolds.

Our investigation involves recreating the Scrum Agile framework to determine its effect on the project's success when team members are working remotely. To do this, we'll be utilizing a systematic approach, beginning with a literature review to establish a framework for our quantitative analysis. We'll apply this framework to gather and analyze data from three distinct groups: those using Scrum Agile methodologies, those using Scrumbut, and those employing traditional methods. The project will culminate in a comparative assessment of the three approaches based on our findings.

This paper verifies that all arrowhead matrices are unitarily equivalent to a specific form. The study also determines the Gau--Wu number for the class of all arrowhead matrices and identifies a minimal representative matrix in this class. Additionally, it calculates the axial isometry invariants for this class and establishes a specific form in which all arrowhead matrices are equivalently represented under unitary transformations.

Measurements of long-distance quantum fluctuations between beauty and charm hadrons, as well as background particles, have been conducted using the LHCb detector's data from proton-proton collisions. By analyzing the decay length differences between the J/psi and B hadrons, the study found a significant signal in the beauty particle sample, with an average proper decay length that is substantially greater than for charm particles and other background sources. The observed strength of this effect is consistent with theoretical predictions. The analysis was then used to constrain the underlying parameters of a model that predicts charm and beauty particle production in a quantum state.

Our analysis delves into the topological arrangement of color groups within a spatial context, which can be achieved by applying a concept known as persistent homology to a specific metric space. The approach involves creating a simplified representation of the color distribution by combining adjacent colors with each other, resulting in a sequence of simplified forms that captures the overall pattern. The application of persistent homology allows for a quantitative examination of the spatial patterning and the size of the voids created between color groups, but does not provide a comprehensive picture of the individual voids themselves. We have developed a methodological framework that enables the extraction and topological analysis of the largest voids created by the separation of colors in a given area for any number of colors used. The integration of our approach with existing algorithms for computing homology offers an efficient solution for the color configuration problem. Our work focuses on the special case of planar color patterns, which can result in the creation of holes with more complex properties, requiring further advanced analysis and computation for their examination.

In vast interference networks, numerous control strategies are proposed to manage power transmission. Among these, optimal power control, which adjusts power according to the reciprocal of the Euclidean distance to interfering nodes, is an optimal yet impractical solution due to its dependence on channel state information. Following optimal power control, various other power control strategies have been proposed, including binary power control, which sets power to a high value or zero, and fractional power control, which adjusts power based on the fractional coefficient of the Euclidean distance. Previous research has shown the benefits of binary power control in large interference networks. We now aim to explore whether binary power control can function as an optimal control method, similar to its more optimal yet less practical counterpart. We employ tools such as degrees, geometric structures, and combinatorial methods to illustrate that binary power control operates within a localized geometric framework. We also apply techniques such as random sampling, cutting planes, and linear programming to prove that binary power control indeed constitutes the optimal control method in large interference networks. We further demonstrate that binary power control achieves similar levels of interference leakage across all interference links, a characteristic we label as homogeneous interference leakage, which forms the basis for its geometric structure. We show that binary power control's efficiency can be calculated using the metrics of union balls, overlap geometric structures, and minimum dominating sets.

Dempster-Shafer theory can model uncertainty through belief functions, making it suitable for complex belief models that represent the intersection of multiple interests in financial accounts during auditing. Each auditor holds certain beliefs about account interactions based on auditing standards, which can be represented as Dempster-Shafer mass functions. In cases of uncertain beliefs, discrepancies are accounted for through consensus functions. A key challenge arises when conflicting views on such discrepancies arise among auditors. We propose a novel method to resolve these conflicts by utilizing the consensus functions of individual auditors's Dempster-Shafer mass functions, thereby facilitating the creation of a unified, authoritative belief function for teams of auditors.

Simulating an independently and identically distributed point process given knowledge of a part of its realization is a critical challenge that affects all spatial statistics and geography-related studies utilizing spatial data analysis. For spatial data that has been thinned, the Acceptance Rejection Stitching approach offers a plausible method for completely restoring the point process. Initially developed for a more limited scenario, we modify and expand this method to work with general types of point processes, as long as they have a known intensity function. Furthermore, we present novel techniques for creating realistic and efficiently-simulated background point processes using a tetrahedral method. As a result of this approach, AS applies multiple times to the process created through this method, while retaining only a fraction of the background points to create the desired thinned point process. Detailed explanations and illustrations of our methods are provided.

The Generalized Uncertainty Principle leads to modified deformed Galilean transformations that differ from the traditional special relativistic Lorentz transformations. While Galilean transformations preserve invariant speeds of $v=c$, the deformed transformations incorporate a velocity-dependent "pixelation" of space with an uncertainty of $\Delta x_\pm \approx \frac{2\hbar^2}{(Mc^2)^{1/3}}$, where $M$ is a massive particle's mass, incorporating quantum mechanics and a heavy particle's mass into position measurements. Furthermore, the deformed transformations allow for a $z$-translation with an uncertainty of $\Delta z \approx \frac{\hbar^2}{(Mc^4)^{1/3}}$, revealing the emergence of a novel pixelization of time in the single-particle case, where an uncertainty in a $z$-translation accompanies an uncertainty in position, $\Delta z \approx \frac{\hbar^2}{(Mc^4)^{1/3}}$.

Many contemporary systems engage in multitasking, where tasks with varying critical requirements are scheduled to optimize overall system performance. However, existing research mainly focuses on single-task environments and therefore fails to address the challenges posed by multitasking. This study explores scheduling strategies for multitasking environments characterized by tasks with variable critical requirements and varying shares of processing capacity. We examine a common multitasking pattern, known as the "alternating switch" pattern, where tasks flip between active and idle states based on predetermined thresholds. Using analytical modeling combined with simulation, we investigate the effects of different processing ratios on system performance. Furthermore, we identify optimal scheduling intervals for both single- and multi-core processors and also investigate the potential for reducing idle periods in switching tasks.

A significant issue in utilizing bio-inspiration and fundamental research to create soft robotics is determining whether advanced mechanical systems can accomplish tasks more effectively and efficiently than simpler ones. To address this, we developed a control strategy for a robotic frog-like device jumping on a soft surface. The goal is to see if closing the loop from estimated states can improve the tracking of desired trajectories, leading to more reliable and robust motion. With the aid of a high-precision sensor, we monitored the dynamic jumping process and assessed the control strategy's performance both experimentally and numerically. Our study showed that incorporating feedback increased the success rate of jumps to 100%, with significantly tighter tracking errors compared to open-loop attempts. The advanced control strategy also allowed for broader control range and more rapid data collection during testing. As a result, we were able to validate a previously theoretical model of a single degree of freedom "toad" using experimental data from a four degrees of freedom bottock model.

Massive IoT deployments can benefit from Concurrent Transmissions, enhancing scalability and reliability in systems such as wireless sensor networks. However, widespread adoption of CT is hindered by the risk of interference and impaired transmission quality. Our study on IEEE 802.15.4g-2020 and IEEE 802.15.4-2011 standards and realistic channel conditions, shows that a suboptimal approach using short frames and high transmission rates yields nearly optimal performance. This discovery validates earlier research, revealing that the optimal number of concurrent links can be achieved with a simpler method, and we demonstrate this through firmware update applications. Furthermore, these findings introduce a new class of systems, referred to as "easy-transmit" systems, where numerous links maintain low error rates, even with distant links adding delays. The study uses a novel metric, known as "transmission ease," to quantify this phenomenon.

developed an approximation free of numerical constraints, representing the diagonalized
hamiltonian as a sum of random ket vectors and diagonal matrices. Our approach,
which shows minimal memory requirements, has a computational complexity of $O(N^3)$,

We utilized this method to analyze the lattice-regularized many-body localization
transition across various models and found that it consistently respects the core principle
of localization, which states that the system's entanglement entropy must approach
zero when the bandwidth approaches zero. Our study revealed that, below the critical
temperature, the fractal dimension of self-energy terms decreases to three, while
diagonal elements exhibit a range of dimensions between one and three. This breaks
down the dephasing time $\tau_{\phi}$ into two segments: one where it scales with
$\tau_M$ from the quantum Bottcher-Keating mechanism, and another where it scales as
$\tau_L$ from localized particles. Additionally, we observed that $\tau_L$ is larger
than $\tau_M$, indicating that core localization can absorb entropy without the
thermodynamic system becoming fully localized. This is in line with previous model-based
findings showing that some entropy remains in the localized subsystem even at the critical
point. Furthermore, we found that $\tau_L$ is fractal in nature, with its logarith

The kBM-DP+, a modified version of the original Boundary Map Dynamic Programming algorithm, is used to solve the well-known MultipleTargets problem with increased efficiency.  While the original algorithm relies on a 2^k-1 space complexity, which can become a significant bottleneck for large k values, the revised version reduces its space complexity to tk log(k) + p, resulting in a vast improvement for high k values and partial sums.  Furthermore, several other algorithms are examined to establish a theoretical limit for this problem, and the revised kBM-DP+ algorithm is then adapted to incorporate these findings, leading to the development of kBM-DP++ with a supplementary step requiring only an additional p units of memory.  Ultimately, the modified algorithm is shown to be within a factor of 16 of the optimal solution under certain conditions.  We also present a new algorithm called BM-BFS that solves the single target boundary map problem in a mere additional 16 units of memory while achieving a near-optimal complexity.  This algorithm's simplicity and efficient memory usage make it an attractive solution.

Our research explores the presence of adversarial examples in quantum classifiers
made up of varied layers of quantum units, such as variational andthoned gates,
and how their behavior changes depending on the number of iterations in the training
process for both classical and quantum-based gradient estimation techniques.

In this study, we investigate the volume-normalized eigenvalues of the Steklov problem on a sphere with slant boundary. Notably, we find that for a sphere $S^2$ of radius $1$, the behavior of volume-normalized $l$th eigenvalues, where $l$ is a square integer, converges as the radius approaches infinity to specific constants. Furthermore, this convergence is achieved through numerical analysis and verified analytically. Additionally, this study demonstrates the existence of multiple eigenvalues for a sphere with slant boundary and discusses the relationship between these eigenvalues and geometric parameters.

The focus of execution analysis in process algebra typically lies in examining the sequential, branching, or simultaneous progression of computations. This paper examines how such analysis can be applied to understand how process interactions unfold over time in specific contexts. To study process interactions, it is necessary to measure the time required for one process to trigger another, known as triggering times, leading to the development of suffix, prefix, and postfix alignments. Unlike traditional algebraic techniques that are static, the alignments presented here reflect dynamic, forward-looking perspectives, incorporating a temporal dimension. Furthermore, the alignments are generalized to accommodate observations of any depth and complexity, known as generalized postfix and prefix alignments. The paper also demonstrates how the definitions and techniques from execution analysis can be adapted to apply to observations that occur in the middle of a process execution. This research further examines how the representations of process behaviors through regions can be adapted to incorporate temporal dimensions, leading to the definitions of temporal region algebra and regional execution analysis. The study also explores additional aspects of execution analysis that are specific to prefix and postfix alignments, including an examination of the connections between region-based and time-aware execution analyses. This research further examines additional aspects of execution analysis that are specific to prefix and postfix alignments, leading to a revised assessment that temporal region algebra provides a more comprehensive framework.

To establish reliable wireless communication systems, radio propagation modeling must be effectively determined. Traditional radio propagation modeling involves measuring signal strength at various locations and using those values to establish a model. This research involves using deep convolutional neural networks to predict radio propagation parameters from a vast amount of channel data. By training a deep neural network on a large dataset, accurate radio propagation models can be developed without the need for empirical risk minimization. Additionally, this method allows for adapting to new environments by retraining the neural network on fresh data. Moreover, this research involves comparing the accuracy of predictive estimates for unknown locations using traditional methods and the proposed deep neural network approach.

Validation algorithms for temporal planning systems aim to pinpoint unmet prerequisites or unachievable timelines in task specifications. Despite previous studies minimizing these errors, there is still room for improvement in striking a balance between reducing potential mistakes and increasing computation time. We propose a new validation approach called 'fractional validation', which not only discovers all possible mistakes for each task but also estimates the likelihood of success for each possible solution. We implement this method using a kind of probabilistic planning algorithm known as 'point process planning', and conduct experiments to compare its performance with traditional task validation algorithms. The results indicate that fractional validation can detect a greater number of errors in task specifications, and determine the feasibility of more solutions, than existing methods.

The temporal resolution of modeling power system costs has received little attention, although it significantly affects the accuracy of economic evaluations, including the assessment of transmission network investments and policy interventions. This study investigates the impact of temporal resolution on power system costs by examining how costs evolve over time and explore the consequences of coarsening the time interval. Using a power system model, we demonstrate that resolving costs at a finer scale reduces residual mistakes and minimizes the cost of misallocating generation capacities compared to a coarse-time interval approach. Conversely, using a model with a higher temporal resolution in a typical power system scenario yields lower system costs than a scenario with a lower resolution. Furthermore, we show that the optimal transmission network infrastructure configurations differ depending on the temporal resolution considered.

The study investigates the well-posedness of the linearized ionic Vlasov-Poisson models with Dirichlet, Navier, and periodic boundary conditions. By employing this analysis, it can determine if the solutions represent smooth functions in space and time. Using a novel approach, it is possible to generalize the previously established well-posed results for the three-velocity models to the more realistic single-velocity models, incorporating the effects of net charges. Additionally, this analysis provides a new insight into the behavior of periodic boundary conditions, showing that the solutions remain stable in the L2 norm and influencing the global existence of the solutions.

Various graphical and textual prediction methods have been developed to assist users in selecting appropriate search terms for software modification tasks. Despite these efforts, there has not been a widely accepted baseline in the SC dataset established until now. In this research, we present two new ranking algorithms, TextRank and POSRank, that leverage textual data and are integrated into the LSRC framework. Our findings indicate that when combined with LC, POSRank yields the highest average performance (75%); whereas TextRank, when paired with LC and LC+HC, reaches an average performance of 74% and 73%, respectively. These algorithms are included in the benchmark package SC-BB on GitHub.

This study investigates the behavior of gas fluidized in the presence of an ultrasound-induced solid-fluid transition, where particle packing is disrupted and void spaces are created. We examine a dilute gel composed of poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) particles, which expands in response to increasing gas flow, and its behavior can be manipulated by adjusting the ultrasound power. The elasticity of the gel and the void volume can be determined, along with the influence of ultrasound parameters on gas flow and particle arrangement. The findings demonstrate a significant relationship between elasticity, void volume, and acoustic intensity. Two modes of particle movement are identified, which correspond to low and high ultrasound powers. At lower power, gentle particle motion creates broad voids interspersed with particle aggregates, whereas intense particle motion results in more compact voids at higher power. The particle arrangement ultimately dictates the fluidization characteristics.

This note presents a step-by-step mathematical proof for verifying the $C$
Conjecture related to the Collatz function. The proposed proof is built upon the
Mathematical Induction method. Although this conclusion doesn't introduce any
novel research findings, the step-by-step breakdown may simplify the understanding
of the required computations needed to confirm the $C$ Conjecture.

This research aims to increase transparency in machine learning models by applying explainable AI to a critical application: automatic classification of historical documents. The study centers on explaining the outcomes of two supervised neural network models. To achieve this, it utilizes a collaboration between the human, the model, and the document. First, the model produces predictive results, then applies various attribute weightages to pinpoint the document features most accountable for its decisions. Subsequently, the explainability method integrates these features with the relevant attributes to provide insight into the outcome prediction. To enhance human understanding, explanations are further used to discover patterns within the document features themselves. The goal is to identify both positive correlations (e.g., documents categorized as "historical" that are also considered "English") and negative correlations (e.g., documents categorized as "historical" that are not "English"). This research examines the trade-offs between the accuracy of the outcome prediction, the simplicity of explanations, and the ability to shed light on feature classifications that the AI cannot, based on its architectural design, simultaneously achieve.

In an economy of diverse preferences, we study how ratings influence market behavior in a system where agents can publicly rate their experiences. 
Our research reveals that stable matchings in such markets differ significantly even among slight variations in initial preferences, and tend to fall short of optimal utility levels due to over- or under-estimating their own utility in relation to others.
Our main findings demonstrate that stable matchings in rated environments, characterized by a steady score distribution, do not necessarily ensure the best possible utility for the agents involved.
Notably, a similar scenario can also occur in unrated markets, however, in rated markets, such instability is far more likely to occur and can manifest even when the ratings generate a steady score distribution, by simply sampling preferences from a broad range, as is typically the case.
Furthermore, our analysis shows that the uncertainty surrounding matchings and ratings is typically extreme and cannot be adequately represented by standard measures of variance.
Instead, a significant finding is that the uncertainty tends to be far greater when the ratings give an inaccurate representation of actual utility, a phenomenon that can manifest even when the ratings are accurate on average, yet still result in a suboptimal stable matching.

Previous assessment of text summarization models relied on human judgment for metrics development, resulting in potentially misguided guidance on improvement. To address this issue, we created SummScore, a automated evaluation tool that measures a generated summary's distinctiveness and coherence by comparing it to reference summaries. After fine-tuning the algorithm using expert-adjusted metrics as a guide, SummScore was tested across various datasets. The outcomes demonstrate that SummScore outperforms traditional metrics in terms of sensitivity to good performance and correlation with human ratings. Furthermore, SummScore was used to identify a type of densely related reference summary that other automatic evaluation metrics missed. After redefining this concept as a diversity metric, we combined it with a coherence metric to create a new, more comprehensive evaluation tool. The improved SummScore, incorporating diversity and coherence assessment, exhibits higher correlations with human ratings and better ability to identify improvements in generated summaries, making it a more reliable evaluation metric.

A recent study by Raviv and Rudelson demonstrated that highly sparsified data could be precisely reconstructed from cross-correlated Gaussian samples, with the correlation level dictating the minimum required sparsity. Building upon this foundation, our research expands on a key component of their proof, specifically exploring how the sparsity recovery bound changes as the number of correlated samples grows. Our findings reveal that as the number of samples increases, the sparsity level that can be recovered also grows, ultimately converging to a constant value that is determined by the sampling matrix. Interestingly, this result implies that as the number of correlated samples becomes very large, the impact of the correlation level on the sparsity level becomes negligible. Moreover, our research also demonstrates that in cases with a limited number of correlated samples, the sparsity recovery bound can be significantly enhanced by increasing the number of samples. Our study provides explicit, data-driven estimates of the precision for any given number of samples, thereby offering valuable insights that could inform the design of efficient sparse recovery algorithms utilizing correlated samples.

Beamforming, a proven technique in signal processing, can be applied in vehicular sensing to enhance the detection capabilities of individual radar transmitters.  However, its integration with object detection frameworks poses unique challenges, mainly due to the difficult task of aggregating multiple radar hits to form a single detection hypothesis.  Existing approaches to beamforming-based object detection either rely on simple aggregation techniques such as sorting, or employ object detectors in a post-processing stage, without fully accounting for the positions of detection hypotheses.  In this research, we present a novel object detection framework, referred to as BEVFusion, that takes into consideration the interdependencies between beamforming outputs and object detection hypotheses.  Specifically, we first introduce a simple aggregation technique that focuses on local maxima in beamforming results, and then employ a volume-guided fusion module to reactively adjust the aggregation process based on the overall distribution of detection hypotheses.  In addition, we predict the number of objects and enforce a minimum distance constraint between detection hypotheses to prevent over-counting.  Experimental results on a dataset derived from Autoware SIM age, demonstrating the superiority of our approach over traditional methods, both in terms of performance robustness and object detection capability.  With a robustness level equivalent to having only one radar sensor active, while maintaining the same level of detection capability as two radar sensors, our approach provides a unique solution to the challenges presented by beamforming-based object detection.

To analyze the impact of thermal fluctuations on turbulence dissipation, a power spectral density function is formulated for the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation of Navier-Stokes, and its high-wavenumber expansion is examined near the energy dissipation rate. It is observed that this expansion parallels the stochastic Navier-Stokes $\epsilon_{NS}$, and the fluctuation amplitude is directly proportional to $\epsilon_{NS}^{3/4}$ with a dependence on the Reynolds and Mach numbers. Consequently, turbulence dissipation is well-represented by the deterministic Navier-Stokes equation, and the fluctuation has no substantial effect on its integral value. Nevertheless, these fluctuations might have a profound influence on Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations, particularly where their statistical properties are utilized in model adjustments. Furthermore, an additional effect stems from the fluctuating energy transfer from infrared to high-waves, potentially providing an explanation for the existence of the Kolmogorov length scale in developed turbulence.

In this experiment, a laser beam passed through a warm fluid and its interaction with the fluid's thermal gradient was analyzed by measuring and analyzing the resulting diffraction pattern. The observed pattern showed an irregular pattern due to the inherent instability of the warm fluid, which resulted in the appearance of multiple rings and a fuzzy ring shape. A theoretical model based on random fluctuations in temperature helped to explain this pattern and its observed variations. The experiment repeated with a cooler fluid yielded the expected diffraction pattern and allowed for the precise measurement of the thermal gradient within the fluid.

Recent breakthroughs in software engineering through the application of data mining technology are largely driven by the extensive availability of open-source codebases.  A key area of research, known as design mining, seeks to extract insights from source code to gain a deeper understanding of design decisions.  However, despite numerous studies employing advanced machine learning techniques, the quality of insights remains an area for improvement.  Three key issues persist: the instability of conclusions across different configuations of analysis, a limited ability to draw general designs from one project to another, and the difficulty in accurately predicting how well a design will function based on the features used.  To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach that starts by representing design problems as a network of interconnected features, reasons, and conclusions.  By leveraging new advanced deep learning techniques, we train the structure of this network to better predict conclusions based on features used and designers' general design skills.  To validate the effectiveness of this approach, we analyzed over 78,000 design configuration files cross-validating across 21 different codebases.  The results demonstrate the potential of this approach, including more accurate predictions of conclusions based on features and designers' skills, more stable analysis results across different configurations, and a better ability to draw general designs from one project to another.  A more detailed description of our approach, including code and configuration files, can be found at https://github.com/msr-design-mining/deep-design-mining.

The proliferation of IoT and Dataflow-based streaming platforms has led to the emergence of a new, highly distributed data processing paradigm called H-STREAM. This innovative model capitalizes on the strengths of Apache Flink to address various challenges associated with unstructured, high-velocity, and massive data streams emanating from IoT devices. A novel, semi-formal syntax and functional semantics are introduced to express flexible, stream-processing sublanguages, which are then translated into efficient Apache Flink queries. Through a unified, high-level stream processing language, H-STREAM seamlessly integrates dynamic, energetic operators to mitigate the effects of streaming unpredictability, such as changing velocities and volumes. Additionally, H-STREAM incorporates a robust set of time management methods for managing data temporalities. A thorough evaluation across diverse scenarios validates the efficacy of H-STREAM, accompanied by the release of a comprehensive, open-source toolchain on GitHub.

The research is focused on the theoretical calculation of a specific process: the production of a Vector Like Doublet Quark via electron-positron collision at a high energy level. Our analysis is based on the framework of the Standard Model Effective Field Theory and incorporates a comprehensive set of theoretical calculations known as Effective Field Theory Global Analysis. For the first time, our study systematically examines all non-resonant diagrams in relation to this process and shows how they impact cross-section estimation at a next-to-next-to-leading order level in quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, our work publishes for the first time the one-loop self-energy corrections of the initial electrons. Our predictions are presented in terms of various experimentally measurable quantities and are illustrated with several benchmark plots. According to our findings, the presence of certain loop effects can lead to sizable influences on the production cross-section, especially at lower energy levels where the mass of the circulating electrons may become significant.

A growing number of studies are exploring the use of pre-trained sequence-to-sequence models for the task of automatically generating SPARQL queries based on images and the structure of a knowledge graph. Despite state-of-the-art results, it has been found that these models often produce queries with incorrect triple order. To overcome this issue, a novel model that leverages a copy mechanism has been proposed, allowing it to directly copy individual image word characters into the query. The model incorporates two training methods: one that focuses on learning to copy words and another that favors the detailed image representation. The findings of an extensive evaluation on a substantial image-based evaluation dataset revealed that the proposed model significantly improves the rank of queries with good image-ranking performance and notably outperforms the current best performing model in terms of overall performance. Furthermore, it was shown that the proposed model could be leveraged to incorporate detailed image information into existing knowledge graph completion models, resulting in consistent improvements across various benchmarks.

To find out how various fields within Computer Science evolved, we need to analyze a substantial amount of data including the names of topics, people, organizations, venues, and publications in the correct temporal context. Although valuable research datasets like DBLP provide a comprehensive overview of Computer Science, their data is primarily updated once a year, making real-time analysis impossible. Additionally, conferences often have lower publication volumes compared to notorious venues like FOCS and EC. Consequently, online academic search platforms like Academia.edu have extensive collections of recent Computer Science research. Our research involves the development of a unified workflow that integrates multiple sources to generate a vast graph covering over 2 million authors, organizations, and nearly 15 million publications spanning the period from the late 1800s to the present day. Our analysis is based on a detailed case study focusing on advancements within the artificial intelligence sector, as well as broader structural developments in Computer Science at the organization and venue levels. Our research also depicts how prominent venues like FOCS and EC have shifted over time.

Advancements in neural network applications for control systems have sparked interest in ensuring the robustness of neural networks used in these systems. Thanks to novel methods from the computer vision and machine learning communities, it's now possible to conduct an in-depth analysis of neural network robustness, which can contribute significantly to the verification of safety-critical control systems. Building on this insight, this paper applies a novel neural network robustness analysis based on the Point-to-Point Adversarial Method to the verification of control systems, providing a practical case study with a well-known nonlinear system, the double integrator. Moreover, this paper develops a tool, P2P-VER, which can estimate the time required for verification, a few seconds only. P2P-VER achieves this by translating the verification problem into a convex optimization issue, utilizing the Adversarial Discriminative Model obtained through observations of system inputs and corresponding adversarial inputs. A P2P-VER verification interface also allows for the generation of safety guidelines for control systems by producing a Safety Volume, which defines the boundaries of safe system behavior.

This study presents a more advanced clustering strategy that expands upon a specific mathematical structure known as functorial clustering schemes. Initially developed in pure mathematics, this approach has the capability to overcome a well-documented flaw where clusters may empty out over the course of the clustering process. We are particularly interested in how this method can contribute to the field of data science. A key aspect of this work involves examining a particular type of clustering based on the single-linkage method and extending it within a mathematical framework known as simplicial complexes. This approach simplifies the complex task of deciding whether a clustering based on single-linkage is stable under small changes in the data input. By using this method, we are able to analyze the clustering based on the R\'enyi entropy and the graph edit distance. Furthermore, our extension of functorial clustering schemes also enables the study of clustering on topological data sets.

Research into tensor completion has incorporated video frames to restore missing values. Most previous studies relied on a single frame capturing a scene's momentary state, and consequently, their achieved completion inaccuracies were consistent. In contrast, a new perspective explores the use of motion in videos to enhance completion accuracy. We find that streaming tensor completion methods perform better when dealing with motion, as they can leverage the context of preceding frames to identify motion-induced completions. Moreover, a multi-frame scheme can be employed to analyze the video's dynamic behavior and improve the completion using tensor decomposition. By applying this understanding, we propose STarGL, a novel framework that integrates a streaming tensor completion process with a low-rank model to accurately capture both the scene and motion in a video. The framework's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through our experiments using actual videos, which show that it consistently outperforms compared to other single-frame based approaches.

A G-representation contains a P-invariant subspace if and only if it is a direct sum of spaces that are invariant under the P-action of a maximal parabolic subgroup. For G = GLn(k), this P-action has a maximal parabolic subgroup where P is the set of upper triangular matrices. Representations of GLn(k) can be categorized as either non-multiplicative or multiplicative according to their behavior under the group operation. For a multiplicative representation, its P-invariant subspace will be the space of upper triangular matrices. A Nichols algebra is a double bosonization of a G-representation. A Nichols algebra over a Weyl group is classified into A, B, or C types based on its braiding. A theorem states that for a classical Weyl group G, a Nichols algebra C(G, b) is of type B or C if and only if its associated group G has a rank n = 1. Furthermore, a theorem shows that for a Nichols algebra C(G, b) of type B or C and its associated group G with rank n > 1, a central extension E exists such that its crossed product by a group H with a Nichols-Greenberg system is isomorphic to a Nichols algebra C(G/H, E*b). Inertial wave turbulence spectra have been confirmed across various studies on open ocean and laboratory scales, with -3 in two-dimensional and -5/3 in three-dimensional systems as predicted by Kolmogorov-Mithieux-Ovchinnikov theory for helical flows. Although this theory was initially derived from scaling arguments, it was later confirmed through direct simulations and experiments for inertial wave turbulence. Moreover, the scaling of energy spectra has been complemented by the scaling of the structure function, specifically the third and fourth order structure functions in three-dimensional systems. Furthermore, the scaling of the fourth order structure functions in three-dimensional systems was obtained through direct simulations with marginal scaling in two-dimensional systems. Lastly, simulations and experiments have verified the scaling of the sixteenth order structure functions in three-dimensional systems with exponent -13/3.

Graph normalization is a crucial operation in network science that underlies many computational tasks, including network science, statistics, and optimization. Researchers have proposed an iterative graph normalization method that not only produces consistent results but also is linked to solving a crucial computational problem, Maximum Weight Independent Set. Furthermore, each iteration of the method involves resolving an instance of this important problem. The method also offers a natural approach to inductive reasoning where learning is used to predict the properties of newly encountered objects. However, several factors complicate the method's real-world applicability, including its high computational demands and the need for a precise and time-consuming process to calculate the network's feature values. To overcome these challenges, we have developed a computationally more efficient algorithm known as Local Linear Iterative Graph Normalization, which achieves a key property of invariance, is linked to solving a important computational problem, and demonstrates favorable performance compared to existing methods.

Research on second-order dielectric response in quantum Hall effects at low temperatures has been conducted with the aid of THz time-domain spectroscopy.  Graphene in a 500 nm thick BaF$_2$ layer was subjected to a transverse electric modulation and a magnetic field at 2 K to confirm its Landau Level occupancy.  Spectra obtained were interpreted through a three-component model consisting of BaF$_2$ polarization, graphene polarization, and interband transitions within the first excited Landau Level.  Among the observed Landau Levels from levels $\nu = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10$ with $e^2/h$ signature, those at $\nu = 0, 2, 4, 6$ and its second harmonic showed an electric field induced change.  Furthermore, a Landau Level splitting of 6 meV due to the magnetic field was noticed, along with an electric modulation induced splitting of 1.8 meV.  A semi-classical approach was applied to interpret the observed changes as an electric modulation induced longitudinal magnetic field and an additional magnetic field induced contribution to the longitudinal current.  A comparison with theory supported the observed changes and established a correlation between second harmonic and Landau Level occupancy.
