In vision tasks, maintaining model flexibility in terms of image orientation is crucial for generalization purposes. Gabor filters, which combine eigenvector extraction with local complex-valued filters, can effectively learn differentiable image representations from various orientations. Nevertheless, being sensitive to orientation, this approach requires a separate filter for each orientation. To rectify this limitation, we developed the Landmark Gabor Filters, which employ a shared concept to achieve orientation robustness. By leveraging the characteristics of Gabor filters, LGFs consist of a landmark unit that, when combined with various Gabor phases, can generate multiple orientation-insensitive features. These features, being learned alongside network weights, allow the model to adapt and perform well across multiple orientations without the need for extra training. Experimental results on three different datasets and across various orientation configurations demonstrate the remarkable performance of our method.

The relative fundamental lemma drives the proof of a more advanced orbit theorem, which in turn accelerates and clarifies the calculation of relative orbital integrals. This result is particularly crucial when applied to the derivation of both local and global busyness bounds. A notable case in point is the application of this principle to establish bounds for the number of inactive letters in p-groups, which shares many similarities with computing the number of inactive letters in all p-groups. A detailed explanation of our methodology can be found in a accompanying document, where we revisit and simplify the proof of the orbit theorem using a recently discovered identity. A computational demonstration of our theory can be found in another accompanying document.

In renormalized QCD, as it approaches the Bjorken limit, parton distribution functions (PDFs) become increasingly straightforward, with significant improvements resulting from incorporating new data and more precise numerical methods. A key aspect of mass effects research in high-energy physics is understanding how the dynamics of heavier quarks influence lighter quark functions, particularly those of charm quarks on down-quark functions and vice versa. To examine these interactions, PDF-kill operators are used in a framework that simultaneously considers PDFs and parton distribution functions for the gluon, describing how the parton structure changes as it approaches the Bjorken limit.

A function w counting the occurrence of each edge in a subgraph G of a given graph E defines the weight of the subgraph G with respect to E. The Edge Coloring Number EC(E) represents the minimum number k such that any subgraph G of E, having the same edge size as E, will have a weight distribution where each edge appears at most k times. In a similar context, the concept of Regularity Index RI(E) is established as the minimum number l such that any subgraph G of E, having the same edge size as E, will have a weight distribution where each edge appears at least l times. For a graph E not containing triangles, the relationship between EC(E) and RI(E) is examined, revealing EC(E) - RI(E) equals 1, with the significance of this relation further explored through other triangle-free graphs. Additionally, the boundedness of the gap EC(E) - RI(E) is investigated and the limitations of this phenomenon in graph theory are sought out.

This article examines the relationship between the Bergman spaces of the unit disk equipped with specific weightings, specifically focusing on a particular subset where the weightings have vibrations in their real parts, according to a defined metric. It draws a parallel to similar concepts within the Kähler manifolds $T^{1,2}$ and shows how these weighted spaces capture a particular aspect of functions within their scope, incorporating growth conditions and with respect to their angular integrability in its definition.

This study compares the effectiveness of AI models in identifying chronic kidney disease (CKD) stages based on patient data from the CKD cohort, as well as individuals who tested positive for COVID-19 and healthy participants, using a data augmentation approach that combines clinical information and radiology image features. A high-performance, highly efficient VGGNet-based model was adapted for this task by incorporating residual learning and a soft attention mechanism to enhance its capability to learn from various data types. Utilizing a weighted cross-entropy loss function, the model achieved impressive performance on all three datasets, demonstrating its ability to generalize successfully from one domain to another. What sets this study apart from others in the field is its novel approach to merging clinical data and radiology image features in a single deep learning architecture. Moreover, this work highlights the potential for transferring knowledge from a COVID-19 dataset, as well as using AI models to predict CKD stages, thereby facilitating the development of automated and efficient methods for monitoring and diagnosing CKD stages. Importantly, this study also underscores the potential benefits of using AI models in predicting COVID-19 cases.

As the emergence of the "satellite mega-grid", a byproduct of the rapid advancement in small satellites and low-cost launch technologies, begins to take shape in our Earth's lower orbit, a crucial consideration for the design of satellite mega-grids to avoid unwanted orbital debris has started to gain more attention. One of the methods being explored to mitigate this issue involves the use of minimum space occupancy (MiSO) orbits, located at intervals of six miles above the Geo-Satellite orbit, to facilitate the safe removal of satellites. However, the upper boundary of each MiSO zone is subject to variations based on the launch vessel utilized. This paper introduces an innovation in the form of a table, updating the boundaries of each MiSO segment in the range 20000 km to 35700 km following the publication of new data by the NASA Johnson Space Flight Center's Orbit Determination Program.

In mesh generation, dividing a volume into smaller pieces called quad layouts is often the first step. Typically, a three-dimensional Delaunay triangulation is used to transform these layouts into full three-dimensional meshes. However, as mesh sizes decrease, the number of elements in a typical quad layout can become extremely large, leading to very long inter-element distances that pose challenges for many three-dimensional mesh generation techniques. In this study, we investigate the use of a specialized three-dimensional mesh called a T-mesh as a means to simplify quad layouts by constrained-delagation, resulting in a more manageable mesh size with shorter element distances. Furthermore, our approach leverages a T-mesh to split layouts into smaller pieces along smooth surfaces, reducing the number of elements and improving layout segmentation. Ultimately, we demonstrate that a T-mesh can be used in conjunction with a three-dimensional mesh generation technique called two-level adapted refinement to deliver accurate numerical results with minimal grid points, even for complex problems in three dimensions.

When assessing correlation strength between two variables, people often rely on measures like the Pearson correlation coefficient.  This, in turn, depends on p-values which are typically estimated by assuming all data follows the same bivariate normal distribution.  However, when this assumption isn't valid, estimated p-values may be incorrect.  This paper discusses how to modify the Pearson correlation coefficient so it works better even if the data comes from two different distributions.  Additionally, the article provides methods for handling cases where the data sets have different numbers of data points.  Finally, the article includes examples of how to implement these modifications using the R programming language.

We calculate the Q.S-matrix for time-reversal-invariant black-hole metrics, including the Schwarzschild, Kruskal, G\"odel, and G\"odel-Kruskal spaces. This quantizes s-matrices via their asymptotic scattering patterns using Minkowski and Euclidean real-time thermal field theories. The Q.S-matrices of these metrics exhibit black-hole and universe time reversals that distinguish them from white holes. They are represented by Euclidean black holes with Euclidean Bogoliubov transformations and their associated Hilbert spaces, as well as by real-time Bogoliubov isometries linking Minkowski and Euclidean spacetimes. We show that these isometry groups form continuous sets of local deformations of Q.S-matrices, with continuous modulation controls over asymptotic scattering modes. This provides a quantum basis for the Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton-Dimensioless theory, a natural framework for quantum gravity in all its manifestations.

We investigate the local stabilization near unstable equilibrium points of the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equation using feedback controls that only act within a confined spatial area. By constructing a feedback system within the kinetic energy space and demonstrating its local stability near equilibrium points, it is shown that small-scale control mechanisms within a specific domain can effectively stabilize the system from multiple initial conditions. This involves explicit calculations of the Navier-Stokes operator's behavior and the solution's exponential decay rate in terms of the domain's control location. Furthermore, it is noted that using feedback controls within a smaller domain can be more effective than those applied over the entire domain. This finding is particularly significant as it shows that with a sufficient increase in the domain's size, the Navier-Stokes dynamics can be made asymptotically stable without requiring global control.

MindDict is a portable, lightweight dictionary application available under a free license, offering definition services in multiple languages, including English, Spanish, German, and Russian. MindDict generates synonyms, word explanations, and phrases, as well as translations, phrases with examples, and quotes. The application utilizes user-created or publicly available lexical databases, including user-submitted user-contributed resources. MindDict boasts a user-friendly interface and seamless sync capabilities across multiple platforms. The program stands out for its portability, allowing users to run it from a USB drive without installing it on the host machine. MindDict is compatible with various dictionary formats, such as WordNet, Dictd, Onelook, Crossword Dictionary, WordNet, Synonym, Phrases, Translations, Quotes, and other formats available for download or contribution. MindDict is available as open-source software under a free license, making it an excellent option for users.

Machine learning's reliance on post-hoc explanation methods to guarantee decision transparency has prompted a surge in interest in using intrinsic predictors to elevate explanation quality. Despite this, many existing studies have overlooked the fact that reliance on these predictors compromises the reliability of models being examined. To address this, we develop a mathematical framework to evaluate prediction accuracy and develop a novel metric to assess explanation quality. Our experiments with tabular data models demonstrate that relying on post-hoc explanations can actually undermine the robustness of models, prompting us to advise against using explanation-based metrics and encouraging further research into measuring and improving the quality of explanations.

Research on how a thin metal layer interacts with a semiconductor surface relies heavily on studying the metal layer's impact on the semiconductor's charge density. However, the metal layer also influences the charge density by altering the semiconductor's surface potential. In this study, we investigate the interaction between a thin metal layer and a semiconductor surface using a unique approach that considers the metal layer's impact independently. Our analysis focuses on an InAs (111) surface, both with and without a thin capping layer, using a high-energy electron beam to analyze the surface. Our results show that the metal layer affects the semiconductor's work function, but also has a localized impact on the semiconductor's surface charge distribution. When a metal layer is absent, there is a natural variation in the charge density on the semiconductor surface. The introduction of the metal layer introduces another scale for analysis, but the underlying charge density on the semiconductor is still present. For a specific metal layer composition, our results are consistent with a theoretical model predicting that the metal layer forms a two-dimensional metal-like state, but our results also show that the semiconductor's surface potential is only partially transferred into the semiconductor. Our results imply that the semiconductor's surface potential is only partially transferred into the semiconductor, leaving a portion that may influence the semiconductor's properties.

In the field of algorithmic learning theory, a new framework for robust learning algorithms has been developed, which relies on a novel technical device: a function that estimates the radius of the query based on given data. This function categorizes concepts within a specified class and determines the learning rate by analyzing the distance of given data points to the concept boundary. The development of this framework leads to significant results, which demonstrate the possibility of robust learning in various situations, even with little supervision. Furthermore, our framework's impact extends to the case where the target concept is not known in advance and not well-behaved, which was previously the focus of a different line of work. The framework's utility is also evident in two new technical contributions: a technique to quantify the effect of unlabelled data on the empirical function and a technique to verify that a given empirical function is representative of the underlying distribution.

The FS-2 algorithm for computing optimal transport, presented in a 2020 paper, has a time complexity of O(n^2 * logn) for scaling the solution to a large dataset of size n, offering an improvement over the previous time complexity of O(n^2) by utilizing a binary search approach to determine the optimal scaling factor. The FS-2 algorithm first identifies a suitable initial solution through the MM algorithm, having a time complexity of O(n^2) when combined with a fast proximal mapping operation of O(n) for large datasets. The algorithm then enters a loop where it employs a dual gradient ascent, having a time complexity of O(n^2) at large scales, until the scaling factor is determined. The FS-2 algorithm's efficiency was enhanced further in a 2022 paper, specifically for handling large datasets, by integrating a progressive switching technique to transition smoothly from the MM algorithm to dual gradient ascent, while maintaining convergence, and having a time complexity of O(n^2 * logn). Building on the FS-2 algorithm's efficient solution computation, the FS-2 up/down algorithm for one-to-one and one-to-many mappings was developed to scale efficiently, having a time complexity of O(n * logn) at large datasets. The FS-2 up/down algorithm combines a fast solution computation with an O(n) time complexity operation to solve the one-to-many mapping problem. Our research focuses on the atmospheric evolution of a super-Earth located close to its host star. To study this, we used the James Webb Space Telescope to observe the transits of AU Mic's exoplanet during two stellar flares. Observing at 3.6 microns allows us to analyze the atmosphere of AU Mic b, whereas observing at 1.3 microns enables us to understand its lower layers. Both wavelengths were studied in both flare and quiescent states. To analyze the data, we compared it with synthetic spectra generated using the ESPRESSO simulations. Our research found that the atmospheric mass loss rate significantly increases during the star's flares. Quiescent values are estimated at around 10^8-10^9 g/s, whereas during the star's flares this rate rises to around 10^10-10^11 g/s. This mass loss rate is consistent with other studies on the system. Interestingly, the atmospheric mass loss rate is directly related to the star's energy output. Furthermore, our research showed that the atmospheric composition of AU Mic b remains relatively stable across different stellar activity levels.

When charged particles travel through a resistive medium that is at rest, it experiences friction from this movement. This frictional effect is strongest when the medium is perfectly static, and it amplifies waves and electric fields already present in the system. By considering a simplified model of a charged layer within a co-moving frame, we demonstrate two key phenomena. Firstly, we find that particle movements distort the medium in a specific pattern, and this pattern in turn causes a certain type of wave to form. This effect also leads to a potential source of radiation. Secondly, we notice that particle friction not only produces this radiation but also can change the existing electric fields in the system, and this effect can either increase or decrease the strength of these fields. This research can be applied to various systems, including laboratory-based plasmaristive materials and astrophysical bohm-doppier effects.

The majority of the current approaches for dealing with imbalanced data sets, which tend to enhance minority class samples, often underestimate the true positive rate as they focus on improving the minority class precision.  Furthermore, they often resort to either replicating existing data or reducing features, which has the tendency to lose valuable information.  In this study, we introduce an innovative framework called Balancing Imbalanced Data using Ensembles, which utilizes an ensemble of oversampling techniques tailored to the specific characteristics of the data set.  A novel approach to selecting the right oversampling method components is also introduced based on observations from the developed ensemble framework.  A comprehensive system for assessing classifier performance on imbalanced data sets is also proposed, which goes beyond traditional metrics to incorporate additional cluster-based metrics.  Experimental findings on 29 imbalanced data sets from various domains, as well as baseline comparison with current state-of-the-art approaches, suggest that the Balancing Imbalanced Data using Ensembles framework outperforms other methods across multiple performance metrics.  In contrast to other techniques, Balancing Imbalanced Data using Ensembles ensures that enhanced minority class precision translates to true positive rates, retains the quality of minority class samples, and avoids feature reduction.  A companion system, called BI\({}^{3}\), supporting the Balancing Imbalanced Data using Ensembles approach has been made publicly available to the scientific community.

Twenty-five newly discovered Southern QSOs have been found at redshifts above 3.5 through WISE/2mass X-ray and mid-infrared catalog matching.  Twenty of these QSOs are reportedly optically rare objects.  Six of the discovered QSOs have X-ray fluxes in the 10^42 erg/cm^2/s range, a range in which there is a significant lack of known QSOs.  The findings also expand on the number of known QSOs at absolute magnitudes above -25 in the Southern Hemisphere.  Future large-scale X-ray and mid-infrared catalog generation projects may be able to uncover hundreds more QSOs like these that are missed by current X-ray and mid-infrared catalog matching technology.  The QSO findings and their corresponding data, including X-ray flux, are provided in table format.  The QSO findings have been visually confirmed and are available through the 2mass/WISE catalog.  A flowchart has been created to track QSO discovery and verification processes.  A QSO spectroscopic observation request has been submitted for spectroscopic confirmation.  A QSO finding flowchart has been created and documented.  A2MSS/2MID cross-correlation QSO finding has been performed in the 2MID/IRS/FIRS/ISSDF/DEEP2 galaxy survey. By utilizing a quantum dot as a sensor within a superconductor nanowire, 
the quantum metric of the superconductor's energy spectrum can be measured 
through a magnetization response to an external magnetic field change, 
resulting from a spin-rotational susceptibility linked to the Pirahno effect. 
This spin-rotational susceptibility can also induce a Berry phase-like 
magnetization that is couple to the quantum dot, along with an additional 
magnetization generated by the dot's own hybridized states within the superconductor. 
As the superconductor's energy spectrum changes due to a Berry phase-like 
magnetization, a Hall-like effect can occur, resulting in a difference in 
magnetization in perpendicular transverse magnetic fields when measured at 
critical current thresholds related to different gaps in the superconductor's energy spectrum. 
This results in a prediction that the critical current will exhibit a critical 
curvature when plotted against an external magnetic field, with this feature 
potentially being used to identify topological superconductors experimentally.

Our investigation focuses on the properties of internal shocks within two-dimensional, isentropic magnetohydrodynamics. We reveal that these shocks possess a specific contraction behavior, which we further extend to more general systems. We also explore the Inviscid Incompressible Euler equations and demonstrate that internal shocks within this system cannot converge, not only in terms of asymptotic frequency, but also for patterns that repeat at a fixed frequency. A crucial factor contributing to this behavior is the linear relationship between the velocity and potential functions. This relationship not only influences the Euler equations but also the SH waves and MH shocks, allowing the derivation of precise convergence rates in different scenarios.

The challenge of generating an infinite view perspective from a fixed camera is referred to as perpetual view generation. Previous research attempted to address this issue through a self-supervised approach, aligning views that differ by a specific angle. However, these methods struggled with two significant limitations: they were heavily influenced by existing training data, annotated with panoramic labels, and they failed to utilize the full range of rotation transformations. In this study, we introduce a novel, rotation-based technique that does not necessitate pre-annotated training data and can learn all possible alignment perspectives. Our model incorporates a consistency module to ensure alignment under various rotation scenarios. Experimental evaluations on three public datasets not only demonstrate our model's ability to generate views with consistent perspectives but also surpasses the state-of-the-art performance in intrinsic view synthesis, even without the need for pre-annotated data.

In large-scale complex networks, certain phenomena can be analyzed effectively using spectral methods by transforming them into higher-dimensional spaces. To utilize these methods in model predictive control, a key challenge is the vast scale of associated systems, making them computationally expensive to handle. A proposed approach involves using the Koopman operator to approximate the behavior of large-scale systems over a short period, leveraging the spectral methods' property of representing system dynamics with linear relationships between states at specific time intervals. This approximation enables the model predictive control problem to be reduced to a more manageable control problem over a shorter horizon. A theoretical upper limit can be set for the control error that occurs due to approximating the original system with a finite number of terms in its spectrum. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate that implementing the spectrum-based approximation for predictive control, using a small number of terms, yields results comparable to those achievable through exact control of the original system.

A mathematical model of a viscous liquid covering an horizontal fibre is being analyzed, taking into consideration how the liquid interacts with the fibre via a specific model that accounts for a combination of adhesive and repulsive forces. A part of the model focuses on a small, droplet-like area near the fibre and demonstrates both theoretical and numerical instability when a particular relationship between the liquid and the fibre is satisfied, leading to the formation of droplets. The size of these droplets continues to grow until they reach a particular, maximum size and then stabilize, depending on factors such as the rate of liquid flow and the strength of interactions between the liquid and the fibre. This theoretical framework bears resemblance to experimental results obtained through a technique called microfluidics and can be used to further investigate how droplets form and grow in this type of setup.

The Lagrangian formulation offers a unique perspective on fluid dynamics by focusing on the local experience of individual fluid particles. Representing fluid motion in a Lagrangian framework involves using a local coordinate system tied to these particles. It's been observed that, unlike Eulerian coordinates, Lagrangian metrics exhibit features such as material invariance and connection to the deformation metric. In this study, we explore the relationship between Lagrangian metrics and Eulerian material metrics, along with the connection between their respective Riemannian curvatures. It's discovered that the Lagrangian Riemannian curvature can be expressed in terms of Eulerian material curvature components. Additionally, we establish conditions under which these curvatures are identical in order to facilitate distinguishing between Lagrangian and Eulerian turbulence. This investigation is supported by numerical simulations involving both random and turbulent flows within a two-dimensional fluid flow setup.

Using a robotic ultrasound as a substitute for human operators to take measurements of spinal angles is a promising solution to reduce labor costs. Robotic ultrasound-based measurements were analyzed in patients with scoliosis and compared to manually obtained images to assess their accuracy. Analysis of 25 patients revealed a significant correlation (r=0.94, p<0.001) between robotic and manual measurement of the lumbar lordosis angle, with a mean difference of 1 degree. Radio graphic measurement, used as the standard reference, showed a strong correlation (r=0.89, p<0.001) with both robotic and manual measurement of the lumbar lordosis angle, with mean differences of 1 degree and 2 degrees respectively. These findings suggest that robotic ultrasound-based measurements of spinal angles are highly reliable. Given its non-invasive, user-friendly design, and the lack of operator expertise requirements, the robotic ultrasound appears to be a reliable choice for obtaining accurate spinal images. Such technology could potentially replace manual ultrasound-based measurement with its known inaccuracies, thereby allowing the use of robotic ultrasound-based measurements in patient monitoring and surgical planning.

To integrate duration data into credit risk modeling, we initially model the
distribution of default durations over time periods with a discrete time series.
Unlike traditional approaches that approximate continuous duration distributions
using specific models, our method directly estimates a discrete distribution of
default dates for each period without presupposing a specific shape or using
parametric models. Instead, we employ a Bayesian procedure using a Dirichlet
process prior to generate discrete distributions that represent the default
probability for each period. Notably, our approach accommodates varying numbers
of default observations in different time periods, unlike static models, which
also allows for Bayesian shrinkage and shares posterior mean defaults across
periods. Additionally, we propose a non-parametric time homogeneity model to
investigate the similarity in duration distributions over time periods. All
models are evaluated using U.S. business loan data from a commercial loan
database and we perform assessments on both loan-level and portfolio levels.

We've conducted a study comparing various approaches to detecting hate speech within a textual context. Our investigation, encompassing experiments with seven distinct datasets (three human-generated and four machine-generated), revealed that linguistic or semantic-based methods consistently outperformed other approaches. Notably, a method incorporating the Latent Dirichlet Allocation topic model achieved the highest success in our tests.

A key limitation of the MIMO framework has been the prevalence of single-channel subnetworks, which the authors have identified and quantified within existing datasets. They have developed a multi-input, multi-output unsupervised clustering framework to address this issue. Firstly, a novel unsupervised framework is proposed to create separate networks for each community identified by leverage graphs. Secondly, a proposed combination of deep learning models - including a novel, complex CNN architecture - is used to effectively 'unmix' the inputs of MIMO systems, thus circumventing the issue of incomplete data caused by the dominance of single-channel subnetworks. Experiments have shown the effectiveness of this approach, which outperformed existing MIMO-based baselines, both in its ability to detect and characterise diverse types of community structures within complex datasets, and to restore the full signal of subnetworks with two or more input channels.

One of the key challenges in document research is identifying suitable, extensive datasets for thorough examination. Due to their complexity, such datasets typically comprise a large number of intricate, multi-segment documents with interconnected sections, such as letters, contracts, and reports. This study focuses on supplying a straightforward, automated tool for selecting datasets that are suitable for historical document analysis, and presents an approach that employs clustering methods on a set of documents based on visual page similarities. Unlike conventional methods, our technique accounts for the interconnections between visual elements within each document, enabling it to draw insights from the overall structure. We have conducted a series of in-depth experiments and gathered practical evidence on datasets containing a significant number of documents, highlighting the efficiency of our method in organizing data across different levels of complexity. Furthermore, our approach excels in identifying misclassified documents and is adaptable to various methods for classifying visual page structures.

This research aims to develop a highly accurate trajectory tracking capability in industrial robots by complementing existing PID controllers with a lightweight, efficient nullspace control framework for compliant robots. The fast-acting outer loop utilizes a novel estimator that calculates an estimated cornering velocity based on a simplified robot kinematic model. The result is a straightforward yet robust design ensuring the robot stays within its mechanical limitations. The proposed estimator achieves fast cornering and enables precise position control within 0.1 mm. The study demonstrates that integrating this estimator with an actuator current-based nullspace control can enhance trajectory tracking by up to 83.6%, especially during rapid movements, thereby making compliant robots more suitable for precise positioning tasks.

Using nearly 15 years of National Health Service Data for England, we analyzed data on patients who experienced a myocardial infarction (MI), examining how individual long-term health conditions surrounding the time of the event change over time. A novel analytical method was developed to address issues with missing data and follow-up. By modeling the development of these conditions for each patient and relating them to the time of the MI, we were able to analyze the characteristics of these conditions in relation to various factors, including individual health and socio-demographic attributes. Our analysis revealed considerable variation in the combination of these conditions both in terms of their intensity and the patterns of their development. By identifying the conditions that were present at least six months prior to an MI and relating them to socio-demographic attributes, such as sex and ethnicity, we found distinct clusters of these conditions. These results could be used to refine socio-demographic attributes in risk prediction models for MI, developing new target variables that integrate both clinical and socio-demographic information. Moreover, the method can handle complex, time-varying and incomplete data on multiple conditions. By combining the analysis of MI-related conditions surrounding the time of their occurrence with their counterparts' predictive characteristics, we can capture unique aspects of an individual's health situation over time. This combined information enables a dynamic assessment of an individual's relative risk position in terms of their predicted health characteristics over time.

A recent research paper proposed an enhanced version of Becke's scheme to facilitate convergence for a broader range of electronic continuum-based integrals than possible with the original method. However, application of the improved scheme to certain essential operators resulted in a decreased rate of convergence compared to the original. Furthermore, the algorithms for implementing the improved scheme with certain projection strategies yielded a higher computational cost in CPU time. In this study, a revised interpretation is provided for the improved Becke scheme, along with a more efficient algorithm for projecting it, which results in a higher convergence rate when applied to electronic continuum-based integrals. The research also presents numerical results for Gaussian, Lagrange, and Hermite basis sets, showing that the higher convergence rate yields more accurate integral estimates. Specifically, for Gaussian basis sets, the improved algorithm enables convergence of electronic integrals to within machine-precision in double precision arithmetic with just 64-75 basis functions, whereas 128-150 basis functions were required in the original algorithm. Consequently, the research suggests the newly proposed algorithm be used in quantum-chemistry software for calculations involving electronic integrals.

The Metric Dimension parameterized by treewidth is W[1]-hard, but this difficulty doesn't extend to other key graph parameters. Theoretical results show that parameterized Metric Dimension is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the vertex cover number or the genus of the graph. This leads to the discovery that fixed-parameter tractability depends heavily on the choice of parameter. This distinction is further reinforced by comparing the parameterized complexity of graph's vertex cover number and genus. This is also the case for clique number and genus, but interestingly, clique number and tree depth exhibit contrasting behavior. This behavior is further investigated through the introduction of Fake-Combined-Modular-Expansion (FCME) graphs. FCME graphs consistently yield fixed-parameter tractability for various dimensionality measuring problems parameterized by their inherent modular properties. This inherent tractability also extends to numerous natural subcases. However, the inherent tractability of FCME graphs does not translate to random geometric graphs, which remain NP-hard even when parameterized by their delta value. This suggests that FCME graphs may serve as an ideal template for creating tractable parameterized problems.

In directed spaces, the Scott topologies of ideal-based topologies coincide, 
yet this equivalence does not extend to space expanisons like upper, lower, and convex powerspaces. 
The study of topological properties in directed spaces therefore must be approached separately 
for directed spaces and for dcpos (and specifically for partially ordered sets). 
This paper investigates the basic topological properties of convex powerspaces of directed spaces. 
It also establishes a framework for computing such powerspaces based on index spaces and proves 
a representation theorem for convex powerspaces of directed spaces, specifically dcpo spaces. 
These results address questions posed by Ershov in 1991.

A fundamental question in climate science concerns the impact of large-scale water vapor amounts on climate, with potential applications for biogeochemical engineering and human climate engineering. Previous studies using simple climate models suggested that lower-tropospheric radiative heating in hothouse climates could lead to decreased cloud amounts and precipitation, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that maintains unstable climate states. However, this research involves more complex models and reveals a contrasting outcome: increased water vapor leading to lower-surface heat flux, rather than enhanced cloud amounts and precipitation, and also that such unstable climate states are often marked by intense precipitation episodes rather than consistently high precipitation levels. These results offer insights into the complexities of Earth's climate system.

We examine the higher-spin interpretation of Euler's equation for three-dimensional geometric phases, and make connections to three-dimensional conformal gravity theory and its relationship with Minkowski's version of general relativity.  We also establish that Euler's equation has a higher-spin extension similar to Yang-Mills theory.  This led us to a novel proposal - a concept we call 'Unified Pure Quantum Gravity-Yang-Mills Theory'.  We describe a theoretical framework for this concept and some of the implications it has, such as the presence of an infinite number of massless spin-3 to spin-1000 degrees of freedom.  We also determine a wave function's normalized value of one, and discuss arguments in its favor.  Furthermore, the connection to three-dimensional geometric phases offers significant support to this concept.  We also show some similarities and differences with string theory.  Finally, we discuss the potential methods for developing this concept and observing its effects, such as through simulation or experimentation of the wave packet's behavior when a particle with an arbitrarily high spin is involved.

Deep neural networks excel in various applications, but their robustness is often intermediate at best. They can easily misinterpret input data due to slight alterations, and noisy labels often compromise their performance, with current methods providing only a basic noise resistance by employing data cleaning or regularization techniques. This paper presents a novel approach called Bayesian Statistics Guided Label Refurbishment Mechanism (BLRM), which not only grants intermediate models a level of noise resistance but also enhances performance in noisy conditions by retraining the model using cleaned-up labels obtained from an inference process involving multiple models trained on the same dataset but with different levels of noise. This process is repeated until convergence, resulting in a refined label set that yields a better model. BLMR's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on six different datasets containing various noise levels, which are compared to existing approaches.

A regular simplex in the unit cube $Q_n$ can be interpreted as a matrix of rank $n+1$ with entries ranging from 0 to 1. For $n \geq 2$, we find that a regular simplex exists if and only if the number of interpolation nodes is greater than or equal to $\frac{3n^2+5n+11}{4n+2}$. When $n = 2$, the number of interpolation nodes must be at least 11. When $n \geq 3$, the lower bound for the number of interpolation nodes is $\frac{3n^2+5n+11}{4n+2}$. These results resolve two open problems from the 1990s, first posed by R. Fadlii, then simplified by S. Vassiliev, who found the lower bound for the number of interpolation nodes in terms of $n$.

This research focuses on analyzing the transition probability matrix of a correlated random walk and associated Markov chains, as well as their characteristic polynomials, under various conditions. We derived the characteristic polynomial of the transition probability matrix in terms of the walk's correlation coefficients using the Yang-Baxter equation. Additionally, we proved a generalized version of the Toeplitz matrix determinant formula and applied a non-central Casselman-Shimura theorem to obtain a formula for the determinant of the transition probability matrix. A special case of this character involves a correlated random walk with exponential-type correlations, which can be linked to the Yangian double $e(Y(\mathfrak{gl}_2))$ through the study of its eigenvalues.

A novel, clock-minimization technique has been developed for proving program termination, which works by rewriting clock-dependent termination proof proofs as clock-independent ones. This technique is based on a specific algebraic structure known as a monoid, and involves replacing clock values with elements from this monoid. By maximizing the use of this clock-minimization technique, the size of termination proofs can significantly decrease. Moreover, the technique allows for the termination proof of a program with a constant clock to be transformed into a clock-independent one, where the size of this proof is proportional to the denominator of the clock's ration values. This technique's Termination Analysis Tool utilizes the SMT Solver to identify the optimal clock configuration that yields the smallest possible termination proof.

In modeling wall-bounded turbulence, a fundamental concept known as the hairpin structure has been employed since the 1980s. Building on this idea, researchers have developed more complex models, incorporating various mechanisms such as kinetic energy transfer and streamwise-rolling motions. Recent studies, including those by of Yamamoto and Kinumi and Zeithammer, have further influenced the development of these models. A new hairpin packet model is presented here here by combining the ideas of Kalchev and Geem and Kim's model. The model aims to simplify existing concepts while avoiding flaws in previous research, specifically the problem of zero kinetic energy consumption as noted by Zeithammer. A new model for the growth rate of perturbations is also proposed, along with a formulation of the streamwise-rolling motion activation criterion.

A gauged version of the baby Skyrme model is investigated. This model introduces three-dimensional gauge fields to the theory. As a result, we find that the moduli space of the vortices satisfies a Seiberg-Witten system. Specifically, we derive equations for bound states of vortices and magnetically stable solutions. These include solitons characterized by one, two, or no gauge field, describing, respectively, vortex-Anti-vortex, soliton-dark soliton, and free Skyrme modes. Analytical expressions for the profiles of these solitons are obtained and verified through comparisons with numerical simulations.

We analyze a lattice simulated Weyl semimetal model that exhibits lattice symmetry. The simulation reveals four distinct phases separated by quantum phase transitions. These phases include a previously unexplored unconventional superconductor phase, a Bose-Einstein condensate of Cooper pairs, a degenerate Pfaffian superconductor, and a Calabrese-Maris pfaffian superconductor phase which is similar to the pfaffian superconductor previously studied. The quantum phase transitions can be detected by monitoring the double occupation or the long range antiferromagnetic correlation among the particles. The phase diagrams can be visualized using a effective model, which incorporates a Z2 gauge field, particle hopping, and a BEC-Coper pair hopping. The study also suggests that the pfaffian superconductor phase can be studied in a experiment using cold atom technology by creating a kagome lattice structure. Furthermore, the study reveals a quantum phase transitions can as well be achived in a kagome lattice structure by includng a next-nearest neighbor hopping.

A novel nanoantenna is proposed that leverages a quantum interference phenomenon between optical modes.  By combining a pair of quantum dots coupled to the nanoantenna, the spectral positions of resonances can be independently fine-tuned.  This is based on the dots' ability to exert local control over the antenna's mode through a quantum "scattering" effect.  The proposed concept offers a promising approach for managing light-matter interaction at the quantum level.  Our study involves a theoretical examination of an experimentally feasible geometry consisting of a silicon nanoribbon paired with silane quantum dots positioned on an air/Ta2O5/silver stack.  The analysis demonstrates a reliable alignment of resonance peaks across the considered spectral range, and spectral positions that can be precisely controlled through a small-sized silver nanoantenna.  By positioning two quantum dots near the antenna's ends, the theory shows that it's possible to implement a multiplexing system operating across the entire 1550 nm spectral range.  This could have significant implications for applications such as enhancing the efficiency of interconnections in photonic integrated circuits, or boosting the efficiency of solar cells by harnessing multiple wavelengths of light.

Amorphous materials have long been recognized for their role in plasitic deformation. Research in physics has focused on theoretical and numerical modeling of their mechanical properties. To improve these models, it is essential to develop a fundamental understanding of the relationship between their microstructure and influence of various stress and strain rates. Current research using simulations often employs simplified thermodynamic criteria to model temperture changes. These criteria sometimes yield unrealistic results and conflict with the experimentally verified principles of thermodynamics. In this study, we introduce a simulation model that adheres to thermodynamics while allowing for complex heat transfer management. Our model is tested on a material typically used in 3D printing and the results demonstrate its compatibility with experimental data. Furthermore, we discover that both thermal and thermomechanical treatments can transform a crystalline material into an amorphous state with distinct mechanical properties that are characterized by a permanent deformation that is not reversible.

The Hubbard model, effective at describing strong correlations between electrons, is studied on silicene surfaces modified by adding Mn atoms in two different arrangements (Mn on top of Si sites or in hollow sites). The focus of this investigation lies in how varying the decoration ratio of Mn on both types of sites affects a parameter in the model, with total Mn counts ranging from one to seven and exploring the difference in electronic properties between Mn on Si sites and Mn on hollow sites. The latter has Mn forming bonds with Si, cascade with Ca, and exhibiting a ligand field band structure. By increasing the ratio of Mn to 100 percent, it is observed that Mn on Si sites transitions from an effective half-filled d-band Hubbard model to a more saturated, multiplexed version. In contrast, Mn on hollow sites remains in a state that initially adheres to a specific, numeric pattern. The number of active d-electrons on Mn determines whether Mn on Si sites or Mn on hollow sites exhibits specific properties. It would be counterintuitive to consider either site as a starting point for exploration using available methods. It would be wise to explore using another method instead of using Mn on Si sites if Mn on Si sites is chosen as a starting point for exploration using that method. It would be wise to explore using another method instead of using Mn on hollow sites if Mn on hollow sites is chosen as a starting point for exploration using that method.

Recent investigations into the activity of the Galactic centre have concentrated on Sgr A East, a double bellows type supernova remnant located just 13.4 parsecs from the centre. Due to its proximity, the radiation from Sgr A East is distinctly visible against the bright luminosity of the Galactic centre. Consequently, estimates of its distance have varied between 8 and 15 parsecs. A thorough examination of the stellar surroundings of the Galactic centre carried out by the Beassort survey in Gaia enabled researchers to determine the latitude of the Galactic centre, allowing for a correction of earlier estimates based on stellar velocities. It was discovered that Sgr A East is situated approximately 9.4 parsecs from the Galactic centre, rather than 13.4 parsecs as previously estimated. Consequently, a study was undertaken to determine the age and evolutionary stage of this supernova remnant using a complex model that accounted for different types of supernovae, cloud expansion, and shock interaction. These analyses revealed that Sgr A East, which exploded approximately 1.0 to 1.5 million years ago, may develop into a historical supernova remnant similar to RX J1703.2+6254 or possibly undergo a shock wave cycle, potentially similar to the circulating remnant of 8E.

This study investigates the effect of class imbalance on various machine learning algorithms, including neural networks, KNN, and SVM, on a specific dataset of Python/seJAR for the purpose of developing an automatic repair system. The aim is to analyze how these methods handle biased datasets and assess their performance using accuracy, precision, and recall metrics. Furthermore, this research examines the impact of data balancing strategies on the performance of these learning algorithms. The results indicate significant disparities in performance among the different algorithms, with neural networks performing better but still struggling with significantly lower repair accuracy for faulty classes. In contrast, SVM outperforms other methods in terms of precision and recall for the minority class. Notably, while data balancing slightly improves performance of neural networks and KNN, this effect is more notable for KNN, suggesting a better integration of underperformance weighting for neural networks but not for KNN. Based on these findings, potential strategies for further improving performance of neural networks, including additional data augmentation, hyperparameter tuning, and more sophisticated repair strategies, are considered.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, a vast amount of coronavirus-related news from 38 European countries was gathered and processed through an infrastructure designed for data collection and pandemic-informed news analysis. This infrastructure relied on multi-dimensional news clustering for conceptualization and visualization. By utilizing dimensional reduction techniques, a comprehensive COVID-19 news visual display was developed, showcasing thematic evolution, country-specific news volumes, and the influence of individual topics across 38 countries. Furthermore, this study examined COVID-19 news coverage, COVID-19-related news coverage in individual countries, and compared it to global pandemic data on new infections and deaths. Despite initial increases in COVID-19 news volume and peak, the analysis found no synchronization between the two curves. Meanwhile, a notable phenomenon observed was the correlation between temperatures and COVID-19 news volume in Southern Europe. Meanwhile, a notable phenomenon also observed was the correlation between temperatures and COVID-19 news volume in Southern Europe.

In addressing complex issues in astrophysical research such as resolving small-scale phenomena while incorporating large-scale data, the University of California, Berkeley's 'Cosmological N-Body Simulations' project presents a crucial challenge. We submit our proposal for using the Fast Multipole Method in N-Body Simulations as a potential solution. By leveraging the FMM, our algorithm reduces computational cost in parallel processing, enabling the replication of results in serial computation that would normally be achieved with quadrature methods. We outline the framework, implications, related work, and anticipated outcomes for our approach.

The double spin asymmetry demonstrated in the ep → e′γ′oγ process has been measured and examined by the COMPASS collaboration using the pp collision data collected at different values of the polarised electron beam, beam's polarisation and target's polarisation. This particular asymmetry is predicted to be significantly affected by the polarised photon's mass and the spin connection between the initial electron and the proton, as well as by the helicity-mixed coupling of the W boson. Despite the small order of the cross-section, an accuracy of a few percent is achievable due to the integration of the collected data over a large range of kinematics. However, the analysis was conducted under the assumption of the initial electron's beam polarisation being uncorrelated with the other measured quantities. As a result, the presented double spin asymmetry remains independent of any assumptions regarding the initial electron's beam polarisation. An accuracy of approximately 20 percent in the integrated cross section has been achieved and the results are in line with the Standard Model predictions.

The challenge of transferring an expert's control skills to a complex robotic system has been identified as policy cloning. Current approaches, however, are limited by their reliance on uninformed behavior cloning techniques. Since the expert's demonstrations may not cover the entire system state space, the student learns suboptimal skills, often resulting in poor performance outside the expert's experience. To improve performance in unknown system conditions, some solutions involve model-based reinforcement learning. However, these methods require extensive model training, which can be particularly demanding for high- degree-of-freedom control problems. To address these limitations, we propose an augmented policy cloning method that leverages data from both successful and failure expert policies. This comprehensive approach enriches the student's training environment, helping them learn robust and optimal control skills. The method's effectiveness was demonstrated on a complex 18-DOF control problem, with the student achieving performance levels matching the expert's capabilities, and often surpassing it.

Leptoquark pair production in proton-proton collisions is examined at the LHC with the collision energy reaching 14 TeV. The research considers three types of leptoquarks - scalar, pseudoscalar, and vector versions - and focuses on how they pair up. The study looks specifically at how these leptoquarks decay into a top quark, a charged lepton, and a $\tau$-lepton. The analysis involves two types of leptoquark charge combinations and two production modes, and it relies on an exclusive decay product final state with just one hard top quark, one charged lepton, and a lot of $\tau$-lepton decay products. The study shows that up to 100 fb for certain leptoquark masses and production modes is within reach with a certain amount of data collected. This study also offers mass limits on heavy $Y$ bosons - a type of leptoquark - in the mass range between 400 and 800 GeV, a certain amount of data was collected, a 700 GeV mass range had a 95% confidence level mass limit.

Research on resonant spin masers is gaining momentum, and so is interest in incorporating digital signal processing into this emerging spin-based phenomenon. Our study delves into the interplay between digital signals and a two-level system, similar to a transverse Ising model, resulting from the interaction between the spin maser's resonant modes and digital signals. Using numerical methods, we investigate the merging of digital signals into the spin maser's spectrum and analyze the complex interactions between their coupled modes. By adjusting the system's parameters, we identify various states with unique characteristics, ranging from singletons to the clustering of digital signals. Our analysis also sheds light on the intriguing relationship between the digital signals and a two-level system. Furthermore, we propose potential applications of this combined digital and resonant spin system.

We provide specific hypergeometric groups, which serve as subgroups of the K3 surface's Siegel modular group, to represent the automorphisms of a K3 surface when the coordinates are defined by hypergeometric functions with common complex multiplicities.

We propose an experimental signature to identify the process of $\gamma$ ray production through the decay of a hidden neutralino that forms a bound state with a $Z'$ boson. This neutralino can transition to a hidden neutralino through the influence of a nonhermitian soft mass. As a result, the hidden neutralino moves to a state of near rest, thereby converting some of its energy into a highly energetic gamma ray, which can be detected by experiments such as XENON1T and future dark matter searches in underground laboratories. We find that neutralino decays within the experiment can contribute significantly to its background. Furthermore, by examining the energy distribution of these gamma rays, we can determine the energy range in which these decays occur and then calculate the associated production cross-sections. Additionally, we find that neutralino decays can, in some instances, dominate the visible decay channel of a $Z'$ boson. We also propose a model that explains the excess in the Fermi-LAT's 3-year $Z'$-related data through the introduction of a small mixing parameter. Finally, by employing future gamma ray sensitivity projections, we establish present and future bounds on the parameter space of our proposed model.

A well-known theorem by F.K. Chung and T. Sotak gives necessary and sufficient conditions for a graph to be representable by edges and faces of equal length on a surface of a specific genus. These conditions are equivalent to another set of requirements related to a graph's embedding in a surface, its facial boundaries, and its chromatic properties. In a related finding, a set of conditions were discovered that are both necessary and sufficient for a bi-colourable graph to be embeddable on a specific surface of genus.

This work offers a set of novel stochastic optimization techniques for large-scale linear optimization problems that incorporate composite objectives and is applicable to diverse problems such as regression, support vector machine, and multi-task learning. By harnessing the capabilities of dual averaging and path-wise methods, these algorithms efficiently minimize complex objectives with non-smooth components at the expense of a slightly increased overall bias. To reduce communication overhead, we incorporate sparsification techniques that selectively send the gradient vector to the server, thereby significantly decreasing data transmission time. This approach is part of a broader optimization framework called COCO, which is rigorously analyzed within a distributed stochastic optimization setting. Our theoretical findings show that under specific conditions, our approach maintains an optimal rate of convergence, even in the presence of weak assumptions about the objective function. Furthermore, we experimentally verify the efficacy of our method on a diversity of problems.

Our research explores the effectiveness of transfer learning in cross-lingual pretraining and fine-tuning of NLP models. Although considerable studies have validated the importance of shared cognitive abilities among languages that have a common ancestral source, the impact of genetic relatedness on NLP model transfer remains an uninvestigated area. To delve into this topic, we examined the NLP tasks of two languages with varying degrees of genetic connection. One language, Cebuano, is a Philistine language closely related to Spanish, while the other languages are Filipino and English. A set of NLP tasks in the Cebuano language were compiled and initially trained on a limited dataset. Our experiments showed the benefits of transferring knowledge from larger, genetically unrelated datasets. Additionally, the performance of our cross-lingual models was assessed under both low-resource and high-resource conditions. Our results suggest that NLP model transfer is more reliable when the source and target languages have a common ancestral source, and that larger, genetically unrelated datasets can enhance NLP model training. To the NLP community's knowledge, our research represents a pioneering study of the association between NLP model transfer and genetic connection.

In the field of low-energy particle detection, particularly when studying dark matter, researchers use Gas Time Projection Chambers to detect particle-recoil interactions. To enhance the sensitivity of these experiments to various types of dark matter interactions, new methods for distinguishing between particle and nuclear recoil observables have been developed. These methods involve analyzing electron-recoil and nuclear-recoil states using multiple observables, rather than relying solely on recoil energy. By employing Machine Learning algorithms, researchers were able to analyze experimental data from the DarkSide-50 experiment and improve the discrimination between particle and nuclear recoil scenarios using the following observables: ionization shape, emission of scintillation light, and event location. Using these new observables in a Boltzmann Transporter model and a Convolutional Neural Network, researchers achieved improved discrimination similar to that achieved with established techniques, along with significant reductions in computational resources needed.

The evaluation of driver behavior is typically conducted by human experts who
consider various factors when making assessments. However, these evaluations are
time-consuming. A potential solution to automate this process could significantly
improve accuracy, as human experts may miss specific driving circumstances.
Research has previously explored the use of machine learning to replicate human
evaluations but often fails to account for the expert's reasoning behind their
decisions. By developing a model that incorporates both the driver's behavior
and the reasons for their behavior, we can create a more effective model for
evaluation. Expert-driven road assessment is particularly applicable to areas
like monitoring traffic lights, signage, and road markings, as these elements are
relatively few in number. By leveraging these characteristics, we can implement a
more efficient model. In this study, we have successfully combined the analysis
of driver behavior with the underlying reasons for their behavior. Using the
reasons behind driver behavior allowed our model to reach the same level of
accuracy as human experts in multiple instances, while outperforming them in
others. Additionally, the model produced relevant explanations for its assessments
when the reasons behind driver behavior were absent. By developing this two-part
model, we hope to have taken the first substantial step towards the mass use of
AI in driver behavior assessment systems.

The past few years have witnessed significant progress in text detection and recognition for scenes, largely fostered by standard benchmarks like ICDAR. A pioneering OOV (out-of-vocabulary) dataset established new benchmarks for recognizing words not seen during model training. A thorough review of papers using this OOV dataset reveals they often isolate it from the underlying training and evaluation datasets, thus preserving the true difficulty of the OOV data and obtaining more authentic performance assessments for scene text recognition models. Furthermore, our analysis indicates certain pre-existing predictions of difficult words are unfairly favored, and we propose a novel word importance measure that more accurately reflects these biases, resulting in more realistic performance evaluations on the OOV dataset. Consequently, we suggest adhering to an unusual, yet authentic, evaluation protocol that distinguishes it from existing models by separately evaluating models on seen, unseen, and out-of-vocabulary words, especially in the out-of-vocabulary case.

Data from two distinct regimes may exhibit a non-trivial connection that can be uncovered by analyzing their statistical similarities and differences. Our research focuses on comparing random fields with either high or low frequency components, and we introduce a novel metric called the generalized field distance (GFD) to quantify their level of association. The GFD metric employs a wavelet-based approach and draws upon the concepts of field correlations, energy spectrum ratios, and power law relationships. By utilizing this metric, we can assess various intermediate states and monitor how these states evolve over time. Our study applies this metric to a detailed data set from 2017, the Santa Barbara Channel, featuring seismometric activity spanning three decades, and it successfully identifies the non-linear dynamics of the system. Our accurate, real-time predictions of earthquake sequences corroborate this finding, and our analysis also enables us to pinpoint the initial points of the system's transition, including the onset of the 2019 sequence, which was triggered by a significant change in the seismic turbulence intensity. Our research opens up opportunities for developing more effective and timely earthquake forecasts and contributes to a deeper understanding of the seismic dynamics.

We conduct an experiment on the hydrodynamic instability of a rotating fluid layer using the semi-arbitrary magnetic levitation technique to assess initial perturbations. This technology allows us to analyze the effect of gravity and anisotropy simultaneously, and it doesn't rely on the assumptions associated with the usual levitation methods. Since the rotating fluid layer in our experiment can be started at any desired rotation rate, we're able to observe a gradual transition from stable to unstable behavior. Moreover, the semi-arbitrary levitation technique enables us to analyze the effect of magnetic levitation on perturbations, such as convective rolls, as well as the decay of unstable spirals. Our experiment shows that the semi-arbitrary levitation technique has several advantages over traditional methods, and it's particularly useful for studying rotating fluid instability.

Building on previous research, we extended T. Church's findings on Hecke L-functions for SL2(Z) to primitive forms in SL2(Z), revealing a link to his, G. Anderson's, and M. Ponger's work on Sp2n(Z) cuspidal Hecke eigenforms. Notably, our results broaden the general case previously established by M. Ponger and one of the authors, incorporating T. Church's work on SL2(Z) as a particular instance. Furthermore, our analysis covered the context of level structures. Utilizing the term "prolongation," we explored how one-type Hecke L-functions sequence evolves as the level increases. Additionally, our general approach led to new information about L-functions moments and the growth rates of Hecke norms. Recent research by R. Ostrowski and one of the authors connects the growth rates to the abundance of one-type Siegel cusp forms.

This research investigates how graphene is joined to conventional conductors, focusing specifically on graphene single atomic layer Schottky contacts. By analyzing electronic structure, which differs significantly from that of conventional materials, we used the non-equilibrium Green's functions method to study transport properties in graphene conductor junctions. Through our calculations, we demonstrated that charge carrier injection is much higher from the conductor into graphene than from graphene into the conductor due to the barrier created. Additionally, we found that graphene's electronic structure has a minimal impact on current-voltage characteristics until a significant threshold, beyond which the carrier injection dynamics switch to a regime where the carrier energy far exceeds the graphene's electronic structure peak. Consequently, this shifts the injection rate to much smaller photon-assisted rates compared to the carrier injection regime. At this switched regime, we showed that the quantum efficiency of photoluminescence can reach nearly 100%, which is much higher than the quantum efficiency of the conventional radiative recombination rate in graphene. Furthermore, we established that the photon-assisted rates follow a logarithmic increase with respect to the radiation intensity.

This study investigates the behavior of half-space algorithms in order to approximate solutions of equations involving potentially nonlinear operators. Initially, we establish a theoretical framework, which includes assumptions applicable to both linear and nonlinear operators, including those with nonlinear components that exhibit Lipschitz-like behavior or other sublinear properties. This theoretical framework enables us to obtain broad, multi-dimensional convergence theorems for Banach lattices, which hold regardless of the norm used. Furthermore, we verify that several nonlinear maps, such as completely positive operators and sublinear operators, meet our established criteria. Building upon these findings, we use the developed theoretical framework to study the convergence of half-space algorithms for several classes of nonlinear operators, including A-proximal mappings, enfolding operators, and asymptotically regular operators. Additionally, we utilize this approach to derive strong convergence results for several algorithms. Multiple illustrative examples are provided to validate the efficacy of our half-space algorithms.

Pancyclic graphs are a fascinating class of cyclic in nature. Researchers have found that many pancyclic graphs also possess another important property - a large number of independent vertices. Specifically, they discovered that for pancyclic graphs with a large number of independent vertices, a smaller number is required for their cyclic nature to be guaranteed. This precise relationship has been formally stated as a claim and proven for pancyclic graphs with a large number of independent vertices for specific types of molecular structure graphs. However, for more general cases of pancyclic graphs with a large number of independent vertices, a precise relationship could not be established through similar means for general cases of pancyclic graphs with a large number of independent vertices. However, for a particular family of pancyclic graphs with a large number of independent vertices, a precise relationship could be established.

The behavior of light hadrons emerging from a hot, dense medium created in high-energy collisions of heavy ions is influenced by pressure gradients, the initial state of the medium, and the characteristics of the medium. A quasi-static analysis reveals that as the density of the medium transitions from its initial to equilibrium states, the gradients of pressure drive the expansion. This dynamic is characterized by an initial phase of acceleration, during which the gradient of velocity is dependent on the gradient of pressure. Partonic states with higher velocity gradients tend to accelerate, whereas collective flow measurements indicate a reverse relationship for photons and mesons. This study provides a unified description of hadron production, collective flow, and the flow-induced energy spectra of these particles, showing that it is primarily the pressure gradient that distinguishes the initial phase of expansion from equilibrium states.

A new technique called SASK has been developed for modeling complex light behavior in various media. This approach employs a specialized light source to accurately represent the desired light patterns, and is based on a combination of two algorithms: a standard finite-difference solver for direct lighting, and a more efficient Monte Carlo-based algorithm for handling complex lighting effects. By separating simple and complex lighting components, SASK reduces the computational cost of simulations, and our results show that it outperforms existing methods by up to 10 times for certain scenarios. We have successfully tested SASK on real-world projects, including the creation of realistic images of medical tissues illuminated by a focused laser beam. Compared to other lighting estimation methods, SASK produces more accurate results with a significant reduction in computational time and memory requirements.

We employed the Gaussian basis set method to investigate the electric resonance of a water molecule in a homogeneous DC electric field, calculating the vibration, rotation, and mixed levels up to 3150 cm$^{-1}$ and 80 MHz. The research yielded resonance parameters of $x_i\mu E$ = 286.06, 57.43, and 2.56 	imes 10^{-40} esu\^2 for the $
u_1$, $
u_2$, and $
u_3$ modes, alongside a significant coupling parameter of $k_{12}$ = 2.31 	imes 10^{-40} esu\^2. These results demonstrated a satisfactory convergence of the system with 2915 Gaussian functions while maintaining a small diagonal element of the mass matrix of less than $-10^{-8}$ amu. Furthermore, we evaluated the effect of symmetry constraints, showing that this method can be an efficient strategy for analyzing vibrational spectra of small molecules, particularly in the presence of electric-dipole moments.

Building upon the OT-based interpolation theory developed by Arjou, Peter and Cuturi in 2021, this study extends its applications to solve nonlinear equations with dissipative effects. Under specific conditions, we demonstrate that an approximation can be achieved by using the Sinkhorn algorithm, even in cases where the original problem has no solution. This research also explores the connections between the OT-based approximation method and a classical numerical approach known as the Galerkin method for nonlinear equations with dissipative effects. Notably, we show that approximating solutions to these equations involves optimizing a dual objective function, even when the original equation does not have a solution. This work further illustrates how the OT-based approximation method can be employed to derive equilibrium states for energy dynamics.

Measurements of the top-quark pair production cross-section, $t\bar{t}$, in proton-proton collisions recorded by the CMS experiment at the LHC are presented. The data, collected at a 13 TeV energy high-energy collision site, amounts to 138 inverse femtobarns, exceeding the theoretical 11 TeV energy threshold previously thought to be the maximum. Using a boosted decision tree method, known kinematic interactions of the $t\bar{t}$ system are determined and used to calculate a cross-section for $t\bar{t}$ production, agreeing with the theoretical standard model predictions within statistical and systematic margins of error. Additionally, $t\bar{t}$ production cross-section measurements in several event kinematic states and top-quark spin polarisation asymmetries are also reported.

Our study explores how the entanglement in a disordered spin system spreads to a central qubit or cavity mode. Initially, the entanglement between the central element and the disordered system decreases and reaches a null point according to a predictable polynomial rate. However, when the central element is replaced with a cavity mode, the decay follows a more complex pattern involving multiple breaks. This phenomenon is attributed to the realignment of the cavity mode with continuously changing collective energy states as the system's components shift due to randomly applied external influences. Furthermore, the breakpoints can be precisely determined by the duration of the collective spin wave packet formation process.

We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for a generalized Bessel function, specifically $R_{\beta,\lambda,\nu}(z)$, to exhibit Janowski convexity and starlikeness in the unit disk $|z| < 1$, also investigating relationships with other convex and starlike functions.

The COVID-19 pandemic marked a turning point in the history of the past century by becoming the first fully global catastrophe.  At its peak in January 2021, the pandemic reached a milestone of 700,000 cases in a single week in Europe, causing immense human suffering, devastating economies, and fundamentally altering people's perspectives worldwide.  Although the pandemic's immediate consequences received extensive coverage in the media, the lasting impact of this event remains largely a subject of inquiry.  Our research investigates how the pandemic altered the diversity of urban encounters and gives rise to resilient communities as measured by clustering properties.  To this effect, we present Epidem, a comprehensive event dataset covering over 480,000 real-time urban encounters along with their geographic locations and diverse interaction contexts.  Within this dataset, we employed clustering to represent individual cities and groups of cities, and by examining the hierarchy of these clusters, we are able to identify long-lasting changes that occurred following the pandemic.  Our visualizations of the city interaction cluster hierarchies reveal the lasting effects of the pandemic by aligning with various public health data across more than 500 major cities around the world.  Moreover, a web-based service that we developed to display and explore these clusters is now made freely accessible to the public.

Developing an efficient solution method for large-scale, three-dimensional mono- or multi-branch fractal submodeling systems of finite element models, particularly those employed in various industries, remains a pressing issue. This paper introduces a novel approach, FSMSN, to accelerate the solution process by leveraging fractal geometry properties. This results in a system of equations that can be broken down into smaller, more manageable sub-systems, each with fewer degrees of freedom and thus quicker convergence times. In contrast to fully implicit methods that involve extensive matrix factorization, FSMSN only factorizes each sub-system's associated matrix, minimizing computational overhead. To take full advantage of parallel processing capabilities, the paper also describes a parallelization strategy, resulting in significantly reduced solution times. Up to 20 times faster than traditional solution methods for complex models, such as a 51-million-element fractal submodel, and offering similar speed-ups for multi-branch systems of similar size, this strategy outperforms its predecessors.

A chiral optical cavity created from a single optical spin (polariton) enables a heightened interaction between light and spinning molecules, which maintains their inherent properties.  Our mathematical model describes how this cavity connects to molecules within the cavity and how it influences the behavior of the polariton's forward and backward movements.
