Using experiments and a mathematical approach called Green's function, we studied a specific configuration of the cavity and molecules and found a range of possible behaviors in this setup.  Our findings also apply to a more complex arrangement of the cavity and molecules called chiral photonic sphere.  In both cases, we discovered a transition from normal to abnormal behavior, which occurs when specific conditions involving the cavity and molecules change.  Normal behavior shows separate forward and backward movements, while abnormal behavior shows a shared forward and backward movements.  These results open pathways to studying similar interactions in other areas of physics, such as condensed matter and particle physics, and provide a basis for understanding similar processes in both living and non-living systems.

Two-dimensional anti de-Sitter spaces within the context of two-dimensional string theory can be thought of as a more fundamental model compared to Schr\"{o}dinger holography. This theory, which expands upon the classical BMS$_3$ framework found in Ashtekar et. al. (2015), incorporates a quantum Hamiltonian constraint. Our work utilizes a more efficient canonical quantization approach compared to the one traditionally utilized in string theory. This alternative method yields a consistent Hilbert space and well-defined operators. As a result, our study provides a precise quantum framework for both primary and secondary observables in two-dimensional string theory. It also offers a novel framework for quantizing anti de-Sitter spacetimes, which can in turn be utilized for holographic Schr\"{o}dinger maps.

Researchers seeking an algebraic warp drive have successfully developed a stable solution without resorting to exotic matters or energies, which could have significant implications for quantum gravity and cosmology. This new solution eliminates the singularity that has long posed a major hurdle in the field, and demonstrates a stable and continuous spacetime within a rocket-shaped region. This particular setup can be viewed as a spacetime domain wall. Furthermore, indicating a potential application in quantum gravity and cosmology, existing theories such as General Relativity and Brans-Dicke theories have been shown to accommodate the algebraic warp drive, which may also provide valuable insights for achieving a warp drive in quantum gravity and cosmology.

The identification of the best options for urban underground infrastructure systems, including energy, water, and telecommunications networks, presents a complex decision-making challenge due to its multifaceted nature. A novel framework known as GUIDES aims to improve the quality of decisions through the utilization of artificial intelligence techniques by providing decision-makers with a clear analysis of the current state of existing infrastructure and potential future requirements. GUIDES achieves this through (1) mapping the physical characteristics of the urban underground space and (2) simulating the behavior and impact of the infrastructure systems within the defined space. Utilizing these simulations, GUIDES runs a series of scenarios to identify the most suitable options for expanding or upgrading the infrastructure. Furthermore, GUIDES facilitates the comparison of various AI-driven planning approaches, such as optimization algorithms, learning-based algorithms, and deep learning methods, to determine their effectiveness and reliability. Through the integration of these methods, GUIDES aims to provide intelligent decision support that can adapt to changing conditions over time.

To evaluate the heat generated by an electromagnetic wave within a two-dimensional plasma arrangement in a Penning trap, we have developed a method combining both direct observation of the plasma confinement and measurements of the ambient temperature. A gas of $^9$Tl$^+$ ions is positioned centrally within a magnetized donut-shaped device. Following initial cooling to near the theoretical minimum energy state through controlled cooling processes, we employ a precise laser beam to increase the internal heat rate. By collecting data from multiple imaging sessions before and after this heating method, we are able to quantify the amount of thermal energy transferred to the two-dimensional Coulomb crystal. Furthermore, these measurements are supported by a numerical model that confirms our experimental findings, establishing a penning trap as an alternative heat source for various scientific studies. This arrangement could also serve a purpose in future research regarding whirling modes of low-temperature plasma arrangements.

A significant Raman spectroscopy technique, tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, can offer extremely detailed insights into materials, especially when an electromagnetic enhancement effect, caused by the way light interacts with materials, dominates over the chemical effect that describes how matter responds to light. Although the electromagnetic effect can significantly impact TEIRS readings, accurately separating and interpreting its contributions can be challenging. Researchers have now devised a method to quantify this effect in TEIRS, using computational models of materials and measuring how the electromagnetic effect impacts Raman spectra after a chemical mapping of the material has been conducted. This approach, demonstrated using an iron oxide nanoparticle, can provide insights into the interactions between materials and their surroundings, making it especially useful for the development and characterization of plasmonic nanoparticles.

Our past study used data from the Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 2 to look for Asymmetrical Massive Elliptical Structures (AMEs) in a diverse set of 73 spiral galaxies. The current paper presented the findings of an extensive search using the Hubble's Advanced Camera for Images to investigate 47 spiral galaxies, focusing on a specific field of view and our previous research on the diversity of galaxy shapes, a key indicator of AME presence. Unlike our previous study, this one supported the idea that the presence of a prominent central bar, interstellar material absorption or a steep central light profile are reliable indicators for the existence of AMEs in spiral galaxies, particularly those with slow rotation rates and significant disk-to-halo mass ratios. Conversely, we found little evidence to support the idea that the galaxy's overall mass or rotation speed are crucial factors. As a result, we established a set of criteria to predict the likelihood of an AME's presence in a galaxy through its projected angular speed.

This study enthalpimetrically investigated the entropy modifications produced by high-pressure treatment of the ammonium sulfate ferroelectric, a material undergoing a second-order phase transition under 3.5 GPa pressure.  We discovered that the entropy alterations primarily stem from the availability of excess energy rather than an alteration in the entropy's statistical distribution.  Additionally, the experiment revealed that the entropy's statistical distribution remains unchanged by the pressure increase.  We computed the entropy's statistical distribution using the thermodynamic relationship $\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T=$$\frac{\Delta S}{\Delta T}$, where $\Delta S$ is measured through a calorimetric approach and $\Delta T$ is measured using a fiber-optic temperature sensor with an accuracy of 0.1 K.  As a result, our research demonstrated that the ferroelectric phase transition's entropy origins are predominantly due to the excess energy.

In a learning scenario involving potential earnings and risk, we found that a key factor influencing people's decisions is not how they calculate probabilities, but rather how they incorporate past losses. Furthermore, we discovered that those who are more likely to engage in probability-matching in the face of uncertainty also tend to give greater weight to recent negative outcomes. Additionally, we found an individual difference that affects learning how to take risks, with those who are more inclined towards risk-aversion initially preferring a safer option, whereas those who are more risk-prone prefer the safer option to a lesser extent. Lastly, we found that those who are more inclined towards risk-aversion also tend to give greater weight to recent negative outcomes when learning how to take risks, whereas those who are more risk-prone give greater weight to recent gains.

The connections among three concepts - nonlocality, contextuality, and entanglement in quantum mechanics are well established. We demonstrate that these concepts are tied to the properties of unitary transformations and geometrically represented in a specific space. The illustration involves multiple boxes, each containing different pairs of qubits, and the relationships between boxes can represent different state configurations. This framework was used to develop a geometric representation of contextuality and nonlocality, and it was applied to the study of six-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states. The results of our analysis, obtained through semi-definite programming, improved our understanding of the quantum properties of these specific entangled states.

For any $\epsilon > 0$, we've developed a novel, randomized approximation algorithm for the $(1+\epsilon)$-near neighbor problem in high-dimensional Euclidean space. This algorithm addresses the issues associated with previous methods, established in our recent work, by significantly reducing both preprocessing time and query time by approximately two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the preprocessing time and query time each exhibit a linear improvement in the 1/\epsilon parameter. Additionally, the algorithm yields a significant approximation factor improvement, specifically $\text{O}(\sqrt{\log n})$-approximation, for the case of preprocessing time. This more closely aligns with the approximation factor that is achieved by previous techniques as well as the constant factor near neighbor search algorithms employing embedding or elimination-based approaches have recently achieved.

Recent advancements in quantum computers have led to the development of sensitive systems, making them highly susceptible to interference from external factors. As a result, measuring quantum systems accurately has become an even more complicated task. To address this issue, researchers are exploring the use of unfolding techniques to mitigate measurement errors. Typically, unfolding involves processing collected data through an inverse mapping to retrieve original distributions, often resulting in high computational costs. To make unfolding more feasible on large datasets, a new approach involves dividing the process into multiple iterative steps that can be executed quickly and efficiently. Each iterative step involves making an educated guess about the original distribution and then evaluating how well that guess aligns with the measured data. The process continues until the predicted and actual distributions converge closely, at which point the predicted distribution is considered to be the original measurement. Theoretical and experimental analysis of this iterative method has demonstrated its effectiveness in producing reliable results even with limited data collection. The algorithm has also shown its capacity to handle complex systems composed of many quantum systems. This work presents the first practical application of Bayesian unfolding in the field of quantum science and technology.

In order to answer this question, we introduce a straightforward robot-assisted method called RoboLIM, which makes clear to users one aspect of a robot's program, such as the specific task inputs it selected. Our study compares the efficiency of humans accomplishing a series of tasks, both with and without access to this information, such as following a leader. Our experiment, conducted with 48 participants over two conditions, revealed a significant and straightforward lesson learned by participants when they new about the robot's chosen input mappings - they could complete our tasks 13% faster. Furthermore, based on the results, we've created a framework that predicts the effectiveness of numerous robot-enabled interfaces based on the degree to which they expose the robot's input program. We also found that, following initial exposure, users began to distrust an imperfect robot, yet discovered their trustfulness when the robot corrected its mistakes. Finally, we found that users preferred a full exposure strategy, but only when other factors such as the robot's accuracy and their own ability, were not factors.

Global metric maps like OctoMap and HRLMap, which represent 3D environments through 2D cell maps, have become a standard for robotic simulation and localization. However, the inherent global focus of these maps leads to inconsistent data management, with large areas consuming more storage and computation. On the other hand, local maps generated by SLAM algorithms like ORB-SLAM3D are dominated by system crashes when they fail to merge into a comprehensive map. To address these issues, we present HiTMap, a new representation and management system for 3D environments. By utilizing a hierarchical structure with a global tree and cell maps, HiTMap balances data representation and navigation. The system's tree, constructed through a customized RRT path, assigns priority to inner nodes which represent the navigation focus, with map cell sets corresponding to these nodes stored in memory. When a new inner node is created, either through direct perception or map fusion, it receives the highest priority, ensuring optimal navigation and memory management. This novel approach also incorporates dynamic tree adaptation, incorporating measures such as tree balance factor and sensor range to optimize the representation. Furthermore, HiTMap integrates a sensor-based fusion filter to merge HiTMap-like maps, constructed from local observations, into a comprehensive and accurate map. The performance of HiTMap has been validated through simulations and real-world experiments, demonstrating its superiority over traditional representations, particularly in terms of memory efficiency, tree balance, and overall performance.

A new approach to creating two-dimensional Z-complementary array code sets (ZCACS) using generalized Boolean functions is presented, providing a fundamental tool for constructing orthogonal wavelet functions. In contrast to traditional generalized Boolean functions with Boolean outputs, this approach involves the use of frequency-domain operators to produce non-Boolean inputs, and subsequent modulation, addition, and shift operations to form the code set's constitutive wavelet functions. Analysis of the wavelet functions' properties, including their autocorrelation and cross-correlation, is performed using the Fourier series of associated generalized Boolean functions. Moreover, it is proven that the inter-code interference ratio (ICIR) increases with the size of the code set, and it is also found that the sum of the ICIRs for all codes in the set is constant. Examples are given to demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in practice.

A novel approach to CT image reconstruction is presented, addressing the limitations imposed by noise in X-ray measurements, such as Poisson and Gaussian noise, under an additional low-dose constraint. This method combines a deep neural network-based image reconstruction technique, originally fabricated for a specific low-dose scenario, with a statistical artefact removal method. The results show that this hybrid approach successfully mitigates statistical errors in CT scans under reduced radiation exposure while preserving image details.

Building upon the well-established effective gap width method, this study expands its applicability to predict the impact of various obstacle shapes and orientations on light traveling through a medium. A novel, more locally relevant approach is introduced, which outperforms the standard model by considering the effects of multiple particles. By analyzing various scenarios, it is demonstrated that the new model efficiently reproduces computational simulations, while significantly reducing the computational costs involved. The developed methodology has immense potential to significantly lower simulation costs in scenarios involving multiple and complex-shaped obstacles.

Contextual named entity retrieval relies on contextual information, like the full text, to guide the selection of relevant entities from candidate suggestions. Current contextual NER approaches face two limitations: the need for massive storage of indexed text, requiring significant time to retrieve candidates, and the necessity of labeled data for training, which can be costly to annotate. To address these challenges, our proposed system uses the distilBERT model to encode the context, enabling the use of pre-trained models despite storage constraints. Additionally, our system allows for user feedback incorporation to refine the retrieval process. Initially tested on a small-scale dataset, our system outperforms the current benchmark contextual NER system, achieving a mean average precision of 0.3616. The combination of pre-trained models and user feedback incudes a large, unlabelled dataset of Wikipedia pages and thousands of possible entity candidates.

This project involves creating a browser extension for visualizing temporal plots 
within interactive temporal representation (ITR) objects, which include time 
charts such as timelines, schedules, and decision tables.  The goal is to expand 
on existing temporal plot functionality by integrating ITR objects with plot 
datasets, enabling linking and syncing between temporal plots and other visual tools, 
like maps and decision tables.  Furthermore, we aim to add features that allow 
users to navigate ITR objects with their browsers and generalize the functionality 
for a broader range of temporal plot types.  The functionality will be based on 
an adapted version of the HyperLinx browser extension, which originally linked and 
synced plot data with other geospatial visualization tools.  Initially, we plan to 
test the extension with decision tables, decision tables with timelines, and law 
review publications.  Hypothesized benefits include greater accessibility and 
utilization of decision-making data among relevant stakeholders.

Recent advancements in heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs) have led to their increasing application in the analysis of Electronic Health Records (EHRs). However, the knotty structure of EHR graphs poses significant challenges to the learning of predictive models using standard inductive representation mechanisms, as seen in transRGNs and graph attention. To overcome these challenges, we employ an extension of the variational graph attention model, combined with a novel message passing strategy, to create MG-VarAG, a graph attention model that operates on heterogeneous graphs through a hybrid approach. This approach applies message passing either at the graph level or at the node level, with weights dynamically determined. We demonstrate MG-VarAG's efficacy in the prediction of patient outcomes for acute kidney injury and admission to ICU from EHR datasets. Research findings confirm MG-VarAG's superior performance when compared to established models, while its explainability capabilities offer valuable insights into the learning process.

We conducted thorough analyses using mean-squared displacement and velocity auto-correlation techniques to examine the behavior of an electrolyte composed of monovalent ions near a soft, charged surface in three-dimensional spaces. This analysis was carried out under the context of a hypernetted-chain approximation. Our research originally employed a two-dimensional model to study the effects of increased ion size on electrolyte behavior, but our present study expands upon this concept by introducing size differences into a three-dimensional model. Our key findings reveal that hypernetted-chain approximations closely align with simulations and existing molecular dynamics data. Moreover, our results demonstrate that hypernetted-chain predictions for a three-dimensional model replicate the well-documented, hypernetted-chain-derived charge density results from a two-dimensional system. This research further shows that increased ion size tends to amplify the hypernetted-chain-derived charge density at the soft surface boundary, a phenomenon that exhibits an inverted relationship with a hyperbolic function as ionic size increases. This research further explores a three-dimensional model by accounting for size differences between oppositely charged ions. This study serves as a fundamental understanding of a three-dimensional model and its applicability to real-world systems.

To determine BERT's performance in analyzing software requirements documentation, we compared it with other cutting-edge models, such as fastText, ELMo, and Bi-LSTM. We also considered deep and shallow Baseline approaches. We evaluated the models using three distinct metrics based on different target variables and found that BERT, with its fine-tuned version, consistently yielded superior results. Specifically, we found that BIRT significantly outperformed other models on two of the three performance measures. Furthermore, we identified key factors that affect the performance of the models, with the quality of the available dataset playing a crucial role. Based on our findings, we recommend using BERT in the development of user interfaces and automated tools to identify software requirements.

This research focuses on reducing energy consumption in cooperative multi-user relay networks. Each user and relay nodes have adjustable power usage and the ability to turn off their transmitters. To minimize energy expenditure while maintaining maximum data transfer rates, a joint optimization technique is applied. This approach involves a two-stage process: the initial stage identifies the subsets of relay nodes with optimal performance through an association procedure, followed by a solution computation that takes into account the initial subsets in the second stage. Consequently, a joint strategy is obtained that achieves the lowest possible energy consumption while maintaining maximum data transfer rates. Furthermore, a solution computation method with a polynomial degree of complexity is provided. Specifically, a computation-laboratory test is performed using a multi-user relay network consisting of 6 users and 10 relay nodes, confirming the efficiency of the proposed algorithm.

The spin-orbit coupling strongly impacts the positions of YSR state peaks at energies lower than the Fermi level. While the positions of the first peak are determined by the spin-orbit coupling of individual magnetic adatoms, those at lower energies are influenced by interactions within the adatom's Kramers' degenerate state. Notably, the spin-orbit coupling causes the second YSR state peak to shift towards higher energies when interacting with pairs of magnetic adatoms, unlike the scenario where the interactions are non-fermionic in nature, which results in the opposite effect. Additionally, the spin-orbit coupling causes the elliptical shape of the second peak to rotate when viewed in a specific direction.

Downsampling point clouds can enhance the accuracy of LIDAR data registration, but current approaches fail to consider the unique challenges posed by dynamic objects. In this study, a simple yet robust method for registering point clouds in dynamic environments is presented. By utilizing a graph-based attribute matching (GAM) technique, the proposed method focuses on downsampled local structures and detects the rigid transformations within the individual point cloud datasets. The GAM method is initialized with a self-consistent registration framework and converges through a process that optimizes graph-based scores. Experimental evaluations conducted on both simulated and real-world data indicate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in registering point clouds in environments with both static and dynamic elements. Moreover, the proposed method is able to achieve registration results comparable to those obtained with superpoint features on real-world data, and it successfully registers point clouds in environments featuring large-scale dynamics, such as traffic cones.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to impressive performance on various satellite image analysis tasks, yet most methods are unsuitable for practical application due to their high computational demands. As a result, they are often too costly and time-consuming to deploy on the latest K210/K286 kits, which offer a combination of CPU and GPU resources. To overcome this challenge, this study presents an efficient method for training and deploying deep learning models, including vectorized Python execution and a detailed analysis of the time required for each model layer. Using this approach, we were able to achieve fast inference times for multiple state-of-the-art benchmark datasets. For instance, we were able to attain $45.65\pm0.87$\% mAP on ImageNet-64k Large Dataset, while also ensuring efficient processing even at a data rate of 1 Gbit/s. Furthermore, we were able to achieve fast model training times, ranging from hours to days, and ultimately succeed in deploying the top-performing model with only 128K parameters on the K210 kit within 15 days of continuous training.

We have studied elastic scattering of 80-fsec pulse pulses from an 80-femtowatt laser with a wavelength of 800 nanometers intersecting with a layer of metallic nickel at a normal angle. An average power density of the laser pulses of approximately 1 gigawatt per square centimeter resulted in a material density reaching nickel's ionization point, triggering nonlinear changes in absorption and subsequent plasma expansion. This led to a laser self-focusing phenomenon, $ {I}_{0} \propto {\rho}_p^{p-1} $ with ${I}_{0}$ and plasma density ${\rho}_p$ parameterized through their spatial integration, exponent ${p}$ approximately equaling 3.2. Notably, when the density reached its peak under low-fluence conditions, the density exponent reduced to 5.8. Increased density due to nonlinear changes at higher fluences resulted in a laser self-focusing enhancement, possibly caused by electron rearrangement within the nonlinear medium. This may have origins in a laser pulse precursor leading to an unusual direction of plasma expansion from the target normal during early stages. Plasma temperature estimates for laser pulses of different peak power densities were calculated by relating their calculated electric field values to their estimated peak and pre-pulse electric field values. This results in estimated ionization thresholds for nickel of approximately 1.38 eV per electron, implying that both ionization and heating thresholds are heavily influenced by high spatial frequency laser field fluctuations, especially

As the reliance on Deep Neural Network-based systems grows, concerns about potential attacks by malicious entities increase. To counter this, researchers have focused on developing metrics and methods to assess the robustness of DNN-based systems. Additionally, there is an ongoing effort to utilize Generative Adversarial Networks as a tool to detect and mitigate adversarial attacks. Our paper introduces ADProve - a tool designed to measure the robustness of control systems against adversarial attacks through simulation proof. ADProve employs a sequence generator produced by a GAN that creates artificial input sequences for testing robustness, similar to real-world adversarial attacks generated by uncertainty-based algorithms. It combines system identification techniques with reachability analysis and verifies robustness through the application of Lyapunov functions and Moura's proof method for discrete-time systems. The evaluation of ADProve's performance reveals its potential for assessing robustness system's performance in real-time.

A novel, multi-hospital, data-driven approach is introduced to segment multiple sclerosis lesions using a strong augmentation method. This approach leverages a replay buffer to segment lesions consistently despite variations in MRI imaging protocols and data across multiple hospitals. The segmentation process utilizes a joint loss function combining both lesion segmentation and image augmentation objectives. The result is a level of consistency in lesion segmentation that approaches that achieved with extensive in-house expertise. Moreover, this method demonstrates superior performance, with results expressed as dice coefficients indicating similarity to clinical standards. The approach showed data-driven evidence for identifying lesions that were not visible to clinical standards, with results quantifying this overlap. The method's effectiveness has been verified through comprehensive evaluations on public datasets and in-house hospital datasets, with notable publications in NeuroImage: Clinical and Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry.

A common approach to evaluating the similarity of metrics involves the use of optimal transport. This method has a direct connection to the continuity of the underlying metric. A recently discovered convergence condition, based on optimal transport, is more relaxed than the standard notion of metric convergence, particularly in a weighted context. In this paper, we explore the existence of such a metric comparison for the Wasserstein distance without weight. Our results show that for any given integer $k$, a metric comparison exists with a comparison constant of $k$, though this value cannot be reduced below $1$. It is also demonstrated that the optimal transport method is capable of detecting more subtle differences in metrics, with a constant of $1/\sqrt{2}$, when those differences are small. Furthermore, we provide a practical technique for calculating these metric comparisons in a universal metric system.

In our research, we investigate how hybrid machine learning techniques can be applied to domain that is mainly governed by physics. Specifically, we develop a new hybrid neural network model that integrates both domain knowledge and data insights. The approach focuses on a system with significant stochastic effects, and we evaluate its performance using data from paused-time Monte Carlo simulations. A comparison with a purely data-driven neural network model reveals that our hybrid approach not only improves accuracy, but also becomes more efficient by utilizing the same resources. Furthermore, we find that our hybrid model is transferable to new scenarios without additional training, including cases with different parameters and concentrations, and that it accurately predicts rare events that are difficult to simulate directly. Overall, this research demonstrates the benefits of a new hybrid algorithm that integrates the strengths of both data and domain knowledge.

Using the 84 GHz Single Dish CO Survey from the Atacama, we evaluated the development of molecular cores and evaluated their possibility of becoming massive stars. We established an empirical model, based on the core mass and radio frequency, to predict the conversion of cores to stars. This analysis revealed that approximately 26% of the studied cores adhere to this model, suggesting that the majority will need more time to transform into stars. Furthermore, we observed a significant increase in the core mass flow rate as it progresses from 64 to 84 GHz. These high-mass cores were also examined using the Submillimeter Array to measure their internal densities and radii, providing insight into their feedback. Compared to the core mass model, we found that the majority feature supersonic spectra, indicating that the core mass flow rate is not the sole determining factor for the development of massive stars. This implies that the mass increase of molecular cores and the formation of massive stars are related but not necessarily simultaneous processes. Massive cores can remain in a state of steady growth before eventually collapsing into stars under conditions of limited turbulence and high density. On the other hand, the rapid increase in the core mass flow rate could be a sign of self-regulation by the tunneling velocity principle, where the increase in the core mass flow rate can help contain the developing star. Current data do not have a specific preferred explanation, so we suggest that the core mass flow rate could be a mix of these two theories.

Using several years of OGLE and KMT data, a comprehensive study of gravitational lensing was conducted, covering a range of magnifications. The analysis provided constraints on supernovae-related gravitational lensing by considering the detection rate of typical magnifications due to accretion by black holes or neutron stars. It was assumed that one out of every 30,000 stars may produce a persistent microlensing event due to a primordial black hole, with an estimated event count ranging from one to eleven. In contrast, the event count for black holes formed through stellar evolution was much higher, assuming an average mass of eighty-three solar masses and yielding around nine hundred to nine thousand events. The analysis also set a lower limit on the density of primordial black holes in the galactic halo at one in ten to one in fifty percent, based on observations of magnifications due to accretion by black holes. Additionally, a previously unpublished calculation was provided regarding the auto-correlation function of the galactic halo, suggesting that the density of primorial black holes should be below a certain threshold, at twenty-five percent, to avoid detecting their effects through the auto-correlation method.

We investigate the equilibrium behavior of polar particles confined to a flat surface, limited by a finite size, using Monte Carlo simulations. As the packing density increases beyond 0.495, we identify two new frustrated crystalline phases: a hexagonal phase and a triangular oblique phase. These structures are confirmed by analyzing the structure factor and the radial distribution functions. Furthermore, we calculate the pressure exerted on the wall by the particles and examine the layer thickness and density to gain deeper insight into the phase behavior.

Recent research highlights the importance of pretrained language models for
downstream tasks. These models rely on various special tokens like start, end,
and null tokens, yet their impact on performance remains unclear. This study
investigates how modifying the set of explicit special tokens affects the performance
of BERT and RoBERTa models. We focus specifically on models trained for German,
a language with complex case marking, morphological changes, and a large case
repertoire. By altering either the set of special tokens or their positioning,
we assess their influence on model performance in targeted areas. Furthermore,
we explore the effect of these modifications on models dealing with out-of-vocabulary
words and languages. The results indicate that using special tokens for specific
morphological cases in German improves the models' performance across many tasks,
including machine translation. Interestingly, the beneficial effect holds even for
English models, when translating German into English, demonstrating the efficacy
of these tokens in translation tasks. Additionally, we found that adjusting token
positions instead of adding null tokens yields better results, as evidenced by
our German-based models. Interestingly, the beneficial effect diminishes for other
tasks without further analysis. Just like many contextual sentence models, these
models can treat single words as sentences by masking case and word order.
Thus, instead of relying on predefined special tokens, German-based models perform
better when using permissive regularization that allows for case and order variations.

We examine candidate networks in the context of a computationally-intensive process - evaluating the results of combining smaller networks via a specific mathematical operation - namely, determining the output of a mathematical operation involving multiple networks. The overarching goal is to assess the efficacy of various network formats for resolving a fundamental problem, namely, identifying the shortest path between two points, using a specific mathematical operation involving multiple networks. We find that networks utilizing multiple tables to represent complex operations outperform other candidates, both theoretically and practically, yielding optimal results in this specific context. This conclusion holds true across different scenarios involving constraints on the operation's parameters. The findings indicate that networks should incorporate diverse - rather than uniform - inputs, and facilitate direct comparisons between related inputs, allowing for the seamless integration of new operations. Notably, the most successful networks were characterized by a hierarchical and modular structure, reflecting the importance of both structural properties and the ability to incorporate external information.

For decades, studying the complex dynamics of glass-forming liquids has been an ongoing challenge. Through theoretical modeling and simulations, researchers have explored how these liquids behave under various conditions, such as changing temperature or chemical composition. One notable concept, thermodynamic scaling, suggests a connection between temperature, chemical potential, and energy at different stages of a process. This study investigates thermodynamic scaling in a specific type of glass-forming mixture made up of atoms interacting via different types of potentials, or interactions. We found that this scaling is consistent with our simulation data but only makes sense in a certain context, or 'window'. We then simulated how this mixture changes over various time frames and observed a transition from one behavioral pattern to another at a specific point. This transition, marked by increased sensitivity to temperature, corresponds with a more predictable pattern in the relationship between temperature and chemical potential. This study contributes to our understanding of how both temperature and chemical potential affect the behavior of these liquids, particularly at different stages of a process. Our work may help guide experiments on various types of glass-forming mixtures, such as those based on silicates.

Recent studies indicate that current NLI datasets favor the inference of denial more than other forms of negation. This work investigates whether this bias is intact when applying similar classification models to new, unlabeled texts. The research compares the efficacy of five transformer-based models across three distinct NLI categorization tasks, utilizing eight contrasting denial categorization datasets as benchmarks. Furthermore, the study examines how susceptible the models are to influence label manipulation. Key findings indicate that the models perform better on denial categorization than other forms of negation but can evade extrinsic negation influence through fine-tuning with an extrinsic negation dataset. Lastly, the study suggests potential reasons why deny-centric NLI datasets have emerged despite their limitations.

The range of translations that a given state in a Neural Machine Translation (NMT) process can explore is hard to predict precisely. Most NMT models generate translations sequentially, navigating a possible but not certain set of translations, guided by past and present states. This work deviates from the sequential NMT approach by also considering future states, a concept referred to as look-ahead attention. Look-ahead attention allows the NMT model to identify which parts of the source sentence are most significant for predicting a state's future translations, thereby informing its decoding trajectory. The proposed look-ahead attention mechanism is validated against time-based attention in two ways: by evaluating its impact on translation quality and by analyzing its speed, investigation methods that rely on attention weights and decoding trajectories. Results show that incorporating look-ahead attention improves translation quality, especially in sensitive domains, and facilitates faster decoding by reducing unnecessary exploration of the translation space in both the initial and final stages of the translation process.

This note examines a cotangent bundle framework for generalized Siksekian manifolds following recent research by Winstein and Guruswamy-Miller.  We demonstrate that this approach naturally leads to a more intricate representation of curvature weights, distinct from the skew-adjoint property in the classical setting.  Additionally, we explore the implications of this framework on the division circle bundle method developed by Krylov and Kapovitch-Schmidt.

We analyze the thermal structure of entanglement entropy using an infrared momentum cutoff in $d$ spatial dimensions and an upper frequency cutoff in the thermal distribution. For small to intermediate coupling strength, we find the thermal entropy of a region can be described by two distinct scaling behaviors, each corresponding to different coupling strengths. In 3D CFTs, we find the thermal entropy is $\mathcal{O}(\ell^d-1)$ for weak coupling, and it transforms into $\mathcal{O}(\ell^d)$ asymptotically for intermediate coupling strengths matching recent simulations. In both cases, we find the thermal entropy is dominated by short-distance physics. We also discuss how our findings on thermal entropy match previous results on entanglement entropy and how they compare with simulations findings. Furthermore, we calculate the thermal structure of entanglement entropy with an upper frequency cutoff and verify the Roberts conjecture that such a quantity is nonnegative for small to intermediate coupling strengths.

This research presents a new approach to pricing Asian options by applying transform techniques that lead to a computationally efficient method, even when the underlying asset follows a geometric Brownian motion with constant volatility. The method starts with a product of two Laplace transforms, one being a polynomial and the other an exponential function, leading to a solution expressible as a finite sum of exponential terms. Each term involves a double integral whose limit allows it to converge as the complex variable moves to a specific value, resulting in an explicit, analytically computable solution. Our contribution lies in the innovative application of transform methods to pricing Asian options, along with a thorough analysis of the resulting expression's convergence. Moreover, a numerical Monte Carlo approach is developed to approximate the double integral, providing a method to achieve high accuracy and efficiency.

The diffuse 0.1 GeV gamma-ray background is primarily studied using observations by the Fermi-LAT, a Cherenkov telescope. Recent analyses with deep field observations have hinted at the presence of individual clusters contributing to this background. We enhance our understanding of the diffuse gamma-ray background by self-consistently modeling its emission from galaxy clusters. We employ two methods: direct calculation and template fitting, with input from numerical simulations. We find that the direct calculation approach is preferable, as it doesn't rely on pre-existing templates which may not account for diverse cluster morphology. Our findings reveal that the diffuse gamma-ray background can be primarily attributed to energy-rich galactic dark matter emissions and intra-cluster gas inverse Compton radiation, with galactic dark matter emissions dominating at lower energy levels below 1 GeV. We find that the linear energy dependence of galactic dark matter emissions significantly impacts the diffuse gamma-ray background spectrum at these lower energy levels, contributing a ~35% share. Furthermore, we calculate that the number density of galaxy clusters within a specified luminosity range is in line with expectations, as clusters with higher energy emissions are less abundant. We also find that galactic dark matter emissions have replaced intra-cluster gas emissions as the dominant source of diffuse gamma-ray background at lower energy levels below 1 GeV. This is consistent with the results of energy-dependent power law emissions of galaxy clusters, as previously reported in the literature.

Inflation models with sharp features in their scalar potentials or equations of state produce distinct primordial non-Gaussianities, which can be modeled through a localized boundary condition in field space. This results in a characteristic signature beyond standard parameters in the spectral shape. Utilizing the polynomial potential of $\phi^p$ with a sharp feature, we identify the associated non-Gaussian parameter through its relation with the derivative of the kernel at the boundary, and then determine the spectral shape by solving the Hele-Shaw equation. Two scenarios are considered: the feature arising from a change in the equation of state versus a change in the mass parameter. While the former produces an $n_2$ shape modulation, the latter results in a $n_3$-shape deformation that significantly differs from the $\delta\rho$-driven effect. Consequently, a feature from a changing equation of state alone is insufficient for distinguishing this scenario from constant-equation-of-state inflation.

We've developed a unique method, called Latent Visual Semantic Explainer (LaViSE), to produce human-readable explanations for the representations learned by convolutional neural networks (CNNs). LaViSE employs a language generator that's trained through reinforcement learning, providing explanations tailored to specific CNN models by mimicking how they process image information in a hierarchical manner. By analyzing its output in conjunction with the representations of CNNs, our method enables foul detection, filters out unimportant details, and provides clear descriptions of the underlying cognitive processes in models like VGG and ResNet, as demonstrated through our work with images of landmines, landscapes, and architecture.

Inspired by the evolving role of entanglement in quantum systems, we propose a new approach to describe high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates. Utilizing the findings of quantum-critical properties in one-dimensional and two-dimensional cuprates revealed by the application of infinite disorder, we establish a fundamental similarity between the two systems. We demonstrate that the similarities in structure and quantum critical behavior among these cuprate systems significantly contribute to the occurrence of high-temperature superconductivity. Furthermore, we show that the mutual influence between electrons and holes plays a crucial part in the formation of vortices in the superconducting state. These insights are applied to the development of a new hypothesis for high-temperature superconductivity in two-dimensional cuprates, which involves the creation of a quantum critical point at a crossover energy. Near this point, the overlap between the electron and hole waves is substantial, and their wave functions are closely intertwined, resulting in the formation of a wave function bound state. We hypothesize that the collective effect of these bound waves in the carrier sea gives rise to a long-waved percolating structure of the wave function, which in turn reduces the cost of entropy and facilitates high-temperature superconductivity in doped two-dimensional insulators. The concept of wave function percolation offers an explanation for various characteristics of high-temperature superconducting cuprates, including the relationship between superconductivity and antiferromagnetism, the decay of superconductivity at a length scale

Uganda has seen notable progress in combating the HIV virus, with improved access to healthcare compared to previous years. For example, more Hagin people know about HIV treatment compared to 2016 numbers. Furthermore, another indicator shows that by 2020, half as many Hagin people were unaware of HIV treatment compared to 2016. The challenge still posed by HIV is, however, the fact that many individuals are yet to receive life-saving treatment. The study investigates the underlying causes of this issue by analyzing data from a innovative travel app used by HIV patients, who report their daily travel details to healthcare facilities. By evaluating these reports through various statistical methods, the analysis reveals a clear correlation between knowledge of travel times and treatment likelihood. Furthermore, an machine learning model predicts patients' familiarity with their local healthcare ecosystem using travel data. The study also presents an innovative travel-based system which aims to assist HIV patients in navigating their local healthcare options through personalized travel itineraries and treatment centers. By providing patients with tailored travel advice, the system aims to improve patients' knowledge of their surrounding environment, ultimately reducing the HIV epidemic.

We study the magnetic response of the fractional quantum Hall system in the presence of a charge imbalance between electrons and holes. Using a hybrid fractional quantum Hall system composed of $^3$He and $^4$He on a substrate, we observe two distinct quantum Hall states: the $^3$He$_{2/3}$ quantum Hall state which exhibits skyrmions and the $^4$He$_{5/2}$ quantum Hall state. Our research shows the interplay between these two quantum Hall states influences the magnetic response of the $^3$He$_{2/3}$ state. Specifically, we found the magnetic field at which the metastable skyrmion lattice transforms into a more stable phase changes due to interactions with the neighboring $^4$He$_{5/2}$ state. Additionally, we found the magnetic response of the $^3$He$_{2/3}$ state changes notably around this field at which the metastable skyrmion lattice transitions.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor models are widely used, but there's a lack of singular ARMA models within this framework. We develop a new class of singular ARMA models, integrate them with time-varying networks and high-dimensional dynamic factor models, and derive estimation and inference methods for key parameters. The theoretical and asymptotic properties of our models and estimation methods are validated through consistent statistical inference. We estimate the graph structure associated with these models using graphical models and the Least Absolute Deviation criterion, but only by assuming certain orthogonality conditions among variables. The performance of our methods is supported by both simulated data and an analysis of the Economic Commissions' macroeconomic data, which reveals insights into the relationships among various macroeconomic variables.

The primary objective of this research is to derive proximal solutions in the context of multi-problems comprising a combination of monotone equilibrium and variational inequalities problems. In doing so, a general framework was established that simplifies the analysis of existing, as well as multiple, interconnected equilibrium problems with variational inequalities. Specifically, the study focuses on the presence of zero-set zeros of a system of equations derived from the Moreau proximal mapping. Remarkably, it was found that these zeros serve as a comprehensive set of solutions to the combined equilibrium and variational inequalities problems under specified, non-strict conditions. Furthermore, the research demonstrates the existence of a zero-zero crossing for a specific mapping, thereby providing a substantial insight into the existence of solutions to the mentioned problems. The study also examines general zero-zero crossings in the sense of Brouwer's degree. Moreover, a path-following algorithm was developed along a more specific and non-linear homotopy for the combination of equilibrium and variational inequalities problems. In the process, it was found that the zeros along this path correspond to a collection of solutions to the problems.

Deep learning's influential advancements have led to a trend of applying Bayesian methods in model evaluation, aiming to quantify models' limitations. However, previous attempts with complex, deep predictive models have been hindered by their high computational demands. To overcome this challenge, we employ a functional Bayesian approximation on a trained network by leveraging its previously computed inference results. By approximating the distribution of hidden layer outputs as normal distributions, we establish an accurate relationship between input data and output predictions. Our method is systematically tested across various computer vision tasks, including classification, regression, and image denoising, resulting in estimations of the prediction accuracy for specific input data with notable speed increases – up to a 290 times improvement compared to conventional Monte Carlo sampling.

This investigation examines the evolution of geodesic magnetic flux tubes in an isotropic magnetic field, where the field lines originate from a dynamo process involving the interaction of inflow regions with turbulent area filling factors. We compare the geodesic magnetic flux tube's behavior to both semi-empirical and direct simulation-based models. By reviewing and discussing the semi-empirical model's predictions and comparing them to numerical simulations results, this study reveals shortfalls in two dynamo models. Firstly, these models consider turbulent effects alongside magnetic diffusivity variations. However, they inaccurately conclude that these two factors cancel each other out. Furthermore, by assuming that turbulent effects can be described using Taylor's hypothesis, they fail to account for time-variant effects. This study challenges these assumptions by showing that individual realizations of turbulent diffusion exponentially outpace mean values. Furthermore, it finds that these realizations' averaging-exponential laws depend on the specific dynamo process in question. Consequently, this study challenges the notion that non-geophysical mean-induced magnetic amplification can be described using a globally applicable exponent. As an alternative, it suggests that simulating and modeling magnetic amplification is contingent on the simulation of downflow regions' specific dynamo physics.

The area around NGC4945 was examined using a powerful radio telescope, ALMA, in search of the molecular gas outflows suspected to exist there. A powerful molecular stream consisting of $600\mathrm{M_\odot/yr}$ that spans a huge distance of $750\,{\rm pc}$, along with lesser yet similar molecular gas outflows, has been discovered. Although the primary molecular stream is largely unimpeded, the other lesser molecular gas outflows appear to be blocked by dense gas around the nucleus, contributing to a substantial outflow rate of $\sim 1200\mathrm{M_\odot/yr}$. This is comparable to 10 times the rate at which the galaxy forms new stars and greatly surpasses the rate at which the galaxy's central area loses gas. As a result, the unimpeded molecular gas outflows appear to be the main factor contributing to a substantial mass loss from the galaxy's central area. A comprehensive picture begins to emerge that shows the interplay between the large-scale viral wind, the galaxy's central area's gas outflows, the galaxy's star formation, the galaxy's central area's gas consumption, the galaxy's central area's heavy element loss, and the surrounding interstellar medium enrichment through the galaxy's central area's gas outflows.

This paper presents a comprehensive derivation of the one-dimensional energy balance model for wave growth in a weakly compressible plasma, applicable to both turbulent and non-turbulent scenarios. By extending the quasilinear theory of wave energy transfer, the model assumes that the rate of change of wave energy at a given wavenumber k is proportional to the rate of change of wave energy in an infinitesimal range dk, multiplied by the probability of finding two particles in the same interval of wave number space. This results in an energy balance equation that depends on the statistical distribution of particle collisions and the energy transfer mechanism, such as wave dispersion or stochastic processes. Two specific cases of this model are examined: the Vlasov-Maxwell equations, which describe wave evolution in an incompressible plasma and rely on two distinct probability density functions, and the Boltzmann-Maxwell equations, which describe wave evolution in a compressible plasma and rely on a single, integrated probability density function. Assuming that wave energy growth follows a logarithmic pattern and that the probability density function follows a Gaussian distribution, the model predicts that the rate of change of wave energy is proportional to the square root of the number of particles involved. Additionally, the study provides a theoretical understanding of the relationship between wave energy transfer and the integrated probability density function, suggesting that the rate of change of wave energy peaks at an intermediate number of particles involved.

In the spectral galerkin level method (SGLM), a family of explicit and implicit finite difference schemes is formulated by taking the derivative of a given smooth, elementary function. These explicit and implicit schemes correspond to the standard finite difference formulas when this elementary function is linear. On uniform grids, the behavior of SGLM approximations mirrors that of standard finite difference approximations. However, when employed on nonuniform grids, SGLM realizations diverge from their standard counterparts. Notably, adapting the standard finite difference formulas to nonuniform grids necessitates a cumbersome selection of appropriate preconditions, whereas achieving a comparable accuracy with SGLM involves a more streamlined set of conditions. Furthermore, SGLM is capable of generating an assortment of derivative approximations that adhere to both the mean value and the boundary value principles. Derivative approximations formulated in this manner are stable when applied to smooth, periodic functions, and their accuracy is quantifiable using the interpolation error theorem. As such, these approximations are suitable for a broad range of applications. The theoretical findings of this paper are illustrated through several examples.

For a bounded self-adjoint operator A within a complex Hilbert space, a study is performed involving the Lyapunov inequality $\lambda > 0, \lambda + \lambda^2 \le c(\lambda I - A)^{-1}(x, (A + \mu I)^{-1}(x))$. Within this context, amplification of A by a strictly positive real number μ is analyzed in relation to resolvent bounds, a bounded C0 semigroup and left invertibility of the semigroup. A novel criterion for exponential stability is formulated and two distinct local and universal approaches are explored using this inequality. The first local approach examines specific perturbations of the form H0 + Δ, where H0 is self-adjoint, non-negative and bounded above, while Δ is a bounded self-adjective operator within a closed sub-space J of the domain of H0. The second universal approach investigates universal resolvent bounds for the uniform Lyapunov inequality across all possible realizations of A and H.

We have developed MuMuPy, a software tool designed to compute the probabilities of significant events related to dimuonium transitions. Based on this framework, we conducted a series of theoretical calculations to determine the probabilities of several important transitions, such as those induced by a photon, electrodisintegration, and other electromagnetic phenomena. These results can be used for a range of applications, including atomic physics-based muon in-initio calculations and phenomenological studies related to the search for dark sectors. The code, along with a detailed user manual and paper, can be accessed online via the following repository: https://github.com/MuMuPy/MuMuPy.

In a multi-period portfolio optimization problem, the investor seeks to maximize a unique utility function, which is based on the average wealth and relative wealth. This function is then used as the candidate for a utility class that includes the absolute and relative wealth case. Next, we convert the optimization issue at hand into a quadratic problem and obtain a dual representation. By analyzing the dual function, we establish a hierarchical investment structure. By solving a particular quadratic problem, we derive a strategy that is consistent with the investor's utility-maximizing goal. We test this strategy using simulation and real data from the NYSE.

Green Pea galaxies, observed through the context of the SDSS, possess compact and blue appearances which make them easily distinguishable. Their relatively small size and high surface brightness lead to a prediction that about 20% of local Green Pea galaxies contain a central black hole with a mass exceeding 10^6 solar masses. This prediction aligns with current understanding that there should be a correlation between the mass of the galaxy and its central black hole. Additionally, the significant number of young and highly active galaxies, including Mr. Pea, Mr. Pea2, and H4n1, have challenged theories of galaxy evolution and prompted further research into the early universe. Using VLT/VIMOS, we collected and analyzed the data from the galaxies H4n1, H4n2, H9n1, and H9n2, whose line emissions, 3-sigma limits of Hbeta and Halpha to Hdelta, and moderate star formation rates deviate from the common star formation rates observed in local galaxies. With line emissions corresponding to a velocity interval of ~500 km/s, these galaxies suggest a significant large-scale structure at z=0.066, implying that Mr. Pea, Mr. Pea2, H4n1, and H4n2 reside within a complex galaxy system. Systematic follow-up observations using VLT/XSHOOTER revealed a high-mass central black hole within Mr. Pea2 with a mass exceeding 10

The research explores fermions interacting with a bosonic field in certain high-temperature conditions, using the Bose-Fermi Einstein condensate model. Initially, the model develops a comprehensive theoretical understanding of fermions accumulating density and bosons condensing in a high-temperature system, particularly in systems such as dilute atomic gases, consisting of cold fermions and bosons, and the electronic states in quantum structures, such as superfluids, semiconductors, and superconductors. Next, the study investigates how advanced mathematical techniques affect fermion-boson systems. These techniques, well-established in theoretical physics, are analyzed with regards to their relevance to both quantum and thermal systems, ultimately providing new insights into fermion-boson interactions. By employing a comprehensive theoretical approach, the model develops a comprehensive understanding of fermion-boson interactions. This research is particularly significant in understanding fermion accumulation and boson condensation in high-temperature systems. The study can be applied to various systems, such as dilute atomic gases, consisting of cold fermions and bosons, and the electronic states in quantum structures, including the phenomena of fermion accumulation, Bose-Einstein condensation, superfluidity, semiconductors, and superconductors.

We establish that the braided Thompson's groups, denoted $V_{r,n}$, exhibit linear divergence. This is achieved by demonstrating that certain words in the group $V_{r,n}$, effectively braided versions of inverse iterated functions, fail to converge to an iterate of a fixed point for sufficiently large $n$. This area of research has seen recent developments in the untangled versions, with most prior results relying on specific computational evidence. In contrast, our approach relies solely on the existing structure of the group $V_{r,n}$ and its explicit tail-reduced presentations, thereby yielding a proof that doesn't rely on computations. This novel method provides a general framework for proving linear divergence in a wide range of groups, particularly those with similar finite-state-automaton-like presentations.

This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of fine-tuning Retrieval Augment Generation (RAG) architecture for downstream tasks. Building upon the foundation of BERT, RAG integrates neural text encoding with the capability to fetch external text, enhancing the potential for adapted models. Yet, incorporating this additional functionality also presents significant challenges in gathering labeled data, given the need to simultaneously process both internal and externally obtained text. Despite initial promise, recent attempts have failed to successfully implement RAG-based models for a range of complex tasks. Our work addresses this gap by proposing a novel pipeline that overcomes critical limitations, thereby enabling significant improvements in the performance of adapted RAG models. Additionally, our paper explores the impact of specific components, such as the type of auxiliary training data and the structure of the retrieval queue, providing valuable insights for future research in the field. Within the realm of scientific literature, our RAG adaptation model surpasses the performance of its counterpart, RAG-1, in the context of the HINDICT benchmark, while also outperforming the latest advancements in the field, including the EDA-Train framework and the Unified English Model.

Riemann-Hilbert methods are powerful tools for unraveling the asymptotic behavior of solutions and other key components in mathematical analysis, often bridging the gap between very late and very early times. Following the successful volumes 1 and 2, this third installment delves into the most complex and cutting-edge applications of these methods, integrating the various approaches with a unified perspective that showcases their potential in driving forward multiple fields of study.

Developing a widely applicable data pipeline to label specific data fields in a diverse dataset collected through crowdsourcing is a complex task. This study focuses on creating labels for automatic summarization by gathering human annotations. To ensure data quality, we employ a multi-stage qualification pipeline, which not only boosts the quality of the annotations but also streamlines the process by reducing the need for subsequent evaluations. Based on the analysis of the collected data, which comprises 55,020 annotations across 6,990 questions, we observed that signal words can predict a summary's relevance in a given document, while frequency-based approaches can identify significant keywords in a summary by indicating word co-occurrence in the mentioned documents. A subsequent statistical evaluation of the collected data reveals that the gathered information is reliable and can be utilized, demonstrating that a qualification pipeline can enhance data quality and reduce the cost of annotation by minimizing the need for subsequent evaluations to 1.57%. This technique can also be applied to other related datasets.

The text-video retrieval task focuses on identifying the most relevant video clips in response to a given query. Our proposed approach, TS2-Net, utilizes a unified network to generate both spatial and temporal queries, utilizing a query encoder to align with video features and enhance video representation quality. Our solution leverages a spatial and temporal attention mechanism to capture key details, and a Swin transformer to unify attention weights and improve performance. By unifying the generation of spatial and temporal queries, and utilizing a Swin transformer, TS2-Net outperforms the existing benchmarks. Our results on the MSRVTT and VATEX datasets demonstrate substantial improvements over state-of-the-art models for text-video retrieval.

The models of a composite Higgs, featuring a narrow light Higgs boson, can be rejected based on the LHC analyses of the channels $t\to hj$ and $h\to \tau\mu$. These studies utilize tagged $t\bar{t}$ events and leverage the $h\to\gamma\gamma, Z\gamma$ branching rates to estimate the model parameters. Moreover, the LHC can search for novel signatures from the decays $h\to \tau\tau, \mu\mu, \mu\mu l\bar{l}$, and $t\to HW, H\bar{b}$ through the $W$ boson and charged leptons produced in hadronic channels. Combining these searches, the LHC should be able to obtain tight constraints on the model parameters, ultimately ruling out any scenario where the composite right-handed up-quark is the source of dark matter in the universe.

In today's network research, scientists study diverse types of networks, like those based on technology, social relationships, and transportation patterns, to name a few.  A specific type of network, known as a pure preferential attachment network, is studied in theoretical research.  However, when measuring a network's nodes, it's often necessary to categorize them based on properties other than the general connectivity.  Combining this with information on network topology can transform a pure preferential attachment network into a hybrid random network, where the in-degree distribution still adheres to a power law, but the out-degree distribution deviates.  To study these networks further, researchers have developed an equation to measure them, known as the telecommunication equation, along with a telecommunication random network model.  Surprisingly, it's discovered that when networks adhere to both models, their characteristics converge towards a unified limit that can be distinct from those of pure preferential attachment networks.  Thus, researchers can use a new approach, combining these two models, to study real-world networks, offering significant insights into these complex structures.

In the context of Internet of Things (IoT), various applications will necessitate massive machine-type communications, driving the need for novel signal processing approaches focused on robust multi-user detection. Researchers have initially explored using deep learning for detecting and separating IoT signals even in the presence of intense random noise. This study builds upon such work by shifting the focus to scenarios involving conflicting technology frequencies. Two such instances are analyzed - scenarios where multiple signals are generated using distinct radio access technologies, and those where signals are designed to be incompatible across different technologies. Notably, our experiments conducted with a large dataset of signals, comprising over 2 million, reveal a substantial distinction in the accuracy of signal classification in the context of compatible versus incompatibile technologies. We have also developed a multi-user detector using a generative adversarial network, first training it on a dataset of compatible signals and then testing its performance in the presence of conflicting technologies. Our findings indicate that while this detector achieves ~90% accuracy in the presence of compatible signals, its performance drops to ~60% in the presence of conflicting technologies. These results suggest that further advancements towards using compatible technologies for IoT applications should be prioritized.

This passage explores the connection between the Klein-Gordon equation and geodesic dynamics in various curved spacetimes, leading to the introduction of a generalized potential function. Considerations of the Klein-Gordon equation as a KG-particle's Lagrangian, including a nonlinear term, are analyzed in static spherically symmetric spacetimes. Research has examined the effects of gravitational fields on KG-particles in scenarios with and without a nonlinear term, resulting in novel concepts such as scalar Aharonov-Bohm-like waves and spinor-like solutions. Additionally, a superposition of states with and without a nonlinear term yields spinor-like solutions with internal degrees of freedom, while a specific alignment of parameters leads to localized superposition states. Conversely, in de Sitter spacetime, KG-particles interact with a potential derived from the geometric properties of the spacetime, and by combining probabilities based on a superposition of states, a localized solution is obtained, resembling a superposition of states in the Schwarzschild spacetime, resulting in a confined particle.
It's proven that any countable locally standard measure algebra can be parameterized with a real number greater than $\aleph_0$.

The process of twist-2, beyond leading-order bosonic parton distribution functions (PDFs) contributes to the electroproduction of virtual photons from partons. As the target's momentum tends towards infinity, this contribution becomes negligible. However, its effect is significant when considering generalized PDFs, especially in infinite-momentum-limit Compton scattering and parton Moore-Dirac equations. The evolution equations of twist-2 generalized PDFs involve a kernel related to the gluon PDF's equation, which can be challenging, especially for function E, the hardest one to measure in fixed target experiments. Luckily, the influence of twist-3 generalized PDFs becomes important at relatively large $t$ and low $x$, allowing for a potential connection between PDFs and parton distribution holography. By leveraging this connection and an earlier findings from an earlier study, a crucial evolution equation can be derived. Moreover, this evolution equation suggests a specific twist-3 contribution/term.

In a multi-dimensional space, achieving precision in a high-stakes classification demands utilizing both initial data and external resources to correct previous inaccuracies, ultimately leading to a proposed utilitarian paradigm which integrates both local fine-tuning and statistical correction processes. Theoretically, our framework shows that even the simplest classifiers can attain nearly perfect accuracy by continuously leveraging this paradigm. The study also conducts a practical investigation into this problem, employing a real-world dataset of sports games, and demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed paradigm by successfully addressing a related prediction challenge.

To examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling on a Bose-Hubbard system with two species, we utilize a multi-component Gross-Pitaevskii model. By introducing a single-body wave function with a spinor component, we account for the inter-species interaction via a pseudo-potential. Our investigation reveals that, under specific conditions of spin-orbit coupling strength and interaction threshold, unique superfluid phases can emerge with distinct spinor wave patterns, including solutions exhibiting one, two, and three domain structures. Moreover, for an exactly solvable limit with separate potentials for individual species, we derive analytical expressions for the energy and stationary states. Our research also develops an innovative energy minimization technique.

The classification of finite abelian $p$-groups can be expressed as a saturated chain of Young diagrams, along with the characterization of which such chains correspond to groups of a specific rank. We establish a generalized version of this concept, representing finite abelian $p_r$-groups through saturated chains of Young diagrams, particularly focusing on the case of $p_r=4$. Our findings lead to the development of a method to identify Young diagrams of a specific size related to groups of rank $r$. As an example, our approach is utilized to list all Young diagrams of rank $3$ that correspond to groups of rank $9$. Furthermore, our method is extended to describe Young diagrams associated with groups of various ranks using a specific arithmetic structure.

Through the AdS/CFT correspondence, topological characteristics in spacetime defects are represented as operator deformations within a associated field theory. This connection offers a detailed interpretation of surface and line defects as well as their relationships. This article will examine how a quantized defect's characteristics influence a related gauge theory's Wilson loop properties. Focusing on defects with a gauge invariant marker, we show how a quantized defect influences the gauge theory's dual, specifically Wilson loop invariant properties. Additionally, we show how a quantized gauge defect impacts string theory branes and surface defects in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence.

Asaso and Vidal (2022) introduced a novel method that efficiently represents kernel functions as trees, leveraging the kernel's properties to analyze data characteristics in a unbiased manner within kernel-based learning techniques. Notably, this method exhibits a favorable computational cost, making it practical for various kernel-based learning disciplines. Although the approach is straightforward, its implementation requires precision to produce an accurate approximation of the original kernel for complex datasets. This method is particularly beneficial when dealing with kernel-based direct optimization methods, such as kernel ridge regression and support tensor regression. To enhance the tree representation's performance, we have also incorporated an efficient bias-correction formula. This addition significantly improves the approximations on challenging datasets. Furthermore, we have implemented a novel initialization technique that adapiously adjusts to diverse data characteristics. This method shows promising results in independent experiments across multiple areas of kernel learning.

A muon collider will likely become a powerful source of high-energy neutrinos, 
producing these particles through the decay of muons in its detectors. Since neutrinos
cannot be detected directly, researchers are studying a novel detector concept that 
uses a magnetized tank filled with liquid xenon, located outside the accelerator's 
interaction point. The aim is to minimize interference from in-flight muon 
decays in the detector by applying magnetic deflection and employing an event 
trigger based on an energy reserve. The liquid xenon detector is evaluated for its 
ability to distinguish muon decays from other types of muon events using a 
simulated model based on a 1000 ton instrument. The concept relies on xenon's 
neutrino-nucleon cross-section and its ability to track muon decays in the detector. 
While this design can significantly reduce noise from in-flight muon decays, it does 
not eliminate them entirely. For this reason, researchers are exploring an alternative 
design, incorporating two energy reserves and magnetic deflection to filter out 
in-flight muon decays. The new concept is being tested in the same model as the 
original, with results indicating a nearly complete elimination of background from 
in-flight muon decays. Despite this, the design presents technical complications,
